families.title: Landscape metrics
families.intro:
The metrics of a **categorical map** (land cover, habitat and not habitat): each cell has a class, a *patch* is a set
of neighbouring cells of one class, and the metrics describe the patches (patch level), the classes (class level) or
the whole map (landscape level). Terraflux computes the metrics of
[landscapemetrics](https://r-spatialecology.github.io/landscapemetrics/) with the same names and the same numbers, and
FRAGSTATS' statistics that package lacks. The names are landscapemetrics' function names (`lsm_c_ca`: the class-level
total area), and the cards that follow list, for each, what it measures, its formula, the call, and the setting of
the application's operators that selects it. They are grouped by theme: area and edge, core area, shape, aggregation,
diversity, complexity (information theory) and contrast.

Two settings change many of the numbers: the patches' **connectivity** (`directions`: 8 neighbours, the default, or 4)
and whether the **map's boundary counts as edge** (`count_boundary`). Patches are found with 8 neighbours unless the
card says otherwise; adjacencies (aggregation, contagion) always use the 4 sides of a cell. The map is in metres:
areas are in hectares and edge lengths in metres, and a distance is the distance between cell centres.

Every patch metric also has class- and landscape-level statistics (the mean, standard deviation, coefficient of
variation, area-weighted mean, median and range of its values over the patches): they are listed in a table on the
card of the patch metric (`lsm_c_area_mn` is on the card of `lsm_p_area`). A few FRAGSTATS metrics need a choice that
only you can make: how far is near (`search_radius` for proximity and similarity, `connect_threshold` for
connectance), how different two classes are (a `contrast` table for the edge contrast metrics, a `similarity` table
for the similarity index) and how many classes the map could have (`classes_max`). Their cards give the call with a
small explicit choice, 300 m (three cells) and weights made up for the example: they show how to call, they are not
recommendations.
families.example:
import terraflux as tf

field = tf.nlm.gaussian_field(30, 30, resolution=100, autocorr_range=8, nug=0.0, seed=7)
landscape = tf.nlm.classify(field, 3)    # three classes; the cells are 100 m, so one cell is one hectare

metrics.name: Patch area
metrics.range: > 0, up to the area of the map
metrics.what:
The size of each patch: how much ground one habitat fragment, one field or one lake covers. It is the base of
most other metrics (a patch's shape, core and isolation all depend on its size) and, summarised over a class, it
tells whether a class is made of a few large patches or of many small ones.

symbols.a_i: the area of patch \(i\), in hectares
symbols.n_i: the number of cells of patch \(i\)
symbols.\\Delta x, \\Delta y: the cell's width and height, in metres (10 000 m² make a hectare)

metrics.use:
Use it to rank patches and to see the size distribution of a class. The mean alone hides that distribution: a
class of one large patch and many single cells has a small mean and a large standard deviation, so read the
summary statistics (below) together, and the median rather than the mean when a few patches dominate.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

Hesselbarth, M. H. K., Sciaini, M., With, K. A., Wiegand, K., & Nowosad, J. (2019). landscapemetrics: an open-source R tool to calculate landscape metrics. *Ecography*, 42(10), 1648-1657. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.04617

metrics.name: Patch perimeter
metrics.what:
The length of the outline of a patch, summing every cell side that faces a cell of another class, a cell without
data or the edge of the map.
metrics.formula: p_i = \ell_h\, e_h + \ell_v\, e_v \quad(= \Delta x\,(e_h+e_v)\ \text{for square cells})

symbols.p_i: the perimeter of patch \(i\), in metres
symbols.e_h, e_v: the number of left/right and top/bottom cell sides of the patch that are not shared with a cell of the same class (or that face a missing cell or the map's edge)
symbols.\\ell_h, \\ell_v: the length of those sides, in metres (the cell's width and height)

metrics.use:
The map border counts as edge here (unlike total edge `te`, which leaves it out by default), so patches cut by
the map frame look more convoluted. Perimeter grows with cell size on staircase outlines: compare maps of one
resolution only.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Radius of gyration
metrics.range: 0 or more (0 for a single cell)
metrics.what:
The mean distance from the cells of a patch to the patch centroid. It grows with the extent of the patch, so a
long thin patch scores higher than a compact one of the same area; it is a measure of how far an organism can
move without leaving the patch.

symbols.G_i: the radius of gyration of patch \(i\), in metres
symbols.n_i: the number of cells of the patch
symbols.(x_k, y_k): the centre of cell \(k\) of the patch, in metres
symbols.(\\bar{x}_i, \\bar{y}_i): the patch's centroid, the mean of its cell centres

metrics.use:
Distances are Euclidean on the map, so use projected data. A patch's own gyrate does not tell whether its shape
is complex: pair it with `shape` or `frac`.
refs: Keitt, T. H., Urban, D. L., & Milne, B. T. (1997). Detecting critical scales in fragmented landscapes. *Conservation Ecology*, 1(1), 4.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Total (class) area
metrics.range: > 0, up to the total area of the map
metrics.what:
The area a class covers in the map: how much forest, pasture or water there is, in hectares. It is the simplest
composition measure, and the quantity the next metric turns into a share.

symbols.\\mathrm{CA}_c: the total area of class \(c\), in hectares
symbols.n_c: the number of patches of class \(c\)
symbols.a_{ic}: the area of patch \(i\) of class \(c\), in hectares

metrics.use:
Use it to report the amount of habitat. It says nothing about how that area is arranged: ten hectares in one
block and ten hectares in a hundred scattered cells have the same value. Pair it with the number of patches or
an aggregation metric.

metrics.name: Percentage of landscape
metrics.range: (0, 100]; the classes of a map add up to 100
metrics.what:
The share of the map that a class covers. Unlike the area in hectares it can be compared between maps of
different sizes, so it is the usual way to say how much habitat a landscape has.

symbols.\\mathrm{CA}_c: the area of class \(c\), in hectares
symbols.\\mathrm{TA}: the total area of the map, in hectares, without the missing cells

metrics.use:
Use it for the habitat amount that many thresholds are stated in (a landscape with less than a given share of
habitat tends to lose species faster). The share is of the cells that have a value: missing cells are left out
of the total.

metrics.name: Largest patch index
metrics.what:
The share of the whole landscape taken by the largest patch of a class, a quick measure of dominance. At
landscape level the largest patch of any class.

symbols.a_i: the area of patch \(i\) of the class, in hectares
symbols.A: the area of the whole map, in hectares (not of the class)

metrics.use:
Unlike PLAND it only sees the largest patch, so a class can have high PLAND and low LPI when fragmented. The
class value divides by the landscape, not by the class.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Total edge (class)
metrics.what:
The length of the boundary between a class and all other classes. By default the map border and cells without
data are not counted as edge.

symbols.h_{ck}, v_{ck}: the number of left/right and top/bottom cell sides between a cell of class \(c\) and a cell of class \(k\)
symbols.\\ell_h, \\ell_v: the length of those sides, in metres

metrics.use:
A shared boundary counts for both of its classes, so the class values add up to twice the landscape's total
edge. Edge length changes with cell size.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Edge density (class)
metrics.range: 0 or more; 0 when the class has no edge with another class
metrics.what:
How much boundary a class has with other classes, per hectare of map. A class with a lot of edge is cut into
many parts or has convoluted outlines, and a lot of its area lies close to a different land cover.

symbols.\\mathrm{TE}_c: the total edge of class \(c\), in metres, that is the length of every cell side shared with a cell of another class
symbols.\\mathrm{TA}: the total area of the map, in hectares

metrics.use:
Use it to compare how fragmented or exposed a class is in maps of different sizes (the density, unlike the total
edge length, does not grow with the map). By default the map's own boundary and the missing cells are not
counted as edge; with `count_boundary=True` they are. The map must be in metres for the unit to hold.

metrics.name: Total area
metrics.what: The area of the landscape, all cells with data.

symbols.A: the total area of the map, in hectares: every cell that has a value
symbols.a_i: the area of patch \(i\), over all patches of all classes, in hectares

metrics.use: Cells without data (NA) are not counted, so it may be smaller than the map extent.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Largest patch index (landscape)
metrics.what:
The share of the map taken by its largest patch, of whatever class: a quick measure of how much one patch
dominates.

symbols.a_i: the area of patch \(i\), over all patches of all classes, in hectares
symbols.A: the area of the map, in hectares

metrics.use:
Unlike the class value it looks at all patches together, so it is the dominance of the single biggest patch of
the map. It says nothing about the other patches.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Total edge (landscape)
metrics.what:
The total length of boundaries between different classes in the landscape. The map border and cells without data
are not edge by default.

symbols.h_{ab}, v_{ab}: the number of left/right and top/bottom cell sides between classes \(a\) and \(b\), each pair of classes counted once
symbols.\\ell_h, \\ell_v: the length of those sides, in metres

metrics.use:
Each boundary counts once here, unlike the class-level TE (twice in total). Sensitive to cell size and
classification detail.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Edge density (landscape)
metrics.what: The edge length between classes per hectare of the landscape, a standard measure of how finely the map is cut.

symbols.\\mathrm{TE}: the total edge of the map, in metres (`lsm_l_te`)
symbols.A: the area of the map, in hectares (`lsm_l_ta`)

metrics.use: Compare landscapes of the same resolution and classification.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Core area
metrics.range: 0 or more, at most the patch area
metrics.what:
The area of a patch that lies farther than an edge depth from its border, the part not exposed to edge effects.
A cell is core when it is at least `edge_depth` cells (city-block distance) from any cell of another class, from
a cell without data or from the map border.
metrics.formula: ca_i = \frac{\Delta x\,\Delta y}{10\,000}\; \#\{\text{cells of } i \text{ with } d(\text{cell}) > \text{edge depth}\}

symbols.ca_i: the core area of patch \(i\), in hectares
symbols.d(\\text{cell}): the city-block distance, in cells, from a cell of the patch to the nearest cell of another class, missing cell or the map's edge
symbols.\\Delta x, \\Delta y: the cell's width and height, in metres

metrics.use:
Choose the edge depth from the species or process, in cells; the default of one cell is only a unit of the grid
and means different distances at 25 m and 1 km.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Number of core areas
metrics.what:
How many separate core areas a patch has, counting connected groups of core cells (with the patch's
neighbourhood rule). A patch with a narrow neck can have several cores or none.
metrics.formula: ncore_i = \#\{\text{connected groups of core cells of patch } i\}

symbols.\\mathrm{ncore}_i: the number of disjunct core areas of patch \(i\)

metrics.use:
A high count means that core is fragmented by edges even if total core is large. Zero for patches without core.
The class and landscape summaries of this count are the `dcore` statistics listed after the core metrics below;
with `convention="fragstats"` they summarise the sizes (in hectares) of all disjunct core areas instead, as
FRAGSTATS' DCORE.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Core area index
metrics.what:
The share of a patch that is core area. It shows how much of a patch is sheltered from the edge, and it drops
for small and elongated patches.

symbols.\\mathrm{CAI}_i: the core area index of patch \(i\), in percent
symbols.ca_i: the core area of the patch, in hectares (`lsm_p_core`)
symbols.a_i: the area of the patch, in hectares

metrics.use:
Depends on the edge depth: report it. Per-class means treat a one-cell patch and a large one alike; use `am` for
the share seen by an average cell.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Total core area
metrics.what: The summed core area of the patches of a class, or of the whole landscape at landscape level.

symbols.ca_i: the core area of patch \(i\) of the class, in hectares (`lsm_p_core`)

metrics.use: Sensitive to the edge depth; give it with the result.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Core area percentage of landscape
metrics.what: The share of the landscape that is core area of a class.

symbols.\\mathrm{TCA}_c: the total core area of class \(c\), in hectares
symbols.A: the area of the whole map, in hectares

metrics.use:
The edge-corrected counterpart of PLAND; the difference between the two is the class area lost to edge effects.
No landscape-level metric of this name in the library.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Number of disjunct core areas
metrics.what: The number of separate core areas of a class, summed over its patches (landscape level: all patches).

symbols.\\mathrm{ncore}_i: the number of disjunct core areas of patch \(i\) (`lsm_p_ncore`)

metrics.use: Many core areas of a small total area signal fragmented cores. Zero if the class has no core.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Disjunct core area density
metrics.what: The number of disjunct core areas of a class per 100 ha of the whole landscape, the density counterpart of NDCA.

symbols.\\mathrm{NDCA}_c: the number of disjunct core areas of class \(c\)
symbols.A: the area of the whole map, in hectares (not of the class)

metrics.use: Allows comparison of maps of different size. The class value divides by the landscape area, not the class area.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Total core area (landscape)
metrics.range: 0 or more, at most the area of the map
metrics.what:
The summed core area of all patches of the map: the part of the map that lies farther than the edge depth from
any patch border.

symbols.ca_i: the core area of patch \(i\), in hectares (`lsm_p_core`)

metrics.use: Sensitive to the edge depth (`edge_depth`, in cells): state it with the result.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Number of disjunct core areas (landscape)
metrics.what: The number of separate core areas of the whole map, summed over all its patches.

symbols.\\mathrm{ncore}_i: the number of disjunct core areas of patch \(i\) (`lsm_p_ncore`)

metrics.use:
Many core areas of a small total core area signal that the cores are fragmented. It is a raw count: use the
density (`lsm_l_dcad`) to compare maps of different size.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Disjunct core area density (landscape)
metrics.what: The number of disjunct core areas of the map per 100 ha: the density counterpart of the number of core areas.

symbols.\\mathrm{NDCA}: the number of disjunct core areas of all patches
symbols.A: the area of the map, in hectares

metrics.use: Allows the comparison of maps of different size.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Shape index
metrics.range: 1 for a square, larger the more irregular; no upper limit
metrics.what:
How far a patch's outline is from the simplest one, a square. A compact patch has a value near 1; a long, thin
or indented patch has a higher one. It measures complexity of the outline relative to the patch's size, so it
can be compared between large and small patches.

symbols.p_i: the perimeter of patch \(i\), in metres, that is every cell side that faces another class, a hole, a missing cell or the edge of the map
symbols.A_i: the area of patch \(i\), in square metres

metrics.use:
Use it to find elongated or ragged patches (riparian strips, patches cut by roads) and to compare how compact
the patches of two classes are. Very small patches take only a few values (a single cell is exactly 1), so a
class of many tiny patches has a mean close to 1 whatever its shape. In the library, `convention="fragstats"`
compares the perimeter with the smallest possible perimeter of as many cells instead (the raster version of
FRAGSTATS).
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.what:

outlines and approaching 2 for very convoluted ones.

metrics.name: Contiguity index
metrics.what:
How connected the cells of a patch are, from the neighbours each cell has within its own patch in a 3x3 window.
Compact, solid patches approach 1; thin, ragged ones and single cells stay near 0.

symbols.n_i: the number of cells of patch \(i\)
symbols.o_i: the pairs of cells of the patch that touch by a side (each pair adds 2 to the weight of both its cells, hence \(4\,o_i\))
symbols.d_i: the pairs that touch by a corner (1 to each of the two cells, hence \(2\,d_i\)); only counted with `directions=8`
symbols.v_k: the weight of cell \(k\): 1 for the cell itself plus its weighted neighbours in a 3 x 3 window (at most 13; the divisor 12 is that maximum minus 1)

metrics.use:
Describes the internal connectivity of the patch (does it have holes or thin arms), not its outline length.
Returns 0 for one-cell patches.

McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Related circumscribing circle
metrics.what:
How much of the smallest circle that encloses a patch it leaves empty. Compact, round patches give values near 0
and elongated or linear patches approach 1.

symbols.a_i: the area of patch \(i\), in hectares (times 10 000: square metres)
symbols.r_i: the radius, in metres, of the smallest circle that encloses the patch

metrics.use:
Good at telling linear features (roads, riparian strips) from blobs; it ignores the outline, so a big indented
patch can score low. Single cells score 0.36 (a square in its circle). As landscapemetrics does, the circle is
fitted to the corners of the cells in the patch's first and last rows and columns only (the same as the circle
around the whole patch for convex outlines); `convention="fragstats"` encloses every cell.

McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Perimeter-area fractal dimension
metrics.what:
A single fractal dimension for all patches of a class (or the map), from the slope of the log-log regression of
patch area on perimeter. Values near 1 mean simple shapes at all sizes, near 2 complex ones.

symbols.a_i: the area of patch \(i\)
symbols.p_i: the perimeter of the patch, in metres
symbols.\\alpha, \\beta: the intercept and the slope of the least-squares line of \(\ln a_i\) on \(\ln p_i\) over the patches (NA below 10 patches)

metrics.use: Needs many patches over a wide range of sizes. It is one regression over the patches, not the mean of FRAC.
refs: Burrough, P. A. (1986). *Principles of geographical information systems for land resources assessment*. Clarendon Press, Oxford.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Perimeter-area fractal dimension (landscape)
metrics.what:
One fractal dimension for all patches of the map, from the slope of the log-log regression of patch area on
perimeter. Values near 1 mean simple shapes at all sizes, values near 2 complex ones.

symbols.a_i: the area of patch \(i\)
symbols.p_i: the perimeter of the patch, in metres
symbols.\\alpha, \\beta: the intercept and the slope of the least-squares line of \(\ln a_i\) on \(\ln p_i\) over all patches (NA below 10 patches)

metrics.use:
Needs many patches over a wide range of sizes. It is one regression over the patches, not the mean of the
fractal dimension index of each patch.
refs: Burrough, P. A. (1986). *Principles of geographical information systems for land resources assessment*. Clarendon Press, Oxford.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Euclidean nearest-neighbour distance
metrics.range: > 0 (NaN for a class with one patch)

The distance from a patch to the closest other patch of the same class, measured between cell centres. Small
values mean patches of a class sit close together, large values mean they are isolated.

symbols.\\mathrm{ENN}_{ij}: the nearest-neighbour distance of patch \(j\) of class \(i\), in metres
symbols.k: runs over the other patches of the same class
symbols.a, b: cells of patch \(j\) and of patch \(k\)
symbols.(x, y): the coordinates of a cell centre, in metres

metrics.use: Isolation of patches; compare classes with similar patch counts. A class with a single patch gives NaN.
refs: Hesselbarth, M. H. K., Sciaini, M., With, K. A., Wiegand, K., & Nowosad, J. (2019). landscapemetrics: an open-source R tool to calculate landscape metrics. *Ecography*, 42(10), 1648-1657. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.04617

metrics.name: Proximity index
metrics.what:
Gustafson and Parker's proximity: how much patch of its own class lies near a patch, weighting each neighbour by
its size and by the inverse square of its distance. Large when big patches of the class are close. A FRAGSTATS
metric that landscapemetrics does not have.

symbols.\\mathrm{PROX}_{ij}: the proximity index of patch \(j\) of class \(i\)
symbols.a_{ik}: the area of patch \(k\) of the same class, in square metres
symbols.h_{jk}: the shortest centre-to-centre distance between the cells of patches \(j\) and \(k\), in metres
symbols.d: the search radius (`search_radius`), in metres; patches farther than \(d\) do not count

metrics.use:
Needs a search radius that suits the species or process. Distances are cell centre to cell centre, not edge to
edge as in some FRAGSTATS versions, so very close patches are at least one cell apart. The summary rows (mean,
standard deviation...) take the same option.
refs: Gustafson, E. J., & Parker, G. R. (1992). Relationships between landcover proportion and indices of landscape spatial pattern. *Landscape Ecology*, 7, 101-110.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Aggregation index (class)
metrics.range: 0 to 100; NA for a class of a single cell
metrics.what:
How clumped a class is. It counts the pairs of side-by-side cells that are both of the class (like adjacencies)
and compares them with the most such pairs that many cells could have, which is when they form the most compact
block possible. It is 0 for a class whose cells never touch and 100 for a class in one compact block.

symbols.g_{cc}: the number of pairs of side-by-side cells that both belong to class \(c\), each pair counted once
symbols.\\max g_{cc}: the largest value \(g_{cc}\) could take for a class of \(n_c\) cells, reached by the most compact block
symbols.n_c: the number of cells of class \(c\)
symbols.s, m: the side of the largest square of \(n_c\) cells, and the cells left over

metrics.use:
Use it to compare the clumping of classes that differ in area: unlike a simple count of patches, it is scaled by
what the class's own area allows. It looks at the four sides of each cell, whatever the patches' connectivity.
refs: He, H. S., DeZonia, B. E., & Mladenoff, D. J. (2000). An aggregation index (AI) to quantify spatial patterns of landscapes. *Landscape Ecology*, 15, 591-601. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1008102521322

metrics.name: Clumpiness index
metrics.what:
Whether a class is more clumped (towards 1) or more dispersed (towards -1) than a random arrangement, taking the
class's share of the landscape into account. 0 is random.

symbols.g_{ii}: the number of ordered pairs of side-by-side cells that are both of class \(i\) (every like adjacency counted twice)
symbols.\\sum_b g_{ib}: the ordered pairs of a cell of class \(i\) with a neighbour of any class, missing cells and the map's outside included
symbols.\\min\\text{-}e_i: the smallest possible perimeter of \(n_i\) cells, in cell sides: \(4s\), \(4s+2\) or \(4s+4\) with \(s = \lfloor \sqrt{n_i} \rfloor\)
symbols.P_i: the share of the map's cells that belong to class \(i\)

metrics.use:
Good for comparing the clumping of classes of different abundance. It follows landscapemetrics' version of the
FRAGSTATS definition, so values can differ slightly from other software.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Patch cohesion index (class)
metrics.what:
Physical connectedness of a class: grows towards 100 when its patches are large and compact (little perimeter
for their size), and falls towards 0 as they split into small, ragged pieces.

symbols.p_{ij}: the perimeter of patch \(j\) of class \(i\), in metres
symbols.n_{ij}: the number of cells of the patch
symbols.N: the number of cells of the map

metrics.use:
Sensitive to the perimeter convention: it uses landscapemetrics' perimeter (cell sides, the map edge counted).
Not comparable across resolutions.
refs: Schumaker, N. H. (1996). Using landscape indices to predict habitat connectivity. *Ecology*, 77(4), 1210-1225.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Connectance index (class)
metrics.what:
The share of all possible pairs of patches of a class that lie within a chosen distance of each other, a yes/no
measure of functional connection. A FRAGSTATS metric that landscapemetrics does not have.

symbols.n_i: the number of patches of class \(i\)
symbols.h_{jk}: the shortest centre-to-centre distance between patches \(j\) and \(k\), in metres
symbols.c_{jk}: 1 when the two patches are within \(d\) of each other, else 0; each pair counted once

metrics.use:
The result depends entirely on the threshold; pick it from the dispersal ability of the species. Not defined for
rasters read out of core.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Landscape division index (class)
metrics.what:
The probability that two random points of the landscape are in different patches of the class (counting a point
outside the class as different). 0 when the class fills the landscape in one patch; near 1 when it is many small
patches.

symbols.a_{ij}: the area of patch \(j\) of class \(i\)
symbols.A: the area of the whole map (not of the class), in the same unit

metrics.use: Compare with mesh and split, which are transformations of the same sum of squared areas.
refs: Jaeger, J. A. G. (2000). Landscape division, splitting index, and effective mesh size: new measures of landscape fragmentation. *Landscape Ecology*, 15, 115-130.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Interspersion and juxtaposition index (class)
metrics.what:
How evenly a class is adjacent to each of the other classes. Low values mean it touches only one or two of them,
100 means it borders all the others in equal amounts.

symbols.e_{ib}: the number of cell adjacencies between class \(i\) and class \(b\)
symbols.E_i: \(\sum_{b \ne i} e_{ib}\), the adjacencies of class \(i\) with other classes (missing cells and the map's outside left out)

metrics.use: Describes the mixing of classes, not their pattern: it ignores patch size. Needs at least three classes.
refs: McGarigal, K., & Marks, B. J. (1995). FRAGSTATS: spatial pattern analysis program for quantifying landscape structure. General Technical Report PNW-GTR-351, USDA Forest Service, Pacific Northwest Research Station.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Landscape shape index (class)
metrics.what:
The total edge of a class compared with the smallest edge a class of the same number of cells could have (a
compact square-like block). 1 means maximally compact, larger values mean a more complex or dispersed class.

symbols.E_i: the total edge of class \(i\), in cell sides: every side towards another class, a missing cell or the map's border
symbols.\\min\\text{-}e_i: the smallest possible perimeter of \(n_i\) cells: \(4s\), \(4s+2\) or \(4s+4\) with \(s = \lfloor \sqrt{n_i} \rfloor\)

metrics.use:
The library lists it under aggregation (as landscapemetrics does); FRAGSTATS calls it a shape metric. The map
border counts as edge whatever `count_boundary` is.
refs: Patton, D. R. (1975). A diversity index for quantifying habitat "edge". *Wildlife Society Bulletin*, 3(4), 171-173.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Effective mesh size (class)
metrics.what:
The size of the patches you would get if the class were cut into equal pieces with the same chance that two
random points of the landscape fall in the same piece (Jaeger 2000). An area-weighted mean patch size.

symbols.a_{ij}: the area of patch \(j\) of class \(i\), in hectares
symbols.A: the area of the whole map, in hectares

metrics.use:
Insensitive to very small patches, unlike the mean patch size, and so suited to monitoring fragmentation. Large
classes dominate because areas are squared.
refs: Jaeger, J. A. G. (2000). Landscape division, splitting index, and effective mesh size: new measures of landscape fragmentation. *Landscape Ecology*, 15, 115-130.

metrics.name: Normalized landscape shape index (class)
metrics.what:
The class's edge placed between the smallest possible edge (0) and the largest possible edge (1) for its number
of cells in a map of this size, a version of LSI that does not grow with class area.

symbols.E_i: the edge of class \(i\) in cell sides (towards other classes, missing cells and the map's border)
symbols.\\min\\text{-}e_i: the smallest possible edge of \(n_i\) cells, as for LSI
symbols.\\max\\text{-}e_i: the largest possible edge of the class in a map of this size: \(4n_i\) if its share \(p = n_i/N\) is at most 0.5, \(3N - 2n_i\) (\(+3\) when \(N\) is odd) up to \(p \le L\) with \(L = (0.5N + 0.5B)/N\), and \(E_i + 4(N - n_i)\) beyond; \(N\) is the number of cells and \(B = 2\,\text{rows} + 2\,\text{cols}\)

metrics.use:
Use instead of LSI to compare classes of very different area. The maximum is a heuristic of landscapemetrics
(after Hesselbarth et al.), not an exact bound.
refs: Bogaert, J., Rousseau, R., Van Hecke, P., & Impens, I. (2000). Alternative area-perimeter ratios for measurement of 2D shape compactness of habitats. *Applied Mathematics and Computation*, 111, 71-85. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0096-3003(99)00075-2

Hesselbarth, M. H. K., Sciaini, M., With, K. A., Wiegand, K., & Nowosad, J. (2019). landscapemetrics: an open-source R tool to calculate landscape metrics. *Ecography*, 42(10), 1648-1657. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.04617

metrics.name: Number of patches (class)
metrics.what: The number of patches of a class, a patch being a group of cells of the class touching each other.

symbols.n_i^{\\text{patches}}: the number of groups of touching cells of class \(i\) (8 neighbours by default, 4 with `directions=4`)

metrics.use: A raw count: it depends on the extent of the map, so compare with patch density when maps differ in size.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Patch density (class)
metrics.what: The number of patches of a class per 100 ha of the whole landscape.

symbols.n_i^{\\text{patches}}: the number of patches of class \(i\)
symbols.A: the area of the whole map (not of the class), in hectares

metrics.use:
Use it to compare fragmentation between maps of different size. The area is in hectares, so the map's cell size
must be right: a raster without a georeference counts each cell as one map unit.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Percentage of like adjacencies (class)
metrics.what:
The share of the cell sides of a class that touch another cell of the same class. High values mean the class is
aggregated.

symbols.g_{ii}: the ordered pairs of side-by-side cells that are both of class \(i\)
symbols.g_{ib}: the ordered pairs of a cell of class \(i\) with a neighbour of class \(b\); the sum covers every class, missing cells and the map's outside, so the map's border counts as an unlike neighbour

metrics.use:
Simple and unbounded by class area, but a large class has a high value by chance; AI and CLUMPY correct for
that.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Splitting index (class)
metrics.what:
The number of equal-sized patches the landscape would be divided into, with the same effective mesh size as the
class. 1 for a class that is the whole landscape; larger means more fragmented.

symbols.a_{ij}: the area of patch \(j\) of class \(i\)
symbols.A: the area of the whole map, in the same unit

metrics.use: Equal to \(A/\mathrm{MESH}\). Easier to read than DIVISION for strong fragmentation, as it has no upper limit.
refs: Jaeger, J. A. G. (2000). Landscape division, splitting index, and effective mesh size: new measures of landscape fragmentation. *Landscape Ecology*, 15, 115-130.

metrics.name: Aggregation index (landscape)
metrics.what: The aggregation index of the classes averaged with the share of the landscape each covers as weights.

symbols.A_i / A: the share of the map covered by class \(i\)

metrics.use:
This is landscapemetrics' definition (an area-weighted mean of the class values); FRAGSTATS computes the
landscape AI from all like adjacencies together, which gives somewhat different values.
refs: He, H. S., DeZonia, B. E., & Mladenoff, D. J. (2000). An aggregation index (AI) to quantify spatial patterns of landscapes. *Landscape Ecology*, 15, 591-601. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1008102521322

metrics.name: Patch cohesion index (landscape)
metrics.what: Physical connectedness of the patches of all classes together.

symbols.p_{ij}: the perimeter of patch \(j\) of class \(i\), in metres
symbols.N: the number of cells of the map

metrics.use: As the class version; here every patch counts, whatever its class.
refs: Schumaker, N. H. (1996). Using landscape indices to predict habitat connectivity. *Ecology*, 77(4), 1210-1225.

metrics.name: Connectance index (landscape)
metrics.what:
The share of all possible same-class patch pairs of the landscape that lie within the threshold distance. A
FRAGSTATS metric that landscapemetrics does not have.

symbols.c^{(i)}_{jk}: 1 when patches \(j\) and \(k\) of class \(i\) are within `connect_threshold` of each other (shortest centre-to-centre distance), else 0
symbols.n_i: the number of patches of class \(i\); pairs of different classes are not counted

metrics.use: As the class version; classes with many patches weigh most because pairs grow with \(n_i^2\).
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Contagion
metrics.range: (0, 100]; NA for a map of one class
metrics.what:
How clumped the classes of the whole map are. Take every pair of side-by-side cells: contagion is high when most
of the pairs are two cells of the same class (a map of a few large patches) and low when classes are mixed up
cell by cell, so that any two neighbours are likely to differ.

symbols.p_{ij}: the share of all pairs of side-by-side cells (counted in both directions) that join a cell of class \(i\) to a cell of class \(j\); a term with \(p_{ij}=0\) is left out
symbols.m: the number of classes present in the map

metrics.use:
Use it to compare the overall grain of landscapes with the same classes. It depends on the number of classes and
on how their areas are shared, so compare it between maps with the same legend. It counts the four sides of each
cell and leaves out edges to missing cells and to the map's boundary.
refs: O'Neill, R. V., Krummel, J. R., Gardner, R. H., Sugihara, G., Jackson, B., DeAngelis, D. L., Milne, B. T., Turner, M. G., Zygmunt, B., Christensen, S. W., Dale, V. H., & Graham, R. L. (1988). Indices of landscape pattern. *Landscape Ecology*, 1(3), 153-162. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00162741

metrics.name: Landscape division index (landscape)
metrics.what: The probability that two random cells of the landscape lie in different patches.

symbols.a_{ij}: the area of patch \(j\) of class \(i\)
symbols.A: the area of the map, in the same unit

metrics.use: Saturates near 1 for fragmented maps; see SPLIT for a measure with no ceiling.
refs: Jaeger, J. A. G. (2000). Landscape division, splitting index, and effective mesh size: new measures of landscape fragmentation. *Landscape Ecology*, 15, 115-130.

metrics.name: Interspersion and juxtaposition index (landscape)
metrics.what:
How evenly the classes are adjacent to one another across the landscape: 100 when every pair of classes shares
the same length of boundary.

symbols.e_{ab}: the number of adjacencies between classes \(a\) and \(b\), each pair of classes counted once (\(a > b\))

metrics.use: Ignores patch size and shape; it is about which classes touch which. Undefined for fewer than three classes.
refs: McGarigal, K., & Marks, B. J. (1995). FRAGSTATS: spatial pattern analysis program for quantifying landscape structure. General Technical Report PNW-GTR-351, USDA Forest Service, Pacific Northwest Research Station.

metrics.name: Landscape shape index (landscape)
metrics.what:
The total edge of the landscape divided by the smallest edge a single block of the same number of cells would
have.

symbols.E: the length of all edges of the map in cell sides: between classes, towards missing cells and along the map's border
symbols.\\min\\text{-}e(N): the smallest possible perimeter of \(N\) cells: \(4s\), \(4s+2\) or \(4s+4\) with \(s = \lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor\)

metrics.use:
Grows with the number of patches and with how intricate the boundaries are; compare landscapes of the same
extent. Listed under aggregation as in landscapemetrics.
refs: Patton, D. R. (1975). A diversity index for quantifying habitat "edge". *Wildlife Society Bulletin*, 3(4), 171-173.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Effective mesh size (landscape)
metrics.what: The area-weighted mean patch size of the landscape; the size of the piece a random point is in, on average.

symbols.a_{ij}: the area of patch \(j\) of class \(i\), in hectares
symbols.A: the area of the map, in hectares

metrics.use: Insensitive to tiny patches; a good fragmentation index for monitoring. Large patches dominate.
refs: Jaeger, J. A. G. (2000). Landscape division, splitting index, and effective mesh size: new measures of landscape fragmentation. *Landscape Ecology*, 15, 115-130.

metrics.name: Number of patches (landscape)
metrics.what: The number of patches of all classes in the landscape.

symbols.n_i^{\\text{patches}}: the number of patches of class \(i\) (8 neighbours by default)

metrics.use: A raw count that depends on the extent of the map; use patch density to compare maps of different size.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Patch density (landscape)
metrics.what: The number of patches in the landscape per 100 ha.

symbols.\\mathrm{NP}: the number of patches of all classes
symbols.A: the area of the map, in hectares

metrics.use:
Use it to compare fragmentation between maps of different size. The area is in hectares, so the map's cell size
must be right: a raster without a georeference counts each cell as one map unit.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Percentage of like adjacencies (landscape)
metrics.what: The share of all cell sides in the landscape that touch a cell of the same class.

symbols.g_{ii}: the ordered pairs of side-by-side cells that are both of class \(i\)
symbols.g_{ib}: the ordered pairs of a cell of class \(i\) with a neighbour of class \(b\); the sum also covers the sides towards the map's outside but, unlike the class level, not those towards missing cells

metrics.use:
Depends strongly on the number and balance of classes (two classes give a higher value by chance than ten);
compare landscapes with similar composition.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Splitting index (landscape)
metrics.what: The number of equal-sized patches into which the landscape would be split to give the same effective mesh size.

symbols.a_{ij}: the area of patch \(j\) of class \(i\)
symbols.A: the area of the map, in the same unit

metrics.use: Equal to \(A/\mathrm{MESH}\); has no upper limit, so it separates strongly fragmented maps that DIVISION cannot.
refs: Jaeger, J. A. G. (2000). Landscape division, splitting index, and effective mesh size: new measures of landscape fragmentation. *Landscape Ecology*, 15, 115-130.

metrics.name: Shannon's diversity index
metrics.range: 0 (one class) to ln m for m classes of equal area
metrics.what:
How many classes the map has and how evenly their areas are spread, in one number. It is the Shannon index of
ecology applied to the area shares of the land-cover classes: it grows with the number of classes and, for a
given number, is highest when they cover equal areas.

symbols.p_c: the share of the map covered by class \(c\), that is \(\mathrm{CA}_c / \mathrm{TA}\)
symbols.m: the number of classes present in the map

metrics.use:
Use it to compare the compositional diversity of landscapes. It ignores where the classes are (a map and its
shuffled cells have the same value), and it is sensitive to rare classes. Its largest possible value depends on
the number of classes, so divide by ln m (Shannon's evenness, `lsm_l_shei`) to compare maps with different
numbers of classes. The logarithm is the natural one.
refs: Shannon, C. E. (1948). A mathematical theory of communication. *Bell System Technical Journal*, 27(3), 379-423. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x

metrics.name: Shannon's evenness index
metrics.what:
Shannon's diversity relative to the maximum for the same number of classes: 1 when all classes cover the same
area, towards 0 when one dominates.

symbols.p_i: the share of the map in class \(i\)
symbols.m: the number of classes (the library returns 0 for \(m = 1\))

metrics.use: Evenness only; use with `pr` or SHDI to know how many classes there are.
refs: Pielou, E. C. (1966). The measurement of diversity in different types of biological collections. *Journal of Theoretical Biology*, 13, 131-144.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Simpson's diversity index
metrics.what:
The probability that two random cells are of different classes (Gini-Simpson): 0 for one class, approaching 1
for many equally common classes.

symbols.p_i: the share of the map in class \(i\)

metrics.use: Weights common classes more than Shannon does, so it is less affected by rare classes. Bounded by \(1-1/m\).
refs: Simpson, E. H. (1949). Measurement of diversity. *Nature*, 163, 688.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Simpson's evenness index
metrics.what: Simpson's diversity relative to the maximum for the same number of classes: how evenly the area is shared.

symbols.p_i: the share of the map in class \(i\)
symbols.m: the number of classes (with one class the denominator is 0 and the result is NA)

metrics.use: Evenness only; its catalogue name in landscapemetrics is spelt "simspon's evenness index".
refs: Simpson, E. H. (1949). Measurement of diversity. *Nature*, 163, 688.
McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Modified Simpson's diversity index
metrics.what:
Simpson's index in the form of a negative logarithm of the probability that two random cells are of the same
class: zero for one class, growing with richness and evenness.

symbols.p_i: the share of the map (by area) in class \(i\)

metrics.use:
Less sensitive to rare classes than the Shannon index. Compare maps that use the same classification and
resolution.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Modified Simpson's evenness index
metrics.what:
The modified Simpson's diversity relative to its maximum for the same richness: how evenly the area is shared
among the classes.

symbols.p_i: the share of the map in class \(i\)
symbols.m: the number of classes; \(\ln m\) is the value for \(m\) equally common classes

metrics.use: Separates evenness from richness; read with `pr`. Undefined with a single class.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Patch richness
metrics.what: The number of classes present in the landscape.

symbols.m: the number of classes with at least one cell (a missing cell is not a class)

metrics.use:
The simplest richness measure; it ignores how much of each class there is, and depends on the extent of the map
(see PRD).
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Patch richness density
metrics.what: The number of classes per 100 ha, so that richness can be compared between landscapes of different size.

symbols.A: the area of the map, in hectares

metrics.use:
Assumes that richness grows linearly with area, which it does not; compare only landscapes of similar extent.
The area is in hectares, so the cell size must be right.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Relative patch richness
metrics.what: The number of classes present as a percentage of the largest number the landscape could have.

symbols.m_{\\max}: the largest number of classes the map could have (`classes_max`, for example the classes of the legend)

metrics.use: Only meaningful if you set `classes_max` from the classification (the potential richness), not from the map.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Shannon entropy (of the adjacencies)
metrics.what:
The compositional complexity of the map: the entropy of the marginal distribution of the classes, as seen
through the cell pairs. High when classes are evenly represented.

symbols.g_{ab}: the ordered pairs of side-by-side cells of class \(a\) next to class \(b\) (4 neighbours; 8 with `neighbourhood=8`)
symbols.p_a: the share of the pairs whose first cell is of class \(a\)

metrics.use:
Not the Shannon diversity index (`shdi`): ENT is computed from the pair counts, in bits by default, SHDI from
class areas in nats. ENT is the starting point of the information-theory set (Nowosad & Stepinski 2019).
refs: Nowosad, J., & Stepinski, T. F. (2019). Information theory as a consistent framework for quantification and classification of landscape patterns. *Landscape Ecology*, 34, 2091-2101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-019-00830-x
Shannon, C. E. (1948). A mathematical theory of communication. *Bell System Technical Journal*, 27(3), 379-423. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x

metrics.name: Conditional entropy
metrics.what:
The uncertainty that remains about the class of a neighbouring cell once the class of a cell is known: the
configurational (spatial) complexity of the map, after removing the part due to composition.

symbols.x, y: the class of a cell and of its neighbour

metrics.use:
Part of the information-theory set of Nowosad and Stepinski (2019): ENT, CONDENT, JOINENT, MUTINF, RELMUTINF.
The values change with `base`, so state it when reporting.
refs: Nowosad, J., & Stepinski, T. F. (2019). Information theory as a consistent framework for quantification and classification of landscape patterns. *Landscape Ecology*, 34, 2091-2101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-019-00830-x

metrics.name: Joint entropy
metrics.what:
The total uncertainty of a pair of neighbouring cells: both the composition and the arrangement of the map add
to it.

symbols.p_{ab}: the share of the neighbour pairs with a cell of class \(a\) next to a cell of class \(b\)
symbols.g: the counts of those ordered pairs

metrics.use: Use together with ENT: JOINENT minus ENT is CONDENT, and the difference between them is MUTINF.
refs: Nowosad, J., & Stepinski, T. F. (2019). Information theory as a consistent framework for quantification and classification of landscape patterns. *Landscape Ecology*, 34, 2091-2101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-019-00830-x

metrics.name: Mutual information
metrics.what:
How much knowing the class of a cell reduces the uncertainty about the class of its neighbour: the part of the
map's composition that is explained by its spatial arrangement. 0 for a random arrangement.
metrics.use:
Larger when the map is more ordered (aggregated) for a given composition. Depends on the number of classes, so
use RELMUTINF to compare maps of different composition.
refs: Nowosad, J., & Stepinski, T. F. (2019). Information theory as a consistent framework for quantification and classification of landscape patterns. *Landscape Ecology*, 34, 2091-2101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-019-00830-x

metrics.name: Relative mutual information
metrics.what:
Mutual information scaled by the marginal entropy: the fraction of the map's compositional uncertainty explained
by the arrangement. 0 is a random arrangement, 1 a perfectly ordered one.
metrics.use:
A unitless measure to compare maps with different class numbers (Nowosad & Stepinski 2019). It does not depend
on the logarithm base.
refs: Nowosad, J., & Stepinski, T. F. (2019). Information theory as a consistent framework for quantification and classification of landscape patterns. *Landscape Ecology*, 34, 2091-2101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-019-00830-x

metrics.name: Edge contrast index
metrics.what:
How strongly a patch contrasts with its surroundings: the share of its perimeter that borders other classes,
each border weighted by how different the two classes are. 100 means every border is maximal contrast. A
FRAGSTATS metric that landscapemetrics does not have.

symbols.\\mathrm{ECON}_j: the edge contrast index of patch \(j\), in percent
symbols.\\ell_s: the length of cell side \(s\) on the patch's border, in metres
symbols.w_s: the contrast weight (0 to 1) between the patch's class and the class beyond side \(s\), from the `contrast` table; `boundary_contrast` for a side towards a missing cell or the map's edge
symbols.P_j: the perimeter of the patch, in metres

metrics.use:
The weights are a judgement (e.g. habitat quality differences); document them. Check that every pair of classes
has a weight, a missing pair gives NaN. The summary rows (mean, standard deviation...) take the same options.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

variants.label: mean
variants.text: the mean over the patches

variants.name: Edge contrast index, standard deviation (class level)
variants.label: standard deviation
variants.text: the sample standard deviation over the patches (n - 1)

variants.name: Edge contrast index, coefficient of variation, in % (class level)
variants.label: coefficient of variation, in %
variants.text: the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean

variants.name: Edge contrast index, area-weighted mean (class level)
variants.label: area-weighted mean
variants.text: the mean weighted by patch area

variants.name: Edge contrast index, median (class level)
variants.label: median
variants.text: the median

variants.label: range
variants.text: the range (largest minus smallest)

variants.name: Edge contrast index, mean (landscape level)
variants.label: mean
variants.text: the mean over the patches

variants.name: Edge contrast index, standard deviation (landscape level)
variants.label: standard deviation
variants.text: the sample standard deviation over the patches (n - 1)

variants.name: Edge contrast index, coefficient of variation, in % (landscape level)
variants.label: coefficient of variation, in %
variants.text: the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean

variants.name: Edge contrast index, area-weighted mean (landscape level)
variants.label: area-weighted mean
variants.text: the mean weighted by patch area

variants.name: Edge contrast index, median (landscape level)
variants.label: median
