metrics.name: Contrast-weighted edge density (class)
metrics.what:
Edge density of a class in which each stretch of edge counts in proportion to the contrast between the two
classes it separates. A FRAGSTATS metric that landscapemetrics does not have.

symbols.e_{ib}: the length of edge between class \(i\) and class \(b\), in metres
symbols.d_{ib}: the contrast weight (0 to 1) between the two classes, from the `contrast` table
symbols.e_{i\\partial}, d_{\\partial}: the edge towards missing cells or the map's border and its weight (`boundary_contrast`); added only with `count_boundary=True`
symbols.A: the area of the map, in hectares

metrics.use:
Edges are counted from the class's own side, so the edge between two classes counts for both. Use it to compare
landscapes of the same classes under the same weights.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Total edge contrast index (class)
metrics.what:
The mean contrast along the edges of a class: its contrast-weighted edge length as a share of its total edge
length. 100 means all the edges are of maximum contrast. A FRAGSTATS metric that landscapemetrics does not have.

symbols.e_{ib}: the length of edge between class \(i\) and class \(b\), in metres
symbols.d_{ib}: the contrast weight (0 to 1) between the two classes, from the `contrast` table
symbols.e_{i\\partial}, d_{\\partial}: the edge towards missing cells or the map's border and its weight (`boundary_contrast`, 0 by default); always counted in TECI

metrics.use:
The border counts as an edge; set `boundary_contrast` to the weight you want it to have (0 treats it as no
contrast and lowers TECI).
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Contrast-weighted edge density (landscape)
metrics.what:
Edge density of the whole landscape with each edge weighted by the contrast between the classes it separates. A
FRAGSTATS metric that landscapemetrics does not have.

symbols.e_{ab}: the length of edge between classes \(a\) and \(b\), in metres, each edge counted once (\(a > b\))
symbols.d_{ab}: the contrast weight (0 to 1) between the two classes, from the `contrast` table
symbols.e_{a\\partial}, d_{\\partial}: the edge towards missing cells or the map's border and its weight (`boundary_contrast`); added only with `count_boundary=True`
symbols.A: the area of the map, in hectares

metrics.use: Counting each edge once makes it comparable between maps; at class level an edge is counted from both sides.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

metrics.name: Total edge contrast index (landscape)
metrics.what:
The contrast-weighted edge of the whole landscape as a percentage of its total edge length. A FRAGSTATS metric
that landscapemetrics does not have.

symbols.e_{ab}: the length of edge between classes \(a\) and \(b\), in metres, each edge counted once (\(a > b\))
symbols.d_{ab}: the contrast weight (0 to 1) between the two classes, from the `contrast` table
symbols.e_{a\\partial}, d_{\\partial}: the edge towards missing cells or the map's border and its weight (`boundary_contrast`); always counted in TECI

metrics.use: Sensitive to the border weight; set `boundary_contrast` deliberately.
refs: McGarigal, K., Cushman, S. A., & Ene, E. (2012). FRAGSTATS v4: spatial pattern analysis program for categorical and continuous maps. University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

families.title: Surface metrics
families.intro:
The metrics of a **continuous surface**: an elevation model, an NDVI image, a canopy-height model, any raster whose
cells are measurements and not classes. They come from the surface texture parameters of ISO 25178 and the R package
[geodiv](https://cran.r-project.org/package=geodiv), which brought them to landscape ecology as *gradient surface
metrics*. They need no classification into patches. A trend (a slope across the whole map) is usually removed first,
so that the metrics describe the texture and not the tilt: `tf.surface.remove_plane`, or use a map that has had it
removed.

A metric is computed on all the cells with a value, or in a moving window with `tf.surface.window_metrics`. Heights
are in the unit of the raster, and the metrics that are not unitless say so on their card.
families.example:
import terraflux as tf

# NDVI of a part of south-western Oregon (371 x 371 cells), the best-fitting trend already removed
z = tf.load_raster(tf.surface.example_data("normforest"))

metrics.name: Average roughness (Sa)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.range: 0 or more; 0 for a flat surface
metrics.what:
The typical distance of a cell's value from the surface's mean: how rough the surface is, in the surface's own
unit. It is the most used amplitude parameter, simple to read and little affected by a few extreme cells.

symbols.N: the number of cells with a value
symbols.\\bar{z}: the mean of the values, \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_k z_k\)

metrics.use:
Use it to compare the roughness of two surfaces in the same unit (the NDVI of two forests, the elevation of two
terrains). It does not tell the shape of the roughness, only its size: pair it with `Ssk` and the spatial metrics
to know whether the roughness comes from peaks or valleys, and how far apart they are.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Root mean square roughness (Sq)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.what:
The standard deviation of the surface's values, in the surface's unit. Like Sa it measures how far the values
spread from the mean, but it squares the differences first, so a few high peaks or deep valleys weigh more.

symbols.N: the number of cells with a value

metrics.use:
Use it as the spread of the heights, and as the scale that the shape metrics (`Ssk`, `Sku`) are divided by. Sq is at
least as large as Sa, and much larger when there are outliers. Terraflux divides by the number of cells, as
ISO 25178 does; the R package geodiv divides by one less (the sample standard deviation), which differs by a
factor of \(\sqrt{(N-1)/N}\), negligible for a real map.

metrics.name: Skewness (Ssk)
metrics.range: no fixed limits; 0 for a symmetric distribution of values
metrics.what:
Whether the surface's values are balanced around the mean or lean to one side. A negative value means that valleys
(values far below the mean) dominate over peaks, as in a plateau cut by gullies or a canopy with gaps; a positive
value means isolated peaks stand out over a flat floor.

symbols.N: the number of cells with a value
symbols.\\mathrm{Sq}: the root mean square roughness, above

metrics.use:
Use it to tell apart surfaces that have the same Sa or Sq but a different shape. It is unitless, so it compares
surfaces in different units. It is sensitive to a few extreme cells, and is defined only when there are more than
two cells with a value. The value of the library is the adjusted one (the correction factor on the right), as the
adjusted Fisher-Pearson coefficient; `adj=False` leaves it out.

metrics.name: Excess kurtosis (Sku)
metrics.range: -2 or more; 0 for a normal distribution
metrics.what:
How much of the spread of the values comes from a few extreme peaks or valleys: the tailedness of the distribution
of values. High values mean a spiky or deeply pitted surface; negative values a flat-topped distribution.

symbols.N: the number of cells with a value

metrics.use:
The library returns the excess form (the fourth moment ratio minus 3), unlike ISO 25178, where a normal surface has
Sku = 3: do not compare it with tables of ISO values without adding 3. `excess=False` gives the ISO form.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Maximum valley depth (Sv)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.what: The absolute value of the lowest value of the surface: the depth of the deepest valley below the zero level.
metrics.use:
It is the absolute value of the minimum, not the depth below the mean, so it means a valley depth only when the mean
or the trend has been removed first. A single cell decides it.

metrics.name: Maximum peak height (Sp)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.what: The absolute value of the highest value of the surface: the height of the highest peak above the zero level.
metrics.use:
Named `sph` in the library (Sp in ISO 25178). Like Sv it needs a surface with the mean or the trend removed to mean a
peak height, and a single cell decides it. When the mean is zero, Sp + Sv is the maximum height Sz.

metrics.name: Mean peak height
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.range: above 0, or NA when no value is positive
metrics.what: The mean of the positive values: the average height of the part of the surface that lies above the zero level.
metrics.use:
Meaningful only when the mean or the trend has been removed, so that zero is the middle level. It is the geodiv
parameter (the mean of the heights above 0), not an ISO 25178 one.
aliases: mean of the heights above zero

metrics.name: Root mean square slope (Sdq)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface per cell
metrics.what:
How steep the surface is on average, from the differences between each cell and its right and its lower neighbour.
It mixes height and spacing: a rough surface with fine texture has a high Sdq.

symbols.M: the number of cells that have both the right and the lower neighbour (the last row and column are left out)

refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Area root mean square slope (Sdq6)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface per cell
metrics.range: 0 or more; NA on a raster with fewer than 7 rows or columns
metrics.what:
The root mean square slope from the seven-point derivative of ISO 25178, which smooths noise more than the
two-point differences of Sdq.

symbols.p_x: the derivative along the row, from the cells 3, 2 and 1 steps to the right (\(z_{+k}\)) and to the left (\(z_{-k}\)) of the cell
symbols.M: the number of cells at least 3 cells away from every edge

metrics.use:
Per cell, not per metre, like Sdq. The stencil of geodiv repeats the term for +2 in place of the one for -2 and takes
the root of the sum, not of the mean; Terraflux corrects both, so its value differs from geodiv's.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Developed interfacial area ratio (Sdr)
metrics.what: How much larger the true surface is than its flat projection: the extra area that the relief adds, in percent.

symbols.A_s: the triangulated area of the surface. Every block of 2 x 2 cell centres is cut into two triangles along each diagonal and the two areas are averaged, summed over the blocks whose four values are present
symbols.A_0: the same sum with every value 0, the flat projection

metrics.use:
As in geodiv, the values are first rescaled to 0 to 1 and the cells are 1 wide, so the value does not depend on the
unit of the surface but is not a physical area ratio, and it changes with the range of the surface: compare surfaces
only after the same rescaling.
The two areas are the [surface area](#surface_area) and the [flat area](#flat_area), which the library gives as
functions of their own.

metrics.name: Density of summits (Sds)
metrics.what: How many peaks the surface has per cell: the number of local maxima above the zero level, over the number of cells.

symbols.n_{\\mathrm{peaks}}: the number of peaks, cells off the edge with all 8 neighbours present that are higher than each of them and higher than 0
symbols.R, C: the number of rows and columns

metrics.use:
Peaks are compared with 0, so remove the mean or the trend first. A high value means a fine, busy texture, but the
count also grows with noise. Per cell, not per square metre: divide by the cell area for a density.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Mean summit curvature (Ssc)
metrics.unit: none (the values rescaled to 0 to 1, as in geodiv)
metrics.range: any real number; positive for rounded peaks
metrics.what:
The average curvature of the peaks: how sharply the summits bend downward around their top. Large positive values
mean pointed peaks.

symbols.z_{x \\pm 1}, z_{y \\pm 1}: its neighbours along the row and the column
symbols.\\Delta x, \\Delta y: the cell width (1) and the ratio of the cell height to its width, as in geodiv

metrics.use:
The sign follows ISO 25178 (positive for rounded-up peaks); geodiv has the opposite sign and uses first differences.
The value depends on the range of the surface because of the rescaling. NA when there are no peaks.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Ten-point height (S10z)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.what:
The mean height of the five highest peaks plus the mean depth of the five deepest valleys: a range measure that uses
several extremes instead of one.

symbols.p_k: the values of the five highest peaks
symbols.v_k: the values of the five lowest valleys (cells lower than their 8 neighbours and lower than 0)

metrics.use:
Less sensitive to a single outlier than Sp + Sv. Peaks and valleys are defined against 0, so remove the mean or the
trend first. Where fewer than five exist, the sum has fewer terms but is still divided by 5.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Surface bearing index (Sbi)
metrics.range: above 0 on a surface with its mean removed
metrics.what:
The root mean square roughness divided by the height that only 5 % of the surface exceeds. A flat-topped, load-bearing
surface has a high Sbi; a surface with sharp peaks has a low one.

symbols.h(0.05): the value at bearing 0.05, the 95th percentile of the values (the bearing is the share of cells at or above a value; type-7 quantile)

metrics.use:
Sensitive to the zero level: it assumes values with the mean removed (a negative \(h(0.05)\) gives a negative index).
Use it on a surface without its trend.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Core fluid retention index (Sci)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.what:
The void volume per unit area of the core of the surface, the part between 5 % and 80 % bearing: how much fluid the
middle of the surface could hold.

symbols.h(t): the value at bearing \(t\), the share of cells at or above it
symbols.integral: Simpson's rule on 1000 intervals; the bracket is the void volume from 5 % to 100 % bearing, and subtracting Svi leaves the core zone

metrics.use:
Defined on the values as they are, with the area measured up to the highest point of the interval; the unit is the
surface's. The areas of geodiv change when the bearing curve dips below 0; Terraflux's do not.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Valley fluid retention index (Svi)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.what:
The void volume per unit area of the valley zone, the lowest 20 % of the surface (80 % to 100 % bearing): how much
the deepest parts could hold.

symbols.h(t): the value at bearing \(t\), the share of cells at or above it
symbols.integral: Simpson's rule on 500 intervals; the first term is the rectangle up to the highest point of the zone, \(h(0.8)\)

metrics.use:
The version of geodiv gives negative values on positive surfaces and its Simpson's rule drops the last point;
Terraflux corrects both, so its value is not comparable with geodiv's.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Core roughness depth (Sk)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.what:
The height range of the core of the surface, read from the flattest 40 % of the bearing curve: the working depth that
remains after the highest peaks and the deepest valleys are taken away.
metrics.formula: \mathrm{Sk} = \left| L(0) - L(1) \right|, \qquad L(t) = b_0 + b_1 t

symbols.L(t): the least-squares line through the points of the bearing curve in the window of bearing fractions that has the smallest mean absolute slope among all windows covering 40 % of the curve (slopes by central differences at 10000 points); so \(\mathrm{Sk} = |b_1|\)

metrics.use:
The search for the flattest window is the slow part of the bearing metrics: avoid Sk, Spk and Svk in moving windows
on large rasters.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Reduced peak height (Spk)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.what:
The height of the peaks that stand above the core: the distance from the top of the surface down to where the core
line begins.

symbols.L(0): the height of the core line at bearing 0 (see Sk)
symbols.t_1: the share of cells at or above that height, so \(h(t_1)\) is the value where the core starts
symbols.B: the bearing, the share of cells at or above a value

metrics.use:
A large Spk means a few high peaks that wear off quickly. Read it with Sk and Svk, which together split the bearing
curve in three.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Reduced valley depth (Svk)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.what: The depth of the valleys below the core: the distance from where the core line ends down to the lowest value.

symbols.L(1): the height of the core line at bearing 1 (see Sk)
symbols.t_2: the share of cells at or above that height
symbols.B: the bearing, the share of cells at or above a value

metrics.use: A large Svk means deep pits that hold fluid or water. The lowest cells dominate it, so noise or a few sinks raise it.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Autocorrelation length (Sal)
metrics.what:
The shortest distance from zero lag at which the autocorrelation of the surface falls to 0.2 or less: the scale over
which the surface still resembles itself. Short values mean a fine texture.

symbols.\\mathrm{ACF}: the areal autocorrelation function of the surface (`tf.surface.aacf`), over the upper half of its image
symbols.\\tau: the lag in x and y

metrics.use:
The threshold 0.2 is ISO 25178's; `tf.surface.scl` gives the lengths for other thresholds (by default 0.2 and 1/e).
On longitude/latitude rasters the distances are haversine metres. geodiv measures from one row above zero lag, with
single-precision proximity, and fails with missing cells; Terraflux does not.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Texture aspect ratio (Str)
metrics.what:
The ratio of the fastest to the slowest decay of the autocorrelation: near 1 for a texture that is the same in every
direction, near 0 for a strongly oriented texture (ridges, stripes).

symbols.\\mathrm{ACF}: the areal autocorrelation function; both distances are measured from zero lag on its image, and the numerator is Sal

metrics.use:
The threshold 0.2 of ISO 25178 is used; `tf.surface.stxr` gives the ratio at several thresholds. When the
autocorrelation has a few gaps the slowest decay can be far away, which makes Str small without a real anisotropy.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Texture direction (Std)
metrics.what:
The dominant direction of the surface texture, from its Fourier spectrum: the angle of the frequency vector that has
the largest summed amplitude.

symbols.\\mathcal{F}(z): the Fourier transform of the surface (no window, mean not removed)
symbols.\\mathbf{f}: a frequency vector in the upper half of the spectrum, within the largest circle around zero frequency that fits (zero frequency itself and the negative side of the zero row are left out)
symbols.\\theta: the direction, from 0 to 179.5 degrees in steps of 0.5 (360 bins); with ties the smallest angle wins

metrics.use:
Meaningful only when one direction dominates: look at Stdi first. The angle is that of the frequency vector: 0 for a
texture that varies along x (stripes running north to south), 90 for one that varies along y. geodiv takes the angles
from one row above zero frequency and counts zero frequency in the 0 degree bin; Terraflux does neither.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Texture direction index (Stdi)
metrics.what:
How strongly one direction dominates the texture: the mean of the amplitude sums over directions, divided by the
largest one. Near 1 means no dominant direction; small values mean a clear one.

symbols.A(\\theta): the amplitude of the Fourier spectrum summed in the direction \(\theta\) (see Std)

metrics.use:
Read it with Std: a direction from a spectrum with Stdi near 1 points at nothing real. Small values mean a strongly
directional texture, the opposite of what the name may suggest.

metrics.name: Dominant radial wavelength (Srw)
metrics.what:
The radius in the Fourier spectrum with the largest summed amplitude: the spatial frequency that carries most of the
texture, given as a distance in the spectrum.

symbols.R(r_k): the amplitude of the upper half of the spectrum (no window, mean not removed) summed over the ring of radius \(r_k\) around zero frequency; the first ring (zero frequency) is set to 0
symbols.K: the number of rings, \(\min(\lfloor n_x/2 \rfloor, 100)\), evenly spaced
symbols.r_{\\max}: the largest distance in the zero row of the spectrum

metrics.use:
The number is a radius in the spectrum, not a ground distance. A texture that repeats \(k\) times across a raster of
\(n\) cells has its peak at \(k\) cell sizes, so its wavelength is \(n/k\) cells: convert before comparing it with a
scale of interest. NA when two rings tie for the maximum.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Radial wavelength index (Srwi)
metrics.what:
How strongly one wavelength dominates: the mean of the ring amplitude sums over the largest. Near 1 means a flat
spectrum with no dominant scale.

symbols.R(r_k): the amplitude summed over the ring of radius \(r_k\) (see Srw)
symbols.K: the number of rings; the mean includes the first ring, which is set to 0

metrics.use: Read it with Srw. Like Stdi it is small when the dominance is strong.

metrics.name: Half-power wavelength (Shw)
metrics.what:
The radius in the spectrum that splits the summed amplitude into two equal halves: the scale below which half of the
texture lies.

symbols.R(r_k): the amplitude summed over the ring of radius \(r_k\) (see Srw); the ring chosen is the one where the cumulative sum comes closest to half the total, not necessarily equal to it

metrics.use:
Like Srw it is a radius in the spectrum, not a ground distance. NA where two rings are equally close to the half.
geodiv measures from one row above zero frequency; Terraflux from zero frequency.

metrics.name: Fractal dimension (Sfd)
metrics.what:
How rough the surface is across scales, by the triangular prism method: 2 for a smooth surface, towards 3 for a
surface that fills space.

symbols.A(\\epsilon): the total area of triangular prisms laid over the central \(n \times n\) square of the surface (\(n\) the largest power of two strictly below the smaller side; values rescaled to 0 to 1), at steps \(\epsilon = 1, 2, 4, \dots, n\) cells. Each \(\epsilon \times \epsilon\) block gives four triangles joining its corners to the corner mean, their areas by Heron's formula
symbols.b: the least-squares slope of \(\ln A\) against \(\ln \epsilon^2\), the log of the cell area

metrics.use:
NA where there are missing cells. Values on smooth rasters sit very close to 2, so differences are small and need a
series of surfaces to be read. geodiv has a typo in one prism side and reads past the raster; Terraflux corrects both.
refs: Clarke, K. C. (1986). Computation of the fractal dimension of topographic surfaces using the triangular prism surface area method. Computers & Geosciences, 12(5), 713-722.

metrics.name: Surface area (triangulated)
metrics.unit: geodiv units (cells of width 1, the values rescaled to 0 to 1)
metrics.what: The area of the surface made of triangles over the cell centres, in geodiv's units: the first part of [Sdr](#surface_sdr).
metrics.formula: A_s = \sum_{\text{blocks}} \tfrac{1}{2} \left( \tfrac{1}{2} (s_1 s_2 + s_3 s_4) + \tfrac{1}{2} (s_1 s_4 + s_3 s_2) \right)

symbols.s_1, s_2, s_3, s_4: the sides of one 2 x 2 block with corner values \(a\) (top left), \(b\) (right), \(c\) (below) and \(d\) (diagonal), on rescaled values: \(s_1=\sqrt{dy^2+(c-a)^2}\), \(s_2=\sqrt{dx^2+(b-a)^2}\), \(s_3=\sqrt{dy^2+(d-b)^2}\), \(s_4=\sqrt{dx^2+(d-c)^2}\)
symbols.dx, dy: the cell width (1) and the ratio of the cell height to its width
symbols.inner terms: the two ways of cutting the block into triangles (half the product of two sides, taken as right-angle pairs)

metrics.use:
Not an area in square metres: use it only as the part of Sdr. Blocks with a missing corner are left out. It is a
function of the library, not one of the metrics of `tf.surface.metrics`.

metrics.name: Flat area (projected)
metrics.what:
The area of the surface projected on a plane: the triangulated area of the same cells with every value 0. It is the
denominator of [Sdr](#surface_sdr), and the [surface area](#surface_area) divided by it is the ratio.

symbols.M_{\\mathrm{blocks}}: the number of 2 x 2 blocks whose four values are present
symbols.dx, dy: the cell width (1) and the ratio of the cell height to its width, as in geodiv

metrics.use: With square cells and no gaps it is (rows - 1) x (columns - 1): 136900 for the 371 x 371 example.

metrics.name: Material ratio height difference (Sdc)
metrics.unit: the unit of the surface (here NDVI)
metrics.what:
The height difference between two bearing fractions of the curve, for instance between 10 % and 80 %: the thickness of
the part of the surface between them.

symbols.h(t): the value at bearing \(t\), the share of cells at or above it (see the [bearing area curve](#surface_bearing_area))
symbols.t_1, t_2: the two fractions you choose, \(0 \le t_1 < t_2 \le 1\)

metrics.use:
There are no default fractions: pass them (ISO often uses 10 % and 80 %). It is not in the library's list of metrics,
so `tf.surface.metrics` does not give it.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Bearing area (Abbott-Firestone) curve
metrics.what:
The share of the surface that lies at or above each value, from the highest value (bearing near 0) to the lowest
(bearing 1). Sbi, Sci, Svi, Sk, Spk and Svk are read from this curve.

symbols.N: the number of cells with a value
symbols.h(t): the inverse, the value whose bearing is \(t\) (the type-7 quantile of the values at \(1 - t\))

metrics.use:
geodiv builds the curve from 1 - z, which puts rounding errors in the values; Terraflux uses z. It is a curve (one row
per distinct value, with the columns `bearing` and `height`), not a single number: the parameters above summarise it.
refs: ISO 25178-2:2021. Geometrical product specifications (GPS) - Surface texture: areal - Part 2: Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters.

metrics.name: Areal autocorrelation function (AACF)
metrics.what:
The correlation of the surface with a copy of itself shifted by every lag in x and y, as an image with zero lag at the
centre. Sal and Str are read from it.

symbols.z: the surface (the mean is not removed)
symbols.w: a two-dimensional Hann window, \(w(r,c) = h_R(r)\,h_C(c)\) with \(h_n(k) = \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n-1}\), zero at both ends
symbols.shift: puts zero lag in the centre; dividing by the maximum cancels the scaling constants, so the value at zero lag is 1

metrics.use:
The image keeps the size of the input: a 371 x 371 raster gives a 371 x 371 image. With missing cells the largest square
without them around the centre is used. A raster with many gaps leaves little to analyse: fill or crop it first.

families.title: Biodiversity (Biodiverse)
families.source: Biodiverse (Laffan, Lubarsky and Rosauer 2010), ported as tf.bio
families.intro:
Species (labels) counted in cells (groups). Every index is computed for each group over its neighbourhood: one or two
sets of groups chosen by spatial conditions (set 1, set 2). The names are Biodiverse's and the values match its output.

The cards show the values of one cell, `3350000:750000`, on Biodiverse's own example: 365 records of 31 species snapped
to cells of 100 km (`tf.bio.example_data("sites")`), with the phylogeny of those species (`"tree"`). The neighbourhood
is `C`, the cells within 200 km; the indices of two sets use `C2`, the cell itself as set 1 and its neighbourhood as
set 2. A call gives a table (`.table`, a row per cell) and list indices (`.lists`); `at` picks what the cell `G` holds
(a list shows its first six entries). The example has no label or group properties and no label matrix, so those cards
use a small toy made with a seeded random generator: a mass between 1 and 50 for each species, an elevation between 0
and 800 for each cell, and random symmetric distances between the species. The numeric-label cards read the record
number of the table as the label. The toy values show how a calculation is called, not a result about the species.

Shared notation: `S` richness (labels in the neighbourhood); `A`, `B`, `C` the labels in both sets, only in set 1 and
only in set 2 (`ABC = A+B+C`); `R_l` the range of a label (the groups holding it in the whole basedata, or its RANGE
property if larger); `r_l` its local range (groups of the neighbourhood holding it); `N_l` and `n_l` the same counts in
samples. Where the code departs from the usual definition the card says so. Moran's I and Geary's C are not here: they
live in `tf.stats`.
families.example:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import terraflux as tf

# Biodiverse's example records: 365 records of 31 species, snapped to cells of 100 km
sites = tf.bio.example_data("sites")
bd = tf.bio.BaseData.from_table(sites, group_columns=["x", "y"], label_columns=["genus", "species"],
                                cell_sizes=[100000, 100000])
tree = tf.bio.read_tree(tf.bio.example_data("tree"))  # the phylogeny of those species
C = "sp_circle (radius => 200000)"                    # the neighbourhood: the cells within 200 km
C2 = ["sp_self_only()", C]                            # two sets: the cell itself (set 1), its neighbourhood (set 2)
G = "3350000:750000"                                  # the cell whose values the cards show

# a small seeded toy where the example has no data: a mass per species, an elevation per cell, a label matrix
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
bd.set_label_properties(pd.DataFrame({"MASS": rng.integers(1, 51, len(bd.labels)).astype(float)}, index=bd.labels))
bd.set_group_properties(pd.DataFrame({"ELEV": rng.integers(0, 801, len(bd.groups)).astype(float)}, index=bd.groups))
v = rng.random((len(bd.labels), len(bd.labels)))
mx = tf.bio.Matrix(bd.labels, (v + v.T) / 2, self_similarity=0.0)
# numeric labels: the record number of the table is the label
bn = tf.bio.BaseData.from_table(sites, group_columns=["x", "y"], label_columns=["num"], cell_sizes=[100000, 100000])


def at(res, *keys, like=None, n=6):
    """What a result holds for the cell G: columns of its table, or the first n entries of a list index."""
    if keys and keys[0] in res.lists:
        d = res.lists[keys[0]]
        return d[d["group"] == G].set_index("key")["value"].head(n)
    row = res.table.loc[G]
    if like:
        return row.filter(like=like)
    return row[keys[0]] if len(keys) == 1 else row[list(keys)] if keys else row

metrics.name: Richness
metrics.what: Number of distinct labels (species) in the neighbourhood. RICHNESS_SET1 and RICHNESS_SET2 give it for each set alone.
metrics.formula: S_{all} = A+B+C,\quad S_{1} = A+B,\quad S_{2} = A+C

symbols.A: the labels in both sets

metrics.use: The base measure of diversity; depends on the cell size and on the neighbourhood. Sampling effort inflates or hides it, see the estimators.

metrics.name: Redundancy
metrics.what: How much sampling exceeds richness, one minus labels per sample. Near 0 every sample is a different label, near 1 most are repeats.

symbols.n_l: the samples of label \(l\) in the neighbourhood. REDUNDANCY_SET1 and _SET2 use their own set.

metrics.use: A cheap check of sample completeness; unlike the estimators it says nothing about unseen labels.

metrics.name: Shared and exclusive label counts (A, B, C, ABC)
metrics.what: Counts of labels in both neighbour sets (ABC_A), only in set 1 (ABC_B), only in set 2 (ABC_C) and in either (ABC_ABC); the inputs of every taxonomic turnover index.

symbols.A: the labels in both sets

metrics.use: Needs two conditions. Read them first when a turnover value looks odd.

metrics.name: Labels in the basedata but not in the neighbourhood (D)
metrics.what: Count of labels of the whole basedata absent from both neighbour sets.

symbols.L: number of labels in the basedata

metrics.use: Completes the 2x2 table of A, B, C, D that presence-absence indices work from.

metrics.name: Element (group) counts
metrics.what: Number of groups in the neighbourhood, EL_COUNT_ALL for both sets, EL_COUNT_SET1 and EL_COUNT_SET2 for each; the nonempty version counts only groups holding at least one label.

symbols.G_1, G_2: the groups of set 1 and set 2

metrics.use: Gives the area in cells behind the other indices (it is the divisor of the normalised endemism indices).
metrics.value:
EL_COUNT_ALL  11
EL_COUNT_SET1  1
EL_COUNT_SET2  10
EL_COUNT_NONEMPTY_ALL  11
EL_COUNT_NONEMPTY_SET1  1
EL_COUNT_NONEMPTY_SET2  10

metrics.name: Element lists (groups of the neighbourhood)
metrics.what: The groups of the neighbourhood as a list (key group name, value 1), for both sets and for each. The "as arrays" version gives the same keys in Biodiverse's array form.

symbols.G_1, G_2: the groups of the two sets

metrics.use: To see or export which cells made up a neighbourhood.

metrics.name: Label count rank (percent)
metrics.what: For each label, the percentage of the other groups in the neighbourhood that hold fewer samples of it than the focal group (groups without it count as 0).
metrics.use: Tells whether the focal cell is rich or poor in a species relative to its neighbours; a label absent from the focal group gets 0.
metrics.value:
Genus:sp1  90
Genus:sp10  0
Genus:sp11  80
Genus:sp12  80
Genus:sp15  100
Genus:sp18  0

metrics.name: Local range statistics
metrics.what: Mean and standard deviation, over the labels of the neighbourhood, of their local range (number of neighbourhood groups holding the label). Per set as ABC2_MEAN_SET1 / _SET2 and ABC2_SD_*.

symbols.r_l: groups of the neighbourhood holding label \(l\)

metrics.use: Separates a neighbourhood of widespread species from one of local ones; the lists ABC2_LABELS_ALL (_SET1, _SET2) give the \(r_l\) themselves (calculation local_range_lists).
metrics.value:
ABC2_MEAN_ALL  2.938
ABC2_MEAN_SET1  1
ABC2_MEAN_SET2  2.571
ABC2_SD_ALL  1.843
ABC2_SD_SET1  0
ABC2_SD_SET2  1.453

metrics.name: Local sample count statistics
metrics.what: Mean, standard deviation and sum of the sample counts of the labels over the neighbourhood (ABC3_MEAN_*, ABC3_SD_*, ABC3_SUM_*, for all, set 1, set 2).
metrics.formula: n_l = \sum_{g \in G} n_{g,l},\quad \bar n = \frac{1}{S}\sum_l n_l,\quad \text{SUM} = \sum_l n_l

symbols.n_l: samples of label \(l\) in the neighbourhood

metrics.use: A summary of abundance; ABC3_LABELS_ALL gives the \(n_l\) (local_sample_count_lists).
metrics.value:

ABC3_MEAN_SET1  3
ABC3_MEAN_SET2  9.214
ABC3_SD_ALL  7.013
ABC3_SD_SET1  2.28
ABC3_SD_SET2  5.206
ABC3_SUM_ALL  162

ABC3_SUM_SET2  129

metrics.name: Local sample count quantiles
metrics.what: The 0, 5, 10 ... 100 percent quantiles (keys Q000 to Q100) of the label sample counts over the neighbourhood, as a list.

symbols.n_l: the sample count of label \(l\) in the neighbourhood

metrics.use: Shows the shape of the abundance distribution. With one set the lists for set 1 repeat the all-set values.

metrics.name: Simpson diversity
metrics.what: Probability that two samples drawn at random from the neighbourhood are different labels (one minus the sum of squared proportions).

symbols.n_l: samples of label \(l\) in the neighbourhood

metrics.use: Weights common species; insensitive to rare ones. It is the Gini-Simpson index (1 − Σp²), not Σp².

metrics.name: Shannon entropy
metrics.what: Entropy of the label proportions with the natural logarithm. The same calculation gives SHANNON_HMAX = ln S and the evenness SHANNON_E = H / ln S.
metrics.formula: H = -\sum_l p_l \ln p_l,\quad H_{max} = \ln S,\quad E = H / H_{max}

symbols.p_l: proportion of the samples that belong to label \(l\)

metrics.use: Sensitive to rare labels more than Simpson. SHANNON_E compares cells of different richness.

metrics.name: Rao quadratic entropy (taxonomic)
metrics.what: Rao's quadratic entropy with every pair of different labels at distance 1; TX_RAO_TN is the number of label pairs counted (S squared), TX_RAO_TLABELS the proportions.

symbols.p_l: proportion of the samples of label \(l\)

metrics.use: With distance 1 it equals SIMPSON_D; use the matrix version MX_RAO_QE for real label distances.
refs: Rao (1982). Diversity and dissimilarity coefficients: a unified approach. Theoretical Population Biology 21: 24-43.

metrics.name: Hurlbert's rarefied richness (ES)
metrics.what: Expected number of labels in a random draw of n samples, for n = 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000 (those not above the total samples), as a list keyed by n.

symbols.N_l: samples of label \(l\); a term is 1 when \(N - N_l < n\)

metrics.use: Compares richness between cells with different sampling effort. A cell with fewer than 5 samples returns nothing.
refs: Hurlbert (1971). The nonconcept of species diversity: a critique and alternative parameters. Ecology 52: 577-586.

metrics.name: Chao1 richness estimate
metrics.what: Lower-bound estimate of the true richness from the singletons and doubletons of the sample counts, with the variance, standard error, 95% interval, undetected labels and the counts f1, f2 (CHAO1_*).
metrics.formula: S_{Chao1} = S + \frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\begin{cases}\dfrac{f_1^2}{2 f_2} & f_2 > 0\\[4pt] \dfrac{f_1 (f_1-1)}{2} & f_2 = 0,\ f_1 > 1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}

symbols.f_1, f_2: labels with exactly one and two samples (CHAO1_F1_COUNT, CHAO1_F2_COUNT)
symbols.z: 1.959964, the normal quantile of the log-normal 95% interval (CHAO1_CI_LOWER, CHAO1_CI_UPPER); CHAO1_META lists the formulas used

metrics.use: Good for sample counts with many rare labels; uses sample counts (see CHAO2 for presence in groups). Unreliable with no singletons.
refs: Chao (1984). Nonparametric estimation of the number of classes in a population. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 11: 265-270.
Chao (1987). Estimating the population size for capture-recapture data with unequal catchability. Biometrics 43: 783-791.

CHAO1_CI_LOWER  16.93
CHAO1_CI_UPPER  54.09
CHAO1_ESTIMATE  21.96
CHAO1_F1_COUNT  4
CHAO1_F2_COUNT  0
CHAO1_SE  7.175
CHAO1_UNDETECTED  5.963
CHAO1_VARIANCE  51.48

metrics.name: Chao2 richness estimate
metrics.what: The incidence-based Chao estimator: it works on the number of groups each label occurs in, so the labels found in exactly one or two groups play the role of singletons and doubletons.
metrics.formula: S_{Chao2} = S + \frac{m-1}{m}\cdot\begin{cases}\dfrac{Q_1^2}{2 Q_2} & Q_2 > 0\\[4pt] \dfrac{Q_1 (Q_1-1)}{2} & Q_2 = 0,\ Q_1 > 1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}

symbols.Q_1, Q_2: labels in exactly one and two groups (CHAO2_Q1_COUNT, CHAO2_Q2_COUNT)
symbols.S_{Chao2} - S: the labels not yet seen (CHAO2_UNDETECTED); the other CHAO2_* values are as for Chao1

metrics.use: Better when the data are presence per group rather than counts; needs several groups in the neighbourhood.
refs: Chao (1987). Estimating the population size for capture-recapture data with unequal catchability. Biometrics 43: 783-791.

CHAO2_CI_UPPER  39.68

CHAO2_Q2_COUNT  3

metrics.name: ACE richness estimate
metrics.what: Abundance-based coverage estimator. Labels with 10 or fewer samples are "rare"; their number is inflated by the sample coverage and a coefficient of variation. Falls back on Chao1 when coverage is 0.

symbols.S_{abund}, S_{rare}: labels with more than / at most 10 samples
symbols.C: the sample coverage of the rare labels, \(1 - f_1/N_{rare}\)
symbols.\\gamma^2: the coefficient-of-variation term, \(\max\left(\frac{S_{rare}}{C}\frac{\sum_i i(i-1)f_i}{N_{rare}(N_{rare}-1)}-1,\,0\right)\) with the sum over 1 to 10; ACE_ESTIMATE_USED_CHAO is 1 when the Chao1 fallback was used

metrics.use: Uses all the rare labels, not only singletons and doubletons; the cutoff 10 is fixed. Variance by the delta method as in EstimateS.
refs: Chao & Lee (1992). Estimating the number of classes via sample coverage. Journal of the American Statistical Association 87: 210-217.

ACE_CI_UPPER  41.14
ACE_ESTIMATE  19.99

metrics.name: ICE richness estimate
metrics.what: The incidence version of ACE: rare labels are those found in 10 or fewer groups, and the coverage and variation use the number of groups t that hold any label.

symbols.S_{freq}, S_{infreq}: labels in more than / at most 10 groups
symbols.N_{infreq}: the sum of the group counts of the infrequent labels
symbols.A: the correction \(\frac{2Q_2}{(t-1)Q_1+2Q_2}\) (a variant when \(Q_2=0\))
symbols.C: the sample coverage of the infrequent labels
symbols.\\gamma^2: the coefficient-of-variation term, with the factor \(t/(t-1)\)

metrics.use: Use with presence data over several groups; needs t > 1 else it returns the observed richness.
refs: Lee & Chao (1994). Estimating population size via sample coverage for closed capture-recapture models. Biometrics 50: 88-97.

metrics.name: Weighted endemism (whole neighbourhood)
metrics.what: Sum over the labels of the neighbourhood of the share of each label's range that lies in it. A label wholly inside counts 1, a widespread one counts little.

symbols.r_l: groups of the neighbourhood (both sets) that hold label \(l\)
symbols.R_l: its range in the basedata (the RANGE property if larger)

metrics.use: Rises with richness as well as with narrow ranges; use the corrected version (ENDW_CWE) to compare cells.
refs: Crisp et al. (2001). Endemism in the Australian flora. Journal of Biogeography 28: 183-198.
Laffan & Crisp (2003). Assessing endemism at multiple spatial scales, with an example from the Australian vascular flora. Journal of Biogeography 30: 511-520.

metrics.name: Corrected weighted endemism (whole neighbourhood)
metrics.what: Weighted endemism divided by richness: the mean proportion of its range the labels of the neighbourhood have there.
metrics.use: Removes the richness effect, so it shows range restriction rather than species numbers. Undefined for empty neighbourhoods.
refs: Crisp et al. (2001). Endemism in the Australian flora. Journal of Biogeography 28: 183-198.

metrics.name: Endemism, single (Rosauer)
metrics.what: Sum over the labels of the neighbourhood of one over its range, each label counted once whatever its local range.

symbols.R_l: range of label \(l\) in the basedata

metrics.use: The range-size-weighted richness used in phylogenetic endemism of single cells; unlike WE it ignores how widely the label occurs in the neighbourhood.
refs: Slatyer et al. (2007). An assessment of endemism and species richness patterns in the Australian Anura. Journal of Biogeography 34: 583-596. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2699.2006.01647.x

metrics.name: Endemism lists (whole neighbourhood)
metrics.what: Per label of the neighbourhood, its range (ENDW_RANGELIST) and its endemism weight r/R (ENDW_WTLIST), the terms behind WE.
metrics.use: To map or rank the species that drive an endemism hotspot.
metrics.value:
Genus:sp1  0.2609
Genus:sp10  0.07143
Genus:sp11  0.1224
Genus:sp12  0.1034
Genus:sp15  0.2667
Genus:sp18  0.05263

metrics.name: Normalised weighted endemism (whole)
metrics.what: WE and CWE divided by the number of groups in the neighbourhood, so neighbourhoods of different size can be compared (ENDW_WE_NORM, ENDW_CWE_NORM).
metrics.use: Only for comparing results between conditions of different sizes; undefined when there are no groups.

metrics.name: Weighted endemism (central)
metrics.what: Weighted endemism of the labels of set 1 only (the central cell), with the local ranges counted over the whole neighbourhood. The calculation also gives ENDC_CWE, ENDC_SINGLE and ENDC_RICHNESS.

symbols.r_l: groups of both sets holding label \(l\)

metrics.use: Needs two conditions (central cell, then the neighbourhood). Shows how endemic the central cell's species are in context.

metrics.name: Endemism lists (central)
metrics.what: Range (ENDC_RANGELIST) and weight r/R (ENDC_WTLIST) per label of set 1; the normalised version ENDC_WE_NORM, ENDC_CWE_NORM divides WE and CWE by the groups in the neighbourhood.
metrics.use: As the whole-neighbourhood lists but for the central cell only.
metrics.value:
Genus:sp1  0.2609
Genus:sp11  0.1224
Genus:sp12  0.1034
Genus:sp15  0.2667
Genus:sp20  0.5556
Genus:sp23  0.16

metrics.name: Absolute endemism
metrics.what: Number of labels of the neighbourhood whose whole range is inside it. END_ABS_ALL_P is their share of the labels; END_ABS1 / END_ABS2 (and _P) count them for set 1 and set 2 alone.
metrics.formula: END_{abs} = \#\{l : R_l \le r_l\},\quad END_{abs,P} = END_{abs} / S

symbols.R_l: range in the basedata; for set 1 alone the test uses its range in set 1

metrics.use: A strict test: one record outside the neighbourhood excludes a label. Depends strongly on neighbourhood size.
metrics.value:
END_ABS1  0
END_ABS1_P  0
END_ABS2  0
END_ABS2_P  0
END_ABS_ALL  1
END_ABS_ALL_P  0.0625

metrics.name: Hierarchical partition of weighted endemism
metrics.what: Splits WE by the levels of a hierarchical label name (here Genus:species): for each level a list of the share of WE contributed by each prefix, the count of labels in it, the expected share and the observed minus expected (_i, _C_i, _E_i, _OME_i; ENDC_HPART_* for the central version).
metrics.formula: O_{k} = \sum_{l \in k} \frac{w_l}{WE},\quad E_k = \frac{n_k}{S},\quad OME_k = E_k - O_k

symbols.S: the number of labels; level 0 is the first name part. OME is expected minus observed, as the code computes it

metrics.use: Shows which genera over- or under-contribute to endemism relative to their species number. Needs labels with ":"-separated parts.
metrics.value:
Genus:sp1  0.06024
Genus:sp10  0.01649
Genus:sp11  0.02827
Genus:sp12  0.02389
Genus:sp15  0.06158
Genus:sp18  0.01215

metrics.name: Hierarchical label ratios
metrics.what: A, B, C counts and their ratios by label level (lists HIER_A, HIER_ARAT, HIER_ASUM, HIER_ASUMRAT, HIER_B, HIER_BRAT, HIER_C, HIER_CRAT), for hierarchical label names.

symbols.A_i: shared labels at level \(i\); likewise B, C. Biodiverse computes the same A, B, C for every level, and so does this port, so the ratios are 1.

metrics.use: Reproduces Biodiverse as it is; the per-level values do not differ between levels. Needs two conditions and a hierarchy.

metrics.name: Weighted rarity (whole neighbourhood)
metrics.what: The endemism calculation with samples in place of groups: sum of the share of each label's total samples that falls in the neighbourhood. The calculation also gives RAREW_CWE and RAREW_RICHNESS.

symbols.n_l: samples of label \(l\) in the neighbourhood
symbols.N_l: its samples in the basedata (the ABUNDANCE property if larger)

metrics.use: Uses abundance rather than range, so it suits sampled data where a cell is not simply present or absent.

metrics.name: Weighted rarity (central)
metrics.what: Weighted rarity of the labels of set 1 with local samples over the whole neighbourhood (RAREC_WE, RAREC_CWE, RAREC_RICHNESS).
metrics.use: Needs two conditions; central version of RAREW_WE. The lists RAREC_RANGELIST / RAREC_WTLIST (rarity_central_lists) and RAREW_* (rarity_whole_lists) give the terms.

metrics.name: Sorenson dissimilarity
metrics.what: Presence-absence dissimilarity between the two neighbour sets: 0 when they hold the same labels, 1 when they share none.

symbols.A: the labels in both sets

metrics.use: Needs two conditions. Undefined (NaN) when both sets are empty; it is 1 when \(A=0\) but both \(B\) and \(C\) are non-zero. Also a `cluster` dissimilarity (the default).

metrics.name: Jaccard dissimilarity
metrics.what: One minus the share of labels the two sets have in common out of all labels found in either.

symbols.A, B, C: the labels in both sets, only in set 1 and only in set 2, as in SORENSON

metrics.use: Same edge rules as SORENSON; counts unshared labels more heavily.

metrics.name: S2 dissimilarity (Lennon)
metrics.what: Turnover that does not depend on differences in richness between the sets: the shared labels are compared with the smaller of the two unshared parts.

symbols.A, B, C: the labels in both sets, only in set 1 and only in set 2, as in SORENSON

metrics.use: Use when the sets differ much in richness, where Sorenson mixes turnover with nestedness. Undefined when no label is found.
refs: Lennon et al. (2001). The geographical structure of British bird distributions: diversity, spatial turnover and scale. Journal of Animal Ecology 70: 966-979. doi:10.1046/j.0021-8790.2001.00563.x

metrics.name: Kulczynski 2 dissimilarity
metrics.what: One minus the mean of the share of set 1 labels found in set 2 and of set 2 labels found in set 1.

symbols.A, B, C: the labels in both sets, only in set 1 and only in set 2, as in SORENSON

metrics.use: Treats the two sets symmetrically while weighting by each set's own richness.

metrics.name: Beta diversity (Whittaker form)
metrics.what: Gamma richness over the larger set richness, minus one.

symbols.A, B, C: the labels in both sets, only in set 1 and only in set 2, as in SORENSON

metrics.use: 0 when one set contains the other; the maximum depends on the set sizes.

metrics.name: Nestedness-resultant dissimilarity
metrics.what: The part of dissimilarity that comes from nestedness, the poorer set being a subset of the richer one (Baselga).

symbols.A, B, C: the labels in both sets, only in set 1 and only in set 2, as in SORENSON

metrics.use: 0 when \(A = 0\) and both \(B, C > 0\) (no overlap), NaN with no overlap and one set empty. Subtract from Sorenson for the spatial turnover part.
refs: Baselga (2010). Partitioning the turnover and nestedness components of beta diversity. Global Ecology and Biogeography 19: 134-143. doi:10.1111/j.1466-8238.2009.00490.x

metrics.name: Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
metrics.what: Abundance-based dissimilarity between the two sets, with sample counts summed over each set. The calculation also gives the parts BC_A, BC_B (totals of set 1 and set 2) and BC_W (shared minimum).

symbols.n_{1l}, n_{2l}: samples of label \(l\) in set 1 and in set 2 (0 when absent)

metrics.use: Sets with many more groups have larger counts; the normalised version divides by group numbers.

metrics.name: Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, normalised by group counts
metrics.what: Bray-Curtis with each set's counts divided by its number of groups, so the sets are compared as mean samples per group (BCN_A, BCN_B, BCN_W are the parts).
metrics.use: Prefer it when the two sets contain different numbers of cells.

metrics.name: Range-weighted turnover
metrics.what: Jaccard-type turnover in which every label counts by its endemism weight, so shared widespread species matter little and shared endemics a lot (RW_TURNOVER_A, _B, _C are the weighted parts).

symbols.A_w: weights of labels in both sets
symbols.r_l/R_l: as in ENDW_WE (local range over the whole neighbourhood)

metrics.use: Turnover that focuses on restricted-range species. NaN when A and B, or A and C, are both zero.
refs: Laffan et al. (2016). Range-weighted metrics of species and phylogenetic turnover can better resolve biogeographic transition zones. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 7: 580-588. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.12513

metrics.name: Labels on the tree
metrics.what: Number of labels of the neighbourhood that are terminals of the tree. PHYLO_LABELS_ON_TREE is the list of them.

symbols.T: the terminal names of the tree

metrics.use: Check it against richness before reading any phylogenetic index: labels missing from the tree are ignored by PD and PE.

metrics.name: Labels not on the tree
metrics.what: Number of labels of the neighbourhood with no terminal on the tree (PHYLO_LABELS_NOT_ON_TREE_N), their proportion (_P) and the list (PHYLO_LABELS_NOT_ON_TREE).
metrics.formula: N_{off} = |\{l \in N: l \notin T\}|,\quad P_{off} = N_{off} / S
metrics.use: A non-zero value means the tree does not cover the data: fix names before trusting PD.

metrics.name: Labels on or off the trimmed tree
metrics.what: As the on-tree counts, against the tree trimmed to the labels of the basedata: PHYLO_LABELS_ON_TRIMMED_TREE (list), PHYLO_LABELS_NOT_ON_TRIMMED_TREE_N, _P and the list.

symbols.T_{trim}: the tree trimmed to the labels present in the basedata

metrics.use: The trimmed tree is the reference of PE and the relative indices.

metrics.name: Last shared ancestor
metrics.what: Properties of the most recent common ancestor of the neighbourhood labels: its depth (LAST_SHARED_ANCESTOR_DEPTH), distance to the root (_DIST_TO_ROOT), to the farthest tip (_DIST_TO_TIP), its own branch length (_LENGTH) and the relative position (_POS_REL).

symbols.d_{root}: the summed branch lengths from the ancestor to the root (0 for the root)
symbols.d_{tip}: the longest path from the ancestor to a label tip (0 for a terminal)

metrics.use: Tells how deep in the tree the group's species diverge, a quick check of clustering by clade.

metrics.name: Phylogenetic diversity (PD)
metrics.what: Total length of the branches of the tree that connect the neighbourhood labels to the root. PD_P is it as a share of the whole tree, PD_per_taxon and PD_P_per_taxon divide by the labels on the tree.

symbols.\\mathrm{span}(N): branches on the paths from the labels of the neighbourhood that are on the tree up to the root
symbols.\\sum_b L_b: the length of the full tree (not trimmed), the divisor of PD_P

metrics.use: Includes the path to the root, so a single species has PD > 0. Rises with richness; compare with relative PD (RPD) or randomisation.
refs: Faith (1992). Conservation evaluation and phylogenetic diversity. Biological Conservation 61: 1-10. doi:10.1016/0006-3207(92)91201-3

metrics.name: Local phylogenetic diversity
metrics.what: PD without the stem: the length shared by all labels from their last common ancestor up to the root is removed (PD_LOCAL, and PD_LOCAL_P as a share of the whole tree).

symbols.a: the last shared ancestor of the neighbourhood labels on the tree, included in the removed path. Not applied if the ancestor is a terminal.

metrics.use: Separates the spread of a group within the tree from how deep its clade sits.

metrics.name: PD node and terminal lists
metrics.what: The branches counted in PD, keyed by node name with their lengths (PD_INCLUDED_NODE_LIST), only the terminal ones (PD_INCLUDED_TERMINAL_NODE_LIST) and their number (PD_INCLUDED_TERMINAL_NODE_COUNT).
metrics.use: To see which clades a cell's PD comes from, or map branch use.

metrics.name: PD clade contributions
metrics.what: For each clade (node) of the neighbourhood's tree, the PD in it (PD_CLADE_SCORE), as a share of the cell's PD (PD_CLADE_CONTR) and of the whole tree (PD_CLADE_CONTR_P).

symbols.L_n: length of node \(n\) if it is on the PD tree
symbols.\\mathrm{kids}(n): the children of the node, summed over the spanning sub-tree
symbols.contr_P: the same share of the total tree length; the values are truncated to 11 decimals as Biodiverse does

metrics.use: Finds the clades that account for a cell's PD.

metrics.name: PD clade loss
metrics.what: PD lost if a clade were removed, counting the unbranched stem above it: nodes with a single child inherit the loss of the first branching ancestor (PD_CLADE_LOSS_CONTR, _CONTR_P, _SCORE). The ancestral version gives the extra loss beyond the clade (PD_CLADE_LOSS_ANC, _ANC_P).

symbols.a(n): the first ancestor of \(n\) (or \(n\)) with more than one child on the PD tree

metrics.use: Ranks the clades whose extinction would cost most PD, stem included.

metrics.name: Phylogenetic abundance
metrics.what: PD weighted by sample counts: each label's samples are multiplied by the length of each branch on its path to the root and summed (PHYLO_ABUNDANCE; PHYLO_ABUNDANCE_BRANCH_HASH by branch).

symbols.n_l: samples of label \(l\) in the neighbourhood
symbols.\\mathrm{path}(l): branches from its tip to the root

metrics.use: Shows how much of the sampling lies in long branches; not scaled by PD.

metrics.name: Phylogenetic endemism (PE)
metrics.what: Endemism summed over branches: each branch of the neighbourhood's PD tree counts its length times the share of its range inside the neighbourhood. PE_WE_P gives it relative to the trimmed tree.

symbols.r_b: groups of the neighbourhood whose labels descend from \(b\)
symbols.R_b: groups in the whole basedata that do (the range of the branch)
symbols.T_{trim}: the tree trimmed to the labels present in the basedata

metrics.use: High where narrow-ranged, long branches concentrate; confounded with richness (compare with CWE or randomisations).
refs: Rosauer et al. (2009). Phylogenetic endemism: a new approach for identifying geographical concentrations of evolutionary history. Molecular Ecology 18: 4061-4072. doi:10.1111/j.1365-294X.2009.04311.x

metrics.name: Phylogenetic endemism, single (PE_WE_SINGLE)
metrics.what: PE counting each branch once, whatever its local range: the sum of branch length over branch range (PE_WE_SINGLE_P relative to the trimmed tree).
metrics.use: The phylogenetic version of Rosauer's single-cell endemism; independent of how many neighbour cells share the branch.

metrics.name: Corrected weighted phylogenetic endemism
metrics.what: PE divided by PD: the average range-restriction of the branches in the neighbourhood, a PE not driven by tree size.
metrics.use: The phylogenetic counterpart of CWE; NaN when PD is 0.

metrics.name: PE lists
metrics.what: Per branch of the neighbourhood: local range (PE_LOCAL_RANGELIST), range (PE_RANGELIST) and weight \(L_b r_b/R_b\) (PE_WTLIST), the terms of PE.

symbols.r_b, R_b: local and global range of the branch

metrics.use: Maps the branches behind a PE hotspot.

metrics.name: Phylogenetic endemism, central
metrics.what: PE of the central cell's tree: the PE of the whole neighbourhood minus the weights of the branches found only in set 2 (PEC_WE_P relative to the trimmed tree).
metrics.use: Needs two conditions (central cell, neighbourhood); the branch ranges still count the whole neighbourhood.

metrics.name: Corrected phylogenetic endemism, central
metrics.what: Central PE divided by the length of the central branches that are in the neighbourhood's PD tree (PEC_CWE_PD).

symbols.PD_C: sum of lengths of the central branches in the PD tree (PEC_CWE_PD)

metrics.use: The central analogue of PE_CWE.

metrics.name: PE lists, central
metrics.what: The PE lists restricted to the central branches: PEC_LOCAL_RANGELIST, PEC_RANGELIST and PEC_WTLIST.

symbols.A, B: branches in both sets and only in set 1 (all when set 2 adds none)

metrics.use: As PE_WTLIST for the central cell.

metrics.name: PD endemism
metrics.what: Total length of the branches found only in the neighbourhood: the part of PD not found in any group outside it. PD_ENDEMISM_P is relative to the trimmed tree, PD_ENDEMISM_WTS the per-branch list.

symbols.r_b: groups of the neighbourhood with the branch
symbols.R_b: groups in the basedata with it

metrics.use: The branch-length analogue of absolute endemism; strict and neighbourhood-size dependent.

metrics.name: PE clade contributions and loss
metrics.what: The clade contribution and loss lists of PD, with PE weights in place of lengths: PE_CLADE_CONTR, _CONTR_P, _SCORE; PE_CLADE_LOSS_CONTR, _CONTR_P, _SCORE; PE_CLADE_LOSS_ANC, _ANC_P.

symbols.w_n: the PE weight \(L_n r_n/R_n\) of node \(n\)
symbols.contr_P: divides by the trimmed tree length; the loss and ancestral lists are as in PD_CLADE_LOSS_CONTR

metrics.use: Shows which clades carry a cell's phylogenetic endemism.

metrics.name: Evolutionary distinctiveness (ED, ES, AED lists)
metrics.what: Per label of the neighbourhood that is on the tree, three distinctiveness scores of its tip: ED (fair proportion), ES (equal splits) and AED (abundance-weighted ED) in the lists PHYLO_ED_LIST, PHYLO_ES_LIST, PHYLO_AED_LIST.

symbols.n: the tip and its ancestors on the trimmed tree
symbols.c_a: children of each ancestor on the way up (ES)
symbols.N_n: total samples (basedata-wide, not local) of the labels below \(n\)

metrics.use: ED/ES/AED rank species by how much unique evolutionary history they carry; AED weights by abundance.
refs: Cadotte et al. (2010). Phylogenetic diversity metrics for ecological communities: integrating species richness, abundance and evolutionary history. Ecology Letters 13: 96-105.
Redding & Mooers (2006). Incorporating evolutionary measures into conservation prioritization. Conservation Biology 20: 1670-1678. doi:10.1111/j.1523-1739.2006.00555.x
Isaac et al. (2007). Mammals on the EDGE: conservation priorities based on threat and phylogeny. PLoS ONE 2: e296. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0000296

metrics.name: AED total
metrics.what: Sum over the labels of the neighbourhood of their samples times their AED. The lists PHYLO_AED_T_WTLIST and _P hold each label's term and its proportion.
metrics.use: Corresponds to the phylogenetic diversity of the sampled individuals; see PHYLO_RARITY_CWR.

metrics.name: Corrected weighted phylogenetic rarity
metrics.what: AED total divided by PD: abundance-weighted distinctiveness of the neighbourhood per unit of its PD.
metrics.use: Phylogenetic rarity corrected for tree size, as CWE is for endemism; NaN when PD is 0.

metrics.name: Phylogenetic Sorenson dissimilarity
metrics.what: Sorenson turnover with branch lengths in place of label counts.

symbols.A: total length of the branches shared by the paths of the two sets (PHYLO_A)
symbols.B: length of those only in set 1 (PHYLO_B)
symbols.C: length of those only in set 2 (PHYLO_C); PHYLO_ABC is their sum

metrics.use: Needs two conditions and a tree. Compares what ancestry two cells share, not just the species.
refs: Bryant et al. (2008). Microbes on mountainsides: contrasting elevational patterns of bacterial and plant diversity. PNAS 105: 11505-11511. doi:10.1073/pnas.0801920105

metrics.name: Phylogenetic Jaccard dissimilarity
metrics.what: Jaccard turnover over branch lengths.

symbols.A, B, C: branch length shared, only in set 1, only in set 2

metrics.use: As PHYLO_SORENSON, weighting unshared branches more.

metrics.name: Phylogenetic S2 dissimilarity
metrics.what: S2 turnover over branch lengths.

symbols.A, B, C: branch length shared, only in set 1, only in set 2

metrics.use: Less affected by differences in PD between the cells than Sorenson.

metrics.name: Phylogenetic A, B, C counts
metrics.what: The branch lengths behind the phylogenetic turnover indices: shared (PHYLO_A), only in set 1 (PHYLO_B), only in set 2 (PHYLO_C) and their sum (PHYLO_ABC).
metrics.formula: A = \sum_{b \in P_1 \cap P_2} L_b,\ B = \sum_{b \in P_1 \setminus P_2} L_b,\ C = \sum_{b \in P_2 \setminus P_1} L_b

symbols.P_k: branches on the paths from the labels of set \(k\) to the root

metrics.use: Read to see what the phylogenetic turnover values are made of.

metrics.name: Phylogenetic range-weighted turnover
metrics.what: Range-weighted turnover over branches: each branch counts by its PE weight, so shared restricted-range lineages weigh most (PHYLO_RW_TURNOVER_A, _B, _C are the parts).

symbols.A_w: sum of the PE weights of the branches in both sets (each set's weight added)
symbols.B_w: the weights of the branches only in set 1
symbols.C_w: the weights of the branches only in set 2
symbols.w_b: the PE weight \(L_b r_b/R_b\), with \(r_b\) the local range of the branch in that set

metrics.use: Needs two non-empty sets; NaN otherwise.

metrics.name: Relative phylogenetic diversity, RPD1
metrics.what: PD as a share of the whole tree, divided by the share expected if all the terminals counted equally (labels on the tree over terminals). PHYLO_RPD_NULL1 is the denominator, PHYLO_RPD_DIFF1 the difference scaled to tree length.

symbols.S_{tree}: labels of the neighbourhood on the tree

metrics.use: Above 1 the cell holds more phylogenetic history than its richness predicts, below 1 less. Use RPD2 on trees with zero-length branches.
refs: Mishler et al. (2014). Phylogenetic measures of biodiversity and neo- and paleo-endemism in Australian Acacia. Nature Communications 5: 4473. doi:10.1038/ncomms5473

metrics.name: Relative phylogenetic diversity, RPD2
metrics.what: PD as a share of the tree divided by the same share on a tree with all non-zero branches of equal length.

symbols.k_{PD}: non-zero-length branches in the PD tree of the cell
symbols.k_T: non-zero-length branches in the whole tree; NULL is \(k_{PD}/k_T\) (PHYLO_RPD_NULL2)

metrics.use: Removes the effect of branch lengths, so it tests whether the cell's lineages are long or short relative to the tree's shape.

metrics.name: Relative phylogenetic endemism, RPE1
metrics.what: PE as a share of the trimmed tree divided by the weighted endemism of the labels on the trimmed tree over the number of terminals, the PE of a star tree.

symbols.WE_{trim}: weighted endemism (ENDW_WE) over the labels on the trimmed tree

metrics.use: Tests whether endemism is on long or short branches given the range sizes. Prefer RPE2 when the tree has zero-length branches.
refs: Mishler et al. (2014). Phylogenetic measures of biodiversity and neo- and paleo-endemism in Australian Acacia. Nature Communications 5: 4473. doi:10.1038/ncomms5473

metrics.name: Relative phylogenetic endemism, RPE2
metrics.what: PE as a share of the tree divided by the PE of the same tree with all non-zero branches set to one equal length. The RPE of the CANAPE test.

symbols.\\bar\\ell: mean non-zero branch length of the trimmed tree
symbols.L_{eq}: total length of the equalised tree
symbols.PE_{eq}: the PE of the equalised tree, summed over the groups of the neighbourhood and over the branches of each group; PHYLO_RPE_NULL2 is \(PE_{eq}/L_{eq}\) and PHYLO_RPE_DIFF2 the scaled difference

metrics.use: Above 1 the lineages are longer than expected (palaeo-endemism), below 1 shorter (neo-endemism); significance by randomisation, see CANAPE.
refs: Mishler et al. (2014). Phylogenetic measures of biodiversity and neo- and paleo-endemism in Australian Acacia. Nature Communications 5: 4473. doi:10.1038/ncomms5473

metrics.name: Relative phylogenetic endemism, central
metrics.what: RPE of the central cell: the central PE (PEC_WE_P) against the PE of the equalised tree restricted to the central branches (PHYLO_RPE_NULLC, PHYLO_RPE_DIFFC).

symbols.PE_{eq,C}: the equal-length PE over the central branches with their local ranges

metrics.use: Needs two conditions; equals RPE2 when set 2 adds no branches.

metrics.name: Mean pairwise distance (MPD), variants 1 to 3
metrics.what: Mean of the tree distances between all pairs of labels of the neighbourhood. Variant 1 counts each label once, 2 weights it by its local range (groups holding it), 3 by its samples. Each gives MAX, MEAN, MIN, N, RMSD and VARIANCE (PMPD1_*, PMPD2_*, PMPD3_*).
metrics.formula: MPD = \frac{\sum_{i \ne j} w_i w_j d_{ij}}{\sum_{i \ne j} w_i w_j}

symbols.d_{ij}: path length between the tips of labels \(i, j\) on the tree
symbols.w: the weight of the variant (1, local range or samples)
symbols.\\mathrm{RMSD}: the root of the mean squared distance

metrics.use: Dominated by deep splits; on trees that are not ultrametric the path cache of PhyloCom matters, and values can depend on the order the groups are processed.
refs: Webb et al. (2002). Phylogenies and community ecology. Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 33: 475-505.
Kembel et al. (2010). Picante: R tools for integrating phylogenies and ecology. Bioinformatics 26: 1463-1464.

symbols.\\mathrm{N}: the labels counted with their weights

metrics.use: Emphasises tip clustering; MPD emphasises the deep structure.

metrics.name: Net relatedness index (NRI), variants 1 to 3
metrics.what: The MPD of the neighbourhood standardised by the expected MPD of random draws of the same number of tips from the tree (PHYLO_NRI1, _NRI2, _NRI3 for the weighting variants).

symbols.\\overline{MPD}_{exp}, SD_{exp}: mean and standard deviation of MPD over random sets of \(k\) tips, computed exactly (Tsirogiannis et al.) or sampled with the seed on non-ultrametric trees

metrics.use: Sign is observed minus expected, so it is the negative of Webb's NRI: here negative means clustered. Use `prng_seed` for repeatable values on non-ultrametric trees.
refs: Webb et al. (2002). Phylogenies and community ecology. Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 33: 475-505.
Tsirogiannis et al. (2012). Efficient computation of popular phylogenetic tree measures. Algorithms in Bioinformatics, LNCS 7534: 30-43. doi:10.1007/978-3-642-33122-0_3

metrics.name: Nearest taxon index (NTI), variants 1 to 3
metrics.what: The MNTD of the neighbourhood standardised by its expectation under random tips (PHYLO_NTI1, _NTI2, _NTI3).

symbols.\\overline{MNTD}_{exp}, SD_{exp}: mean and standard deviation of MNTD over random sets of \(k\) tips

metrics.use: Same sign convention as NRI (observed minus expected). Negative means closer relatives than random.
refs: Webb et al. (2002). Phylogenies and community ecology. Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 33: 475-505.

metrics.name: NRI and NTI expected values
metrics.what: The expected mean and standard deviation of MPD (PHYLO_NRI_SAMPLE_MEAN, _SD) and MNTD (PHYLO_NTI_SAMPLE_MEAN, _SD) for the number of labels on the tree, and the sample size (PHYLO_NRI_NTI_SAMPLE_N).

symbols.\\bar d: the mean pairwise distance between all terminals; the other expected values come from the exact formulas of Tsirogiannis et al.
symbols.N_{sample}: the sample size (PHYLO_NRI_NTI_SAMPLE_N), 0 when the values are exact

metrics.use: The reference NRI and NTI are measured against.

metrics.name: Net variance of pairwise distances (net VPD)
metrics.what: The variance of the pairwise distances of the neighbourhood standardised by its expected variance under random tips; PHYLO_NET_VPD_SAMPLE_MEAN, _SD and _N give the expectation.

symbols.VPD_{obs}: variance of the tree distances between label pairs (variant 1, the PMPD1_VARIANCE)
symbols.\\overline{VPD}_{exp}, SD_{exp}: their expectation for \(k\) random tips (sampled with the seed)

metrics.use: Captures unevenness of relatedness rather than its mean; randomness depends on `prng_seed`.

metrics.name: RWiBaLD branch codes
metrics.what: Classifies each branch of the neighbourhood's PD tree against a tree of equal branch lengths: code 0 for branches that are not range-restricted, 1 for shorter than the equalised length, 2 for about equal, 3 for longer. The lists give the codes (RWIBALD_CODES), counts (RWIBALD_CODE_COUNTS), the length differences (RWIBALD_DIFFS, RWIBALD_RR_DIFFS for the range-restricted ones) and the thresholds (RWIBALD_METADATA).

symbols.R_b: branch range; a branch is range-restricted when \(1/R_b\) reaches an elbow threshold of the sorted \(1/R\) values
symbols.d_b: the length difference; codes 1 and 3 are \(d\) at or beyond the negative and positive elbow thresholds of the sorted \(d\)

metrics.use: A branch-level counterpart of RPE; thresholds are found per tree by the elbow rule, so they vary with the data.

metrics.name: Label property statistics
metrics.what: For each label property (set with `set_label_properties`), summary statistics over the labels of the neighbourhood, each label counted once: COUNT, MEAN, MIN, MAX, MEDIAN, SUM, SKEWNESS, KURTOSIS, SD, IQR (keys PROP_MEAN etc.). The _abc2 version weights each label by its local range.

symbols.x_l: the property value of label \(l\); values that are not numbers are dropped

metrics.use: To summarise traits, body mass, threat scores per cell. Needs label properties set on the basedata.

metrics.name: Getis-Ord Gi* of label properties
metrics.what: Z-score of the sum of a label property over the neighbourhood against its global mean and spread; positive when the neighbourhood holds unusually high values (LBPROP_GISTAR_LIST per property; the _abc2 version weights labels by range).

symbols.x_l: property of label \(l\) in the neighbourhood
symbols.n: the number of labels in the basedata (weights summed)
symbols.\\bar x, s: the global mean and standard deviation, with weight 1 (or the label range for abc2)

metrics.use: Uses the labels, not the groups, as the units, so it is a hotspot measure of trait values rather than of space. Undefined when \(w=0\).
refs: Getis & Ord (1992). The analysis of spatial association by use of distance statistics. Geographical Analysis 24: 189-206. doi:10.1111/j.1538-4632.1992.tb00261.x

metrics.name: Group property statistics
metrics.what: The same statistics as LBPROP_STATS for group properties over the groups of the neighbourhood (COUNT, MEAN, MIN, MAX, MEDIAN, SUM, SD, IQR), quantiles (GPPROP_QUANTILE_LIST, keys GPPROP_STATS_PROP_Q05 ...) and Gi* (GPPROP_GISTAR_LIST).
metrics.formula: \bar x = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} x_g,\quad G^* = \frac{\sum_g x_g - |G|\bar x_{glob}}{s\sqrt{\dfrac{n|G| - |G|^2}{n-1}}}
metrics.use: To summarise a cell attribute (elevation, rainfall) over the neighbourhood; Gi* marks hot and cold spots.

metrics.name: Numeric label statistics
metrics.what: When the labels themselves are numbers (for example sizes), the weighted statistics of the label values, each weighted by its sample count: N, MEAN, SD, MIN, MAX, RANGE, CV, SKEW, KURT (NUM_*). Geometric and harmonic means come from numeric_label_other_means (NUM_GMEAN, NUM_HMEAN).
metrics.formula: CV = \frac{s}{\bar x},\quad \bar x = \frac{\sum_l n_l x_l}{\sum_l n_l}

symbols.n_l: its samples in the neighbourhood; skewness needs N > 2 and kurtosis N > 3

metrics.use: For data where the label is a measurement (a size class, an altitude). Not for names such as species codes.

symbols.x_{(i)}: the sorted numeric labels of group \(g\) (at least two labels)
symbols.n_l: samples of a label; each label with \(n_l > 1\) adds \(n_l - 1\) zero intervals

metrics.use: From BiodiverseX; for time-stamped or ordered labels. The geometric mean is NaN if any interval is negative.

metrics.name: Numeric label dissimilarity between two sets
metrics.what: Weighted mean absolute difference (NUMD_ABSMEAN) and mean squared difference (NUMD_VARIANCE) between the numeric labels of set 1 and those of set 2, over all pairs weighted by their samples; NUMD_COUNT is the weight total.
metrics.formula: ABSMEAN = \frac{\sum_{i,j} a_i b_j |x_i - y_j|}{\sum_{i,j} a_i b_j},\quad VAR = \frac{\sum_{i,j} a_i b_j (x_i - y_j)^2}{\sum_{i,j} a_i b_j}

symbols.x_i, y_j: numeric labels of set 1 and set 2
symbols.VAR: the mean square, not a variance about the mean difference (NUMD_VARIANCE)

metrics.use: Needs two conditions; compares the value distributions of two neighbourhoods (for example cell against surroundings).

metrics.name: Matrix statistics
metrics.what: Statistics of the values of a label matrix (distances, similarities) over the pairs of labels in the neighbourhood, diagonal included: N, MEAN, MEDIAN, SD, MIN, MAX, RANGE, SKEW, KURT, and the 5, 25, 75, 95 percent quantiles (MX_*). MX_LABELS and MX_VALUES list the labels and values.

symbols.v_{ij}: the matrix value of labels \(i, j\) of the neighbourhood that are in the matrix

metrics.use: Needs `matrix=` (for example functional or genetic distances). Labels outside the matrix are ignored.
