metrics.name: Matrix comparison of two sets
metrics.what: Mean (MXD_MEAN) and mean square (MXD_VARIANCE) of the matrix values between each label of set 1 and each label of set 2, with MXD_COUNT pairs; MXD_LIST1 and MXD_LIST2 hold the labels used.
metrics.formula: MXD = \frac{1}{|A||B|}\sum_{i \in A}\sum_{j \in B} v_{ij},\quad MXD_{var} = \frac{1}{|A||B|}\sum v_{ij}^2

symbols.A: the labels of set 1 that are in the matrix
symbols.B: the labels of set 2 that are in the matrix
symbols.v_{ij}: the matrix value; a missing pair or \(i = j\) counts 0. MXD_VARIANCE is the mean square, not a variance

metrics.use: Needs two conditions and a matrix: the mean distance between the species of a cell and those of its neighbours.

metrics.name: Rao quadratic entropy from a matrix
metrics.what: Rao's quadratic entropy with the pairwise distances taken from a label matrix; MX_RAO_TN is the number of pairs counted (n squared) and MX_RAO_TLABELS the label proportions.
metrics.formula: Q = \sum_{i \le j} 2\, v_{ij}\, p_i p_j,\quad p_i = 1/n

symbols.n: labels of the neighbourhood that are in the matrix
symbols.p_i: \(1/n\), as presence only; the sum includes \(i=j\) with the factor 2, so the diagonal values count double

metrics.use: Needs `matrix=`. Presence-only (label weights are 1/n); with a zero diagonal it equals the usual quadratic entropy of equal proportions.
refs: Rao (1982). Diversity and dissimilarity coefficients: a unified approach. Theoretical Population Biology 21: 24-43.

metrics.name: P-rank of an index (randomisation)
metrics.what: Where the observed index lies among its randomised values. High (near 1) means the observed value is larger than most random ones, low means smaller.

symbols.C: number of randomisations in which the observed value exceeds the random one (by more than a tolerance)
symbols.Q: comparisons made (those with both values defined)

metrics.use: The significance test of Biodiverse: rank above 0.95 or below 0.05 for a two-tailed 10% test. Counts, p-ranks and z-scores come from `randomise(...)` on a SpatialResult; they are not calculations to list in the analysis.
metrics.python: rn = tf.bio.randomise(tf.bio.spatial_analysis(bd, C, ["pe", "phylo_rpe2"], tree=tree), "rand_structured", iterations=99, seed=1); rn.p_rank().loc[G]

metrics.name: Z-score of an index (randomisation)
metrics.what: Observed index minus the mean of the randomised values, over their standard deviation (the population form, divided by Q).

symbols.Q: their number; z is 0 when they do not vary

metrics.use: Complements the p-rank when the null distribution is roughly normal; `rn.comparison()` also gives the counters C, T, Q, P, SUMX, SUMXX.
metrics.python: rn = tf.bio.randomise(tf.bio.spatial_analysis(bd, C, ["pe", "phylo_rpe2"], tree=tree), "rand_structured", iterations=99, seed=1); rn.z_scores().loc[G]

metrics.name: CANAPE categories
metrics.what: Categorical analysis of neo- and palaeo-endemism: each cell is classed from the p-ranks of PE, the PE of the equalised tree (the null PE) and RPE as not significant (0), neo-endemism (1), palaeo-endemism (2), mixed (3) or super (4); also as indicator columns NEO, PALAEO, MIXED, SUPER.
metrics.formula: code = \begin{cases} 0 & p_{PE} \le 0.95 \ \wedge\ p_{null} \le 0.95\\ 1 & p_{RPE} < 0.025\\ 2 & p_{RPE} > 0.975\\ 4 & p_{PE} > 0.99 \ \wedge\ p_{null} > 0.99\\ 3 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}

symbols.p: the p-ranks (missing counted 0.5) of PE_WE, PHYLO_RPE_NULL2 and PHYLO_RPE2 (the diff variant uses PHYLO_RPE_DIFF2; `central=True` uses PEC_WE, PHYLO_RPE_NULLC, PHYLO_RPEC). Tests are applied in the order shown.

metrics.use: Needs `pe` and `phylo_rpe2` in the analysis and randomisations (use rand_structured). Palaeo cells are rich in long-branch endemics, neo cells in short-branch ones.
refs: Mishler et al. (2014). Phylogenetic measures of biodiversity and neo- and paleo-endemism in Australian Acacia. Nature Communications 5: 4473. doi:10.1038/ncomms5473

families.title: Terrain and hydrology
families.source: spatialEco (R), terra::terrain, GRASS r.geomorphon, WhiteboxTools, InVEST, riverconn (R), hydrographr (R)
families.intro:
Indices computed cell by cell from an elevation model (DEM): slope and aspect, ruggedness, topographic position,
curvature, landforms, the hydrological indices that combine the slope with the area that drains through a cell, and the
connectivity of rivers. They need no classification: every cell gets a value, and the metrics of the
[surface family](../surface-metrics/) (roughness, texture) are the ones that describe a whole surface.

The cards show their values on the SRTM elevation of south-western Oregon that ships with the library, put on a 30 m grid
in UTM zone 10N (369 x 270 cells, 440 to 1388 m), and, for the hydrological indices, the same DEM with its depressions
filled. A value on a card is the mean and the range of the raster the call returns. The two dendritic connectivity
indices have no river in the example, so their cards use the three-cell toy river of the library's own documentation.
Cells at the edge of the raster, or whose window reaches a missing cell, have no value. Windows are odd numbers of cells,
heights are in metres and slopes in degrees unless the card says otherwise.
families.example:
import numpy as np
import xarray as xr
import terraflux as tf

# SRTM elevation of south-western Oregon on a 30 m grid in UTM zone 10N (369 x 270 cells)
dem0 = tf.load_raster(tf.surface.example_data("orelevation"))
grid = xr.DataArray(np.zeros((369, 270)), dims=("y", "x"),
                    coords={"y": 4771920 - 15 - 30 * np.arange(369), "x": 500010 + 15 + 30 * np.arange(270)})
dem = tf.reproject(dem0, like=grid.rio.write_crs("EPSG:32610"), resampling="bilinear")

filled = tf.hydro.fill(dem)                           # depressions filled, for the hydrological indices
acc = tf.hydro.flow_accumulation(filled)              # D8 accumulation, in cells
rivers = tf.hydro.streams(acc, 500)                   # the cells that drain at least 500 cells
link_map, links = tf.hydro.stream_links(filled, rivers)

# the NDVI of the same area, as an illustrative cover weight (a USLE C factor) for the connectivity index
ndvi = tf.reproject(tf.load_raster(tf.surface.example_data("orforest")), like=grid.rio.write_crs("EPSG:32610"),
                    resampling="bilinear")
cover = xr.where(ndvi > 0.55, 0.003, 0.05)

metrics.name: Slope
metrics.what:
The steepness of the ground at a cell: the angle of steepest descent, from the elevations of the 3 x 3 window around
it.

symbols.\\partial z / \\partial x: Horn's derivative along the row, \([(z_3+2z_6+z_9)-(z_1+2z_4+z_7)]/(8\,\Delta x)\), for the window \(z_1 \dots z_9\) read row by row from the top left
symbols.\\partial z / \\partial y: Horn's derivative down the column, \([(z_7+2z_8+z_9)-(z_1+2z_2+z_3)]/(8\,\Delta y)\)

metrics.use:
The same as `terra::terrain`. The edge cells have no value. Slope depends on the cell size: the same hill is steeper on
a fine DEM than on a coarse one. On longitude/latitude rasters the cell sizes are in metres (geodesics on WGS84) and
the elevation must be in metres.
refs: Horn, B. K. P. (1981). Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE, 69(1), 14-47.
metrics.value: a map: mean 18.07, from 0.1181 to 58.2; 1274 cells without a value

metrics.name: Aspect
metrics.what: The compass direction that the slope faces, clockwise from north: 0 north, 90 east, 180 south, 270 west.

symbols.\\partial z / \\partial y: Horn's derivative toward the north (the window of Slope with the sign of its rows reversed)
symbols.\\alpha: the downhill direction clockwise from north; a surface rising to the east gives 270, one rising to the south gives 0

metrics.use:
Aspect is circular (359 and 1 are neighbours): do not average it or use it in a regression as it is. Use the
transformed aspect (TRASP), the heat load index, or its sine and cosine. A flat cell (both derivatives 0) gets 90, not
a missing value.
refs: Horn, B. K. P. (1981). Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE, 69(1), 14-47.
metrics.value: a map: mean 178, from 0.003801 to 360; 1274 cells without a value

metrics.name: Transformed aspect (TRASP)
metrics.what:
Aspect folded into a number from 0 on the cool, wet north-north-east slopes to 1 on the hot, dry south-south-west
ones, so that it can enter a linear model.

symbols.\\alpha: the aspect in degrees, clockwise from north (Horn, 3 x 3 window, 8 neighbours)

metrics.use:
It ignores the slope: a flat cell still gets a value from a meaningless aspect. Combine it with the slope, or use the
heat load index, which includes both.
refs: Roberts, D. W., & Cooper, S. V. (1989). Concepts and techniques of vegetation mapping. In Land classifications based on vegetation: applications for resource management (pp. 90-96). USDA Forest Service General Technical Report INT-257.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.5458, from 0.0000000023 to 1; 1274 cells without a value

metrics.name: Heat load index (HLI)
metrics.unit: ln(MJ cm-2 yr-1), or MJ cm-2 yr-1 with scaled=True
metrics.range: about -1.7 to 0.1 (log scale) on the example
metrics.what:
The potential annual direct radiation that a slope receives given its steepness, its orientation and the latitude, after
McCune and Keon. In the northern hemisphere it is highest on south-west slopes.
metrics.formula: \ln H = -1.467 + 1.582 \cos L \cos S - 1.5 \cos A \sin S \sin L - 0.262 \sin L \sin S + 0.607 \sin A \sin S

symbols.A: the aspect \(\alpha\) folded about the north-east to south-west line, \(|\pi - |\alpha - 5\pi/4||\) (with `direct=True` about north-south, \(\pi - |\alpha - \pi|\); in the southern hemisphere about north-west to south-east, with the absolute latitude)

metrics.use:
The latitude is that of the centre of the raster unless you give it, so give it for rasters of large extent.
`equation=2` and `3` use other coefficients (3 for latitudes of 30 to 60 degrees). spatialEco has errors in the
southern hemisphere branch, which Terraflux corrects.
refs: McCune, B., & Keon, D. (2002). Equations for potential annual direct incident radiation and heat load. Journal of Vegetation Science, 13(4), 603-606.
metrics.value: a map: mean -0.2838, from -1.68 to 0.06991; 1274 cells without a value

metrics.name: Terrain ruggedness index (TRI)
metrics.unit: the unit of the elevation (here m)
metrics.what:
How much the heights in a window differ from the central cell: the square root of the summed squared differences, so a
flat surface has 0 and a pit or a peak a high value.

symbols.z_0: the elevation of the central cell
symbols.z_i: the elevations of the other cells of the window (3 x 3 by default) that have a value, so the edge cells get a value from the cells they have

metrics.use:
This is the original of Riley et al. (the root of the sum of squares). It grows with the size of the window and does
not subtract the slope: a smooth steep plane has a high TRI. For a roughness that ignores steepness use the vector
ruggedness measure.
refs: Riley, S. J., DeGloria, S. D., & Elliot, R. (1999). A terrain ruggedness index that quantifies topographic heterogeneity. Intermountain Journal of Sciences, 5(1-4), 23-27.

metrics.name: Vector ruggedness measure (VRM)
metrics.what:
Ruggedness as the scatter of the surface normals in a window: 0 for a plane however steep, towards 1 where the ground
faces many directions. It separates roughness from steepness.

symbols.x_i, y_i, z_i: the unit normal of cell \(i\) of the window, \(x_i=\sin\alpha_i\sin\beta_i\), \(y_i=\cos\alpha_i\sin\beta_i\), \(z_i=\cos\beta_i\), from its aspect \(\alpha_i\) and slope \(\beta_i\) (Horn)
symbols.n: the number of cells of the window (3 x 3 by default)

metrics.use:
The normals need the slope and the aspect of every cell, so the window loses one more ring of cells at the edge than
TRI. Values are small on gentle terrain (mean 0.006 on the example).
refs: Sappington, J. M., Longshore, K. M., & Thompson, D. B. (2007). Quantifying landscape ruggedness for animal habitat analysis: a case study using bighorn sheep in the Mojave Desert. Journal of Wildlife Management, 71(5), 1419-1426.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.005678, from 0.00001502 to 0.1031; 2540 cells without a value

metrics.name: Surface relief ratio (SRR)
metrics.what:
Where the mean elevation of a window lies between its lowest and its highest point: the hypsometric shape of the
relief. A low value means that most of the area is near the bottom.

symbols.\\bar z: the mean elevation of the window (5 x 5 cells by default)
symbols.z_{\\min}, z_{\\max}: the lowest and the highest elevation of the window

metrics.use: NA where the window is flat (maximum equal to minimum). It describes the shape of the relief, not its size.
refs: Pike, R. J., & Wilson, S. E. (1971). Elevation-relief ratio, hypsometric integral, and geomorphic area-altitude analysis. Geological Society of America Bulletin, 82(4), 1079-1084.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.5019, from 0.1661 to 0.8628; 2540 cells without a value

metrics.name: Dissection (Martonne)
metrics.what:
The position of the central cell between the lowest and the highest elevation of its window: 0 at the lowest, 1 at the
highest.

symbols.z_0: the elevation of the central cell
symbols.z_{\\min}, z_{\\max}: the lowest and the highest elevation of the window (5 x 5 by default)

metrics.use:
It is the value of the cell, not the window mean (as in SRR); it behaves like an elevation rescaled in the window and
reads as a relative height. NA on a flat window.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.5029, from 0 to 1; 2540 cells without a value

metrics.name: Spherical standard deviation (terrain heterogeneity)
metrics.what:
The spread of the surface normals in a window as a spherical standard deviation: 0 where all normals point the same
way (a plane), larger where the slope and the aspect change.

symbols.\\mathbf{n}_i: the unit normal of cell \(i\) of the window, from its aspect and slope (see VRM)
symbols.n: the number of cells of the window (3 x 3 by default)
symbols.R: the length of the mean normal; with `variance=True` the value is \(1 - R^2\), without the root

metrics.use:
Built from the same normals as VRM, which measures 1 - R instead of the root of 1 - R squared; the two rank the cells
almost alike, so use one of them.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.09473, from 0.00548 to 0.4421; 2540 cells without a value

metrics.name: Topographic position index (TPI)
metrics.unit: the unit of the elevation (here m)
metrics.range: any real number; 0 on a flat or an even slope
metrics.what:
The elevation of a cell minus the mean elevation of a window around it: positive on ridges and hilltops, negative in
valleys and hollows, about zero on flats and even slopes.

symbols.\\bar z_W: the mean elevation of the window \(W\) around the cell, which includes it (a square of 3 cells by default)

metrics.use:
The scale decides what you see: a small window picks out gullies and bumps, a large one valleys and mountains, so
report it. Cells whose window reaches the edge or a missing cell have no value. With `win="circle"` the scale is a
radius in map units; `normalize=True` divides the value by the standard deviation of the window.
refs: Weiss, A. D. (2001). Topographic position and landforms analysis. Poster, ESRI International User Conference, San Diego.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.008564, from -23.96 to 26.11; 2540 cells without a value

metrics.name: Hierarchical slope position (HSP)
metrics.range: any real number, or 0 to 1 with normalize=True
metrics.what:
The position on the slope across several scales at once: the standardised topographic position summed over a series of
window sizes.

symbols.\\mathrm{TPI}_k: the topographic position index at scale \(k\), with window sides 3, 7, 11, ... up to 27 by default (`min_scale`, `inc`, `max_scale`)
symbols.\\mu_k, \\sigma_k: its mean and standard deviation over the whole raster

metrics.use:
The z-scores use the whole raster, so the value of a cell depends on the extent you process. spatialEco computes the
TPI minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation, by operator precedence and not as a z-score; Terraflux
computes the z-score.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.5266, from 0 to 1; 6290 cells without a value

metrics.name: Planform curvature
metrics.range: any real number; negative on concave (converging) ground, positive on convex
metrics.what:
The curvature of the ground across the slope, perpendicular to the direction of steepest descent: positive on spurs,
where flow diverges, and negative in hollows, where it converges.
metrics.formula: C_{\mathrm{plan}} = -\frac{q^2 r - 2pqs + p^2 t}{(p^2 + q^2) \sqrt{1 + p^2 + q^2}}

symbols.p, q: Zevenbergen and Thorne's first derivatives of the window \(z_1 \dots z_9\): \(p=(z_6-z_4)/2L_x\), \(q=(z_2-z_8)/2L_y\)

metrics.use:
No value on flat cells (p = q = 0) or on the edge. Use a projected raster. spatialEco halves the second derivatives,
pads the edges with 0 and rounds to 6 decimals; Terraflux does none of that, so its values differ from spatialEco's.
refs: Zevenbergen, L. W., & Thorne, C. R. (1987). Quantitative analysis of land surface topography. Earth Surface Processes and Landforms, 12(1), 47-56.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.00004045, from -0.03188 to 0.02263; 1274 cells without a value

metrics.name: Profile curvature
metrics.range: any real number; negative on concave, positive on convex ground
metrics.what:
The curvature of the ground along the direction of steepest descent: positive where the slope steepens away from a
crest, negative where it flattens toward a foot. It controls whether flow speeds up or slows down.

symbols.p, q, r, s, t: Zevenbergen and Thorne's derivatives of the 3 x 3 window (see planform curvature)

metrics.use:
As for planform curvature, no value on flat cells and on the edge, and spatialEco's halving and rounding are not
reproduced. Check the sign on a known shape before comparing with other software: here a dome is positive and a bowl
negative.
refs: Zevenbergen, L. W., & Thorne, C. R. (1987). Quantitative analysis of land surface topography. Earth Surface Processes and Landforms, 12(1), 47-56.
metrics.value: a map: mean -0.00003844, from -0.02988 to 0.02059; 1274 cells without a value

metrics.name: Total curvature
metrics.range: any real number; positive on convex, negative on concave ground
metrics.what: The sum of the planform and the profile curvatures: one number for how convex or concave the ground is at a cell.
metrics.use:
It is the sum of the two curvatures above, as spatialEco defines it, not the Laplacian of the surface. Flat cells and
the edge have no value.
refs: Zevenbergen, L. W., & Thorne, C. R. (1987). Quantitative analysis of land surface topography. Earth Surface Processes and Landforms, 12(1), 47-56.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.000002008, from -0.03743 to 0.03583; 1274 cells without a value

metrics.name: McNab curvature
metrics.what:
How much a cell stands above or below its eight neighbours: the mean difference to them, divided by the largest such
mean difference on the raster, so that the most convex cell is 1.

symbols.z_j: the elevations of its neighbours that have a value (the sum is still divided by 8)
symbols.denominator: the largest numerator over the whole raster

metrics.name: Bolstad curvature
metrics.range: any real number; positive on convex ground
metrics.what: The difference between a cell and the mean of its 3 x 3 window, scaled by the cell width: a simple local convexity.

symbols.\\bar z_{3 \\times 3}: the mean of its 3 x 3 window, the cell included
symbols.L_x: the cell width in map units

metrics.use:
The factors 10000 and 1000 are those of the spatialEco code, which fails on this option; Terraflux gives the same
formula as intended. The result is in odd units, so compare cells within one raster only.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.0001391, from -3.394 to 3.63; 1274 cells without a value

metrics.name: Geomorphons (landforms)
metrics.what:
The landform of each cell, from its lines of sight in the 8 compass directions up to a search radius: the numbers of
directions that look up (higher) and down (lower) name the form. Unlike the slope or the curvature it sees the
terrain at the scale of the search radius.

symbols.n_{+}, n_{-}: the numbers of the 8 directions that are higher and lower than the cell. In each direction, from \(skip+1\) cells away while the distance is below the search distance (the search in cells times the cell size), the highest elevation angle (zenith) and the lowest (nadir) are found. With the default comparison, the direction is level if neither \(|\text{zenith}|\) nor \(|\text{nadir}|\) exceeds the flatness threshold (`flat`, 1 degree), otherwise higher if \(|\text{nadir}| < |\text{zenith}|\) and lower if it is greater. A direction whose first neighbour is missing or off the raster counts as neither

metrics.use:
The result depends on the search radius (`search`, in cells; 3 by default) and on the flatness threshold: record both
and test several radii. It needs a projected DEM. The result also holds a table `share` of the cells per form, and
`measures=True` adds intensity, exposition, range, variance, elongation, azimuth, extend and width. It is a port of
GRASS r.geomorphon 8.4 with four of its errors corrected.
refs: Jasiewicz, J., & Stepinski, T. F. (2013). Geomorphons - a pattern recognition approach to classification and mapping of landforms. Geomorphology, 182, 147-156.

metrics.name: Flow accumulation
metrics.unit: cells, or area (map units squared), or specific contributing area (map units)
metrics.what:
The area that drains through each cell, the cell itself included: the basis of every drainage index. D8 sends all of a
cell to its steepest neighbour; the multiple-flow methods split it among the lower neighbours.
formula:
A_i = w_i + \sum_{j \to i} p_{ji}\, A_j
a = \frac{A \,\Delta x\, \Delta y}{(\Delta x + \Delta y)/2}

symbols.w_i: the contribution of the cell itself (1, or a weight raster)
symbols.p_{ji}: the share of the flow of cell \(j\) that goes to \(i\), which is 1 for the steepest neighbour with `d8` and proportional to the slope to the power 1.1 with `fd8` (D-infinity, Quinn and `mfd` split it differently)
symbols.a: the specific contributing area (`units="sca"`), the area per unit contour width

metrics.use:
Best on a DEM with its depressions filled (`tf.hydro.fill`). D8 draws artificial parallel lines on hillslopes; the
multiple-flow methods avoid them and are the default for the wetness indices.
refs: O'Callaghan, J. F., & Mark, D. M. (1984). The extraction of drainage networks from digital elevation data. Computer Vision, Graphics, and Image Processing, 28(3), 323-344.
Freeman, T. G. (1991). Calculating catchment area with divergent flow based on a rectangular grid. Computers & Geosciences, 17(3), 413-422.
Tarboton, D. G. (1997). A new method for the determination of flow directions and upslope areas in grid digital elevation models. Water Resources Research, 33(2), 309-319.

metrics.name: Topographic wetness index (TWI)
metrics.unit: none (log of m2 per m per tangent)
metrics.what:
High where much area drains through a gentle slope (valley floors, hollows, flats) and low on steep ridges: a proxy for
soil moisture and saturation.

symbols.a: the specific contributing area, the area draining through a cell per unit of contour width (from the FD8 accumulation by default, exponent 1.1)
symbols.\\tan\\beta: the tangent of the slope from Horn's gradient (a missing neighbour takes the value of the cell itself); with `min_slope` it has a floor, for instance 0.001, so that flat cells get a finite value

metrics.use:
There is no value where the slope is exactly 0 unless you give `min_slope` (as WhiteboxTools does): the flat floors of
filled depressions are empty. The DEM should have its depressions filled. The value depends on the accumulation
method, so record it.
refs: Beven, K. J., & Kirkby, M. J. (1979). A physically based, variable contributing area model of basin hydrology. Hydrological Sciences Bulletin, 24(1), 43-69.
metrics.value: a map: mean 6.834, from 3.844 to 19.04; 155 cells without a value

metrics.name: Stream power index (SPI)
metrics.unit: m2 per m (specific area times tangent)
metrics.what:
The erosive power of overland flow: large where much water drains and the slope is steep, as in gullies and at channel
heads.

symbols.\\tan\\beta: the tangent of the slope (see TWI)

metrics.use:
Heavy-tailed (median 69, maximum 4.4 x 10^5 on the example), so map it on a log scale or take the logarithm. It is zero
on flat cells.
refs: Moore, I. D., Grayson, R. B., & Ladson, A. R. (1991). Digital terrain modelling: a review of hydrological, geomorphological, and biological applications. Hydrological Processes, 5(1), 3-30.

metrics.name: Sediment transport index (STI)
metrics.what:
The capacity of flow to carry sediment, the LS factor of the USLE written from the contributing area: large on long,
steep, convergent slopes.

symbols.22.13, 0.0896: the length (m) and the slope (9 %) of the USLE reference plot

metrics.use:
Compare it with the RUSLE LS factor only with the same exponents. Heavy-tailed (median 17.8, maximum 664 on the
example).
refs: Moore, I. D., & Burch, G. J. (1986). Physical basis of the length-slope factor in the Universal Soil Loss Equation. Soil Science Society of America Journal, 50(5), 1294-1298.

metrics.name: Height above the nearest drainage (HAND)
metrics.unit: the unit of the elevation (here m)
metrics.what:
The height of each cell above the stream cell where its water reaches the drainage, following the D8 directions
downhill: 0 on the streams, small on floodplains and valley floors, large on hilltops. A terrain descriptor of soil
water and flood susceptibility, developed at INPE.

symbols.s(i): the first stream cell reached from \(i\) along the D8 flow path; the streams are given as a raster or as the cells with D8 accumulation at or above `threshold`

metrics.use:
It depends on what you call a stream, so record the threshold. The DEM needs its depressions filled; cells that reach
no stream have no value.
refs: Rennó, C. D., Nobre, A. D., Cuartas, L. A., Soares, J. V., Hodnett, M. G., Tomasella, J., & Waterloo, M. J. (2008). HAND, a new terrain descriptor using SRTM-DEM: mapping terra-firme rainforest environments in Amazonia. Remote Sensing of Environment, 112(9), 3469-3481.

Nobre, A. D., Cuartas, L. A., Hodnett, M., Rennó, C. D., Rodrigues, G., Silveira, A., Waterloo, M., & Saleska, S. (2011). Height Above the Nearest Drainage - a hydrologically relevant new terrain model. Journal of Hydrology, 404(1-2), 13-29.
metrics.value: a map: mean 118, from 0 to 441.7; 4976 cells without a value

metrics.name: Distance to channel (flow path length)
metrics.unit: cell lengths (or the units of the weights)
metrics.what:
The mean distance that water travels from a cell to a stream along the multiple flow directions of pygeoprocessing,
as InVEST's sediment model measures its downslope component.
metrics.formula: d_i = \sum_k p_{ik} \left( d_k + \ell_{ik} \right), \qquad d_i = 0 \text{ on streams}

symbols.p_{ik}: the share of the flow of cell \(i\) that goes to its neighbour \(k\) (only flow that reaches a stream counts)
symbols.\\ell_{ik}: the step, 1 for a side, \(\sqrt{2}\) for a diagonal, or the value of the weight raster at the cell stepped onto

metrics.use:
No value where no flow reaches a stream. The unit is the cell length, so multiply by the cell size for metres. It needs
the streams raster (1 on the streams) and a filled DEM.
metrics.value: a map: mean 19.66, from 0 to 76.92; 1908 cells without a value

metrics.name: Index of connectivity (IC)
metrics.what:
How well each cell is connected to the streams for sediment: the upslope component (how much material is produced above
it, and how fast) over the downslope component (how much impedes it on the way to a stream).

symbols.\\bar W, \\bar S: the weight and the slope (in m/m) averaged over the contributing area \(A\) of the cell (accumulation times cell area)
symbols.W_i, S_i: the weight and the slope of each cell \(i\) on the flow path down to a stream
symbols.W: usually the USLE C factor of the land cover

metrics.use:
There is no value on the streams or where the flow reaches none. It is a relative index: compare cells of one run. It
needs a weight raster on the DEM grid (here two illustrative C factors by cover) and the streams or a `threshold` of
accumulation. InVEST's way is followed: the DEM is filled and routed by pygeoprocessing (multiple flow or D8), the
slopes are kept between 0.005 and 1, the weights from 0.001 up, and the step weights are those of the cell stepped
onto.
refs: Borselli, L., Cassi, P., & Torri, D. (2008). Prolegomena to sediment and flow connectivity in the landscape: a GIS and field numerical assessment. Catena, 75(3), 268-277.
Cavalli, M., Trevisani, S., Comiti, F., & Marchi, L. (2013). Geomorphometric assessment of spatial sediment connectivity in small Alpine catchments. Geomorphology, 188, 31-41.
metrics.value: a map: mean -5.477, from -8.547 to -1.716; 4949 cells without a value

metrics.name: Dendritic connectivity index, potamodromous (DCI p)
metrics.what:
The chance that a fish placed at random in the river network can reach another random point of it, with the barriers
(dams, weirs, culverts) cutting the network into segments.

symbols.i, j: the segments, the stretches of river between barriers
symbols.w_i: the weight of a segment, its length (or its length times the habitat raster)
symbols.W: the weight of the whole network
symbols.c_{ij}: the product of the passabilities (0 to 1) of the barriers on the way between segments \(i\) and \(j\), with \(c_{ii} = 1\); with `direction="symmetric"` each barrier counts as the product of its up and down passabilities, `"asymmetric"` uses the one of the direction of travel

metrics.use:
One row per network with barriers. The barriers are moved onto the streams (`snap`). The card is run on the library's toy
river of three cells with one barrier of passability 0.5 in the middle: segments of 2 and 1 cells give
(2^2 + 1^2 + 2 x 2 x 1 x 0.25) / 3^2 = 66.67 %. The DEM of the example has too few barriers to show.
refs: Cote, D., Kehler, D. G., Bourne, C., & Wiersma, Y. F. (2009). A new measure of longitudinal connectivity for stream networks. Landscape Ecology, 24(1), 101-113.
metrics.python:
dem3 = np.array([[5, 4, 5], [5, 3, 5], [5, 2, 5], [5, 1, 5]], float)
toy = tf.hydro.streams(tf.hydro.flow_accumulation(dem3), 2)
tf.hydro.dci(dem3, toy, [(1.5, 1.5)], passability=0.5).table.dci_p

metrics.name: Dendritic connectivity index, diadromous (DCI d)
metrics.what:
The chance that a fish that enters the network at its mouth can reach a random point of it: connectivity for species
that migrate between the sea (or the main river) and the headwaters.

symbols.m: the segment at the mouth of the network
symbols.c_{mj}: the product of the passabilities of the barriers between the mouth and segment \(j\)
symbols.W: the weight of the network (see DCI p)

metrics.use:
Read it with the potamodromous index. The barriers table of `tf.hydro.dci` also gives, for every barrier, `d_index` (the
percent that DCI p of its network grows if the barrier is removed) and a `rank`, to decide which barrier to remove first.
The card is run on the toy river of DCI p.
refs: Cote, D., Kehler, D. G., Bourne, C., & Wiersma, Y. F. (2009). A new measure of longitudinal connectivity for stream networks. Landscape Ecology, 24(1), 101-113.
metrics.python:
dem3 = np.array([[5, 4, 5], [5, 3, 5], [5, 2, 5], [5, 1, 5]], float)
toy = tf.hydro.streams(tf.hydro.flow_accumulation(dem3), 2)
tf.hydro.dci(dem3, toy, [(1.5, 1.5)], passability=0.5).table.dci_d

metrics.name: Stream magnitude (Shreve)
metrics.what:
The number of headwater links upstream of a stretch of river, itself included if it is a headwater: a measure of the size
of the network above it.

symbols.v: a link of the stream network, the stretch between sources, junctions and outlets

metrics.use:
It is the column `magnitude` of `tf.hydro.centrality` (on the links table of `tf.hydro.stream_links`), with `upstream`
(the number of links flowing in), `degree` and `upstream_length` (the summed length of the link and all above it). The
card shows its summary over the links of the example.
refs: Shreve, R. L. (1966). Statistical law of stream numbers. Journal of Geology, 74(1), 17-37.

metrics.name: Link betweenness
metrics.what:
The number of pairs of other links whose path in the network goes through this link: how much a stretch of river lies in
the way between the parts of the network.

symbols.k: a branch left when the network is cut at link \(v\), one per link flowing in and the rest of the network below it
symbols.s_k: the number of links of branch \(k\); the formula counts the pairs of links in different branches

metrics.use:
The column `betweenness` of `tf.hydro.centrality`. High values mark the stretches that a dam would cut into large parts.
There are no weights, only the topology of the links. The card shows its summary over the links of the example.

metrics.name: Link closeness
metrics.what:
The inverse of the summed number of steps from a link to all other links of its network: high for central links and low
for those on the periphery.

symbols.d(v, u): the number of steps along the network between the links \(v\) and \(u\) (links crossed from one to the other)
symbols.u: every other link in the same network

metrics.use:
The column `closeness` of `tf.hydro.centrality`, not normalised by the size of the network, so networks of different
sizes are not comparable. The card shows its summary over the links of the example.

families.title: Connectivity
families.source: Conefor Sensinode (Saura & Torne 2009; Saura & Pascual-Hortal 2007; Pascual-Hortal & Saura 2006) and Makurhini (MK_dPCIIC, MK_dECA, MK_RMCentrality, MK_Focal_nodes, MK_ProtConn)
families.intro:
Indices of a habitat graph: the nodes are habitat patches with an attribute (usually the area) and the links join patches
that are close enough for the species to disperse between them. They are the measures of the
[habitat networks tutorials](../../tutorials/habitat-networks/connectivity-as-a-graph/), and of Conefor Sensinode and
Makurhini.

The cards show their values on the forests (CORINE classes 23, 24 and 25) of the 50 x 50 km excerpt around Lake Steinhude
and Hannover, Lower Saxony, that those tutorials use, on 100 m cells: `net` is the graph of its 154 forest patches
(51 569 ha of forest in a landscape of 250 000 ha), with edge-to-edge distances, read at a dispersal distance of 1000 m
and, for the probabilistic indices, a probability of 0.5 at that distance. `scrub` is the same graph with the
transitional woodland-shrub of class 29 as habitat too. The importance of a node or a link comes as a row for each of the
154 nodes, so the cards show the three highest, with the small function `top`. The ProtConn cards use the 18 forests of
500 ha or more as hypothetical reserves (they are not the real protected areas of the region) in the whole square; the
cards that need a transboundary zone use a region 30 x 30 km inside it, with a zone of 5 km around.

Conventions: the default `makurhini` convention links pairs closer than the distance (`d < t`), derives the probability
of a direct link as \(p_{ij} = P^{d_{ij}/t}\) and drops it below `pij_min` (0.01); the `conefor` convention links pairs
up to the distance (`d <= t`) and keeps every probability. Node importance is the percent loss of an index when the node
is removed.
families.example:
import geopandas as gpd
import numpy as np
import rasterio.features
import shapely
import terraflux as tf

# CORINE land cover of the Steinhude-Hannover excerpt (EPSG:3035) on 100 m cells; the forests are the habitat
land = tf.reproject(tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("clc")), res=100, resampling="mode")
kw = dict(area_unit="ha", distance="edge", landscape_area=250_000)       # ha, edge-to-edge distances, a 50 x 50 km landscape
net = tf.HabitatGraph.from_raster(land, habitat=[23, 24, 25], **kw)
scrub = tf.HabitatGraph.from_raster(land, habitat=[23, 24, 25, 29], **kw)   # with transitional woodland-shrub as habitat too
nodes = tf.conn.node_table(land, habitat=[23, 24, 25], area_unit="ha")
candidate = (nodes["attribute"] >= 40).astype(int).to_numpy()            # 0 marks the forests under 40 ha, candidates to add

# hypothetical reserves: the forests of 500 ha or more as polygons, in the whole square and in a region inside it
ids = net.to_raster(nodes[nodes["attribute"] >= 500], "id")
grid = np.nan_to_num(ids.values).astype("int32")
shapes = rasterio.features.shapes(grid, mask=grid > 0, transform=land.rio.transform(), connectivity=8)
reserves = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[shapely.geometry.shape(s) for s, _ in shapes], crs=land.rio.crs)
x0, y0, x1, y1 = land.rio.bounds()
region = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[shapely.box(x0, y0, x1, y1)], crs=land.rio.crs)
inner = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[shapely.box(x0 + 10_000, y0 + 10_000, x1 - 10_000, y1 - 10_000)], crs=land.rio.crs)


def top(table, by, *cols, n=3):
    """The n rows of a table with the highest value of a column, with some other columns."""
    return table.nlargest(n, by)[["id", by, *cols]].round(4)

metrics.name: Total node attribute (A)
metrics.what:
The sum of the attributes of all nodes, normally the total habitat area. It is the denominator of CCP and of the
node importance dA.

symbols.a_i: attribute of node \( i \)

metrics.use: Context for the other indices. Not a connectivity measure by itself.
refs: Saura & Torné (2009). Conefor Sensinode 2.2: a software package for quantifying the importance of habitat patches for landscape connectivity. Environmental Modelling & Software 24: 135-139. doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2008.05.005

metrics.name: Number of components (NC)
metrics.what:
How many groups of nodes are connected to each other by links at the chosen distance. A single component means
any patch can be reached from any other through stepping stones.
metrics.formula: NC = \#\{\text{connected components of the link graph}\}

symbols.l_{ij}: 1 when nodes \(i\) and \(j\) are linked, that is when \(d_{ij} < t\) (\(d_{ij} \le t\) with the Conefor convention)

metrics.use: A coarse indicator; it ignores patch size and the strength of connections. Use IIC, PC or CCP when sizes matter.
refs: Pascual-Hortal & Saura (2006). Comparison and development of new graph-based landscape connectivity indices: towards the prioritization of habitat patches and corridors for conservation. Landscape Ecology 21: 959-967.

metrics.name: Number of links (NL)
metrics.what: The number of node pairs that are linked at the chosen distance.

symbols.l_{ij}: 1 when nodes \( i \) and \( j \) are linked

metrics.use: Grows with the threshold; it does not tell whether the links join separate groups or only add redundancy.
refs: Pascual-Hortal & Saura (2006). Comparison and development of new graph-based landscape connectivity indices: towards the prioritization of habitat patches and corridors for conservation. Landscape Ecology 21: 959-967.

metrics.name: Harary index (H)
metrics.what:
The sum, over node pairs, of the inverse of the number of links on the shortest path. Pairs in different
components contribute nothing; closely linked pairs contribute most.

symbols.nl_{ij}: number of links on the shortest path between \( i \) and \( j \) in the link graph; pairs without a path add 0.

metrics.use: Topological only (ignores areas). Sensitive to the number of nodes, so compare graphs with the same nodes.
refs: Pascual-Hortal & Saura (2006). Comparison and development of new graph-based landscape connectivity indices: towards the prioritization of habitat patches and corridors for conservation. Landscape Ecology 21: 959-967.

metrics.name: Class coincidence probability (CCP)
metrics.what:
The probability that two random points in the habitat fall in the same component. It is 1 when all habitat is in
one component and falls as the habitat splits into pieces.

symbols.A_k: sum of node attributes in component \( k \); \( A = \sum_i a_i \).

metrics.use:
Normalised by the habitat present, not by the landscape. Use LCP when different landscapes (or habitat amounts)
are compared.
refs: Pascual-Hortal & Saura (2006). Comparison and development of new graph-based landscape connectivity indices: towards the prioritization of habitat patches and corridors for conservation. Landscape Ecology 21: 959-967.

metrics.name: Landscape coincidence probability (LCP)
metrics.what: Like CCP but divided by the whole landscape area, so it also drops when habitat is lost.

symbols.LA: landscape attribute (`landscape_area`). Without `landscape_area` Makurhini gives only the numerator (here NaN), Conefor uses \( LA = 1 \). The numerator is also returned as `LCPnum`.

metrics.use: Needs a landscape area. Good for comparing landscapes or scenarios of the same extent.
refs: Pascual-Hortal & Saura (2006). Comparison and development of new graph-based landscape connectivity indices: towards the prioritization of habitat patches and corridors for conservation. Landscape Ecology 21: 959-967.

metrics.name: Integral index of connectivity (IIC)
metrics.what:
Habitat available in the landscape, counting each pair of patches weighted by their sizes and discounted by the
number of links between them. It rises with larger patches and with shorter link paths, and is 1 when all the
landscape is one habitat patch.

symbols.a_i: node attribute
symbols.nl_{ij}: links on the shortest path (0 for \( i = j \))
symbols.LA: landscape attribute. Pairs without a path add 0 (Conefor); with the `makurhini` convention they add \( a_i a_j/(1+16443701) \) (Makurhini's stand-in for an unreachable pair, practically 0), and the value is capped at 1. The numerator is `IICnum`.

metrics.use:
Binary links: it does not use dispersal probabilities. Prefer PC for graded dispersal. Needs `landscape_area`,
otherwise NaN.
refs: Pascual-Hortal & Saura (2006). Comparison and development of new graph-based landscape connectivity indices: towards the prioritization of habitat patches and corridors for conservation. Landscape Ecology 21: 959-967.

metrics.name: Equivalent connectivity of IIC (EC(IIC))
metrics.what:
The size of a single habitat patch that would give the same IIC as the real graph. It puts IIC back in area
units (also called ECA).

symbols.IIC: the integral index of connectivity (the card above)
symbols.LA: landscape attribute; with the `makurhini` convention the result is capped at it

metrics.use: Easier to read than IIC and comparable across scenarios; changes of EC in % are what `eca_change` reports.
refs: Saura et al. (2011). Network analysis to assess landscape connectivity trends: application to European forests (1990-2000). Ecological Indicators 11: 407-416.

metrics.name: IIC fractions (intra, direct, step)
metrics.what:
Splits the IIC numerator into the part from within the patches themselves, the part from directly linked pairs
and the part from pairs reached through stepping stones.
metrics.formula: IIC_{intra} = \frac{100\sum_i a_i^{2}}{IIC_{num}},\quad IIC_{direct} = \frac{100\sum_{i\neq j,\, nl_{ij}=1}\frac{a_i a_j}{2}}{IIC_{num}},\quad IIC_{step} = 100 - IIC_{intra} - IIC_{direct}

symbols.IIC_{num}: numerator of IIC; direct pairs are those one link apart (the sum runs over ordered pairs). Columns `IICintra(%)`, `IICdirect(%)`, `IICstep(%)`.

metrics.use: Shows how much connectivity depends on patch size alone, on neighbours, or on stepping stones.
refs: Saura & Rubio (2010). A common currency for the different ways in which patches and links can contribute to habitat availability and connectivity in the landscape. Ecography 33: 523-537.

metrics.name: Flux (F)
metrics.what:
The total dispersal flux between patches: the sum of the direct dispersal probabilities over all ordered pairs
of different nodes.

symbols.p_{ij} = P^{d_{ij}/t}: probability of direct dispersal at distance \( d_{ij} \) (\( P \) is the probability at the threshold \( t \)); values below `pij_min` are dropped.

metrics.use: Uses direct links only (no stepping stones) and no areas; AWF adds the areas. Needs distances or probabilities.
refs: Saura & Torné (2009). Conefor Sensinode 2.2: a software package for quantifying the importance of habitat patches for landscape connectivity. Environmental Modelling & Software 24: 135-139. doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2008.05.005

metrics.name: Area-weighted flux (AWF)
metrics.what:
Like the flux, but each pair of patches is weighted by the product of their attributes, so exchange between
large patches counts most.

symbols.a_i: attribute of node \(i\)
symbols.p_{ij}: probability of direct dispersal between \(i\) and \(j\) (as F)

metrics.use: Direct dispersal only. PC extends it with the best path through stepping stones and adds the intra-patch term.
refs: Saura & Torné (2009). Conefor Sensinode 2.2: a software package for quantifying the importance of habitat patches for landscape connectivity. Environmental Modelling & Software 24: 135-139. doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2008.05.005

metrics.name: Probability of connectivity (PC)
metrics.what:
The probability that two random points of the landscape fall in habitat areas that are connected, taking into
account the best dispersal path (possibly through stepping stones) between every pair of patches.

symbols.p^{*}_{ij}: the highest product of direct probabilities \( p_{ij} = P^{d_{ij}/t} \) along any path between \( i \) and \( j \) (1 for \( i = j \), 0 if no path stays above `pij_min`)
symbols.LA: landscape attribute. The numerator is `PCnum`; the Makurhini convention caps PC at 1.

metrics.use:
The preferred index when dispersal probabilities are known. Needs `landscape_area` for the 0-1 value (NaN
otherwise); depends on the probability chosen at the distance.
refs: Saura & Pascual-Hortal (2007). A new habitat availability index to integrate connectivity in landscape conservation planning: comparison with existing indices and application to a case study. Landscape and Urban Planning 83: 91-103.

metrics.name: Equivalent connectivity of PC (EC(PC))
metrics.what: The size of a single patch with the same PC as the graph, in area units. It is the ECA most often reported.

symbols.PC: the probability of connectivity (the card above)
symbols.LA: landscape attribute; with the `makurhini` convention the result is capped at it

metrics.use:
Compare habitat-area changes with `eca_change`. A drop of EC larger than the drop of habitat area means
connectivity was lost too.
refs: Saura et al. (2011). Network analysis to assess landscape connectivity trends: application to European forests (1990-2000). Ecological Indicators 11: 407-416.

metrics.name: PC fractions (intra, direct, step)
metrics.what:
The share of PC due to the area of the patches themselves, to direct dispersal between patches, and to dispersal
through stepping stones.
metrics.formula: PC_{intra} = \frac{100\sum_i a_i^{2}}{PC_{num}},\quad PC_{direct} = \frac{100\sum_{i\neq j} a_i a_j p_{ij}}{PC_{num}},\quad PC_{step} = 100 - PC_{intra} - PC_{direct}

symbols.PC_{num}: numerator of PC, \(\sum_i\sum_j a_i a_j p^{*}_{ij}\)
symbols.p_{ij}: probability of direct dispersal between \(i\) and \(j\); the columns are `PCintra(%)`, `PCdirect(%)`, `PCstep(%)`

metrics.use: A high step share means the network works through stepping stones; removing the middle patches would hurt most.

metrics.name: Node importance of area (dA)
metrics.what: The share of the total attribute held by the node: what is lost if only its area counted.

symbols.a_i: attribute of node \( i \)
symbols.A: total attribute.

metrics.use: The baseline against which dIIC and dPC show the extra weight of connectivity.
refs: Saura & Rubio (2010). A common currency for the different ways in which patches and links can contribute to habitat availability and connectivity in the landscape. Ecography 33: 523-537.

metrics.name: Node importance for NC (dNC)
metrics.range: can be negative (removal splits a component)
metrics.what:
The percent change in the number of components when the node is removed. Negative when removing it splits its
component in two or more, positive when it was a component on its own.

symbols.NC_{-i}: components of the graph without node \( i \). An isolated node gives \( +100/NC \).

metrics.use: Finds cut nodes (negative values). Ignores sizes.

metrics.name: Node importance for NL (dNL)
metrics.what: The share of all links that are lost when the node is removed, i.e. its degree relative to NL.

symbols.k_i: number of links of node \( i \).

metrics.use: A degree measure; blind to the sizes and to what lies behind the links.

metrics.name: Node importance for H (dH)
metrics.what:
The percent of the Harary index lost when the node is removed, both from its own pairs and from pairs whose
shortest path went through it.

symbols.H_{-i}: Harary index of the graph without node \( i \).

metrics.use: Topological importance; needs the links only.

metrics.name: Node importance for CCP (dCCP)
metrics.what:
The percent change of CCP when the node is removed. Negative when removing the node leaves a more concentrated
habitat, as for a patch that was poorly connected to the rest.

symbols.CCP_{-i}: CCP of the graph without node \( i \) (recomputed with \( A - a_i \)).

metrics.use:
Because CCP is normalised by the remaining habitat, a negative sign can reflect that the removed node was poorly
connected.

metrics.name: Node importance for LCP (dLCP)
metrics.what: The percent of LCP lost when the node is removed (its component's area leaves the sum of squares).

symbols.LCP_{-i}: LCP of the graph without node \( i \), with the same landscape area.

metrics.use: Rates nodes by their weight in the largest components.

metrics.name: Node importance for IIC (dIIC)
metrics.what:
The percent of IIC lost when the node is removed. It is the node's own area, its flux with other nodes and its
role as a connector (stepping stone) between others.

symbols.IIC_{-i}: IIC of the graph without node \( i \), same landscape area.

metrics.use:
The standard priority ranking for habitat patches with binary links. With the `makurhini` convention unreachable
pairs count in the whole graph but not in the reduced graph, which slightly changes flux and connector.
refs: Pascual-Hortal & Saura (2006). Comparison and development of new graph-based landscape connectivity indices: towards the prioritization of habitat patches and corridors for conservation. Landscape Ecology 21: 959-967.
Saura & Rubio (2010). A common currency for the different ways in which patches and links can contribute to habitat availability and connectivity in the landscape. Ecography 33: 523-537.

metrics.name: dIIC fractions (intra, flux, connector)
metrics.what:
Splits dIIC into the loss of the node's own area, of pairs that have the node as an endpoint, and of pairs whose
shortest path passed through it.
metrics.formula: dIIC^{intra}_i = 100\frac{a_i^{2}}{IIC_{num}},\quad dIIC^{flux}_i = 100\frac{2 a_i \sum_{j\neq i}\frac{a_j}{1+nl_{ij}}}{IIC_{num}},\quad dIIC^{connector}_i = dIIC_i - dIIC^{intra}_i - dIIC^{flux}_i

symbols.dIIC^{intra}_i, dIIC^{flux}_i, dIIC^{con: the columns `dIICintra`, `dIICflux`, `dIICconnector`; the connector part is the loss of the pairs that do not contain \(i\) but whose shortest path used it
symbols.nl_{ij}: links on the shortest path between \(i\) and \(j\)

metrics.use: A large connector part flags a stepping stone; a large intra part flags a patch important by size alone.
refs: Saura & Rubio (2010). A common currency for the different ways in which patches and links can contribute to habitat availability and connectivity in the landscape. Ecography 33: 523-537.

metrics.name: Node importance for F (dF)
metrics.what: The percent of the flux lost when the node is removed (all its direct links).
metrics.use: Direct links only; sizes ignored.

metrics.name: Node importance for AWF (dAWF)
metrics.what: The percent of the area-weighted flux lost when the node is removed.

symbols.a_i: attribute of node \(i\)
symbols.AWF: area-weighted flux of the whole graph

metrics.use: Like dF but weighted by areas.

metrics.name: Node importance for PC (dPC)
metrics.what:
The percent of PC lost when the node is removed, combining its area, its direct exchange with other nodes and
its role as stepping stone.

symbols.PC_{-i}: PC of the graph without node \( i \), same landscape area.

metrics.use: The standard ranking of patches for conservation priority with probabilistic dispersal.
refs: Saura & Rubio (2010). A common currency for the different ways in which patches and links can contribute to habitat availability and connectivity in the landscape. Ecography 33: 523-537.

metrics.name: dPC fractions (intra, flux, connector)
metrics.what: The parts of dPC due to the node's own area, to the flux with other nodes and to its role as connector.
metrics.formula: dPC^{intra}_i = 100\frac{a_i^{2}}{PC_{num}},\quad dPC^{flux}_i = 100\frac{2 a_i\sum_{j\neq i} a_j p^{*}_{ij}}{PC_{num}},\quad dPC^{connector}_i = dPC_i - dPC^{intra}_i - dPC^{flux}_i

symbols.PC_{num}: numerator of PC, \(\sum_i\sum_j a_i a_j p^{*}_{ij}\)
symbols.p^{*}_{ij}: highest product of direct probabilities along a path between \(i\) and \(j\)

metrics.use: As for IIC: separates size, position and stepping-stone value.

metrics.name: Absolute loss of PC (varPC)
metrics.what: The absolute drop of PC (not in percent) when the node is removed.

symbols.PC_{-i}: PC of the graph without node \(i\), with the same landscape area
symbols.dPC_i: the percent loss of the card above

metrics.use: Use when absolute changes of PC are summed across nodes or scenarios.

metrics.name: Betweenness centrality (BC)
metrics.what:
How often the node lies on the shortest link path between two other nodes (Freeman betweenness), normalised by
the number of pairs of other nodes. Asked for by name; it is not in the default metric list.

symbols.\\sigma_{jk}: number of shortest paths between \( j \) and \( k \)

metrics.use: Topological. For graph-theory ranking of stepping stones. Zero for n < 3.
refs: Freeman (1977). A set of measures of centrality based on betweenness. Sociometry 40: 35-41.
Bodin & Saura (2010). Ranking individual habitat patches as connectivity providers: integrating network analysis and patch removal experiments. Ecological Modelling 221: 2393-2405.

metrics.name: Betweenness importance for IIC (dBC_IIC)
metrics.what:
The part of the IIC numerator that flows over the shortest paths running through the node, in percent. It
isolates the stepping-stone role of the node.

symbols.varBC_{IIC,i}: the betweenness contribution to IIC of node \(i\) (the next card)
symbols.IIC_{num}: IIC numerator (the Conefor value, without the unreachable-pair term)

metrics.use: Compare with the connector part of dIIC; it is the betweenness-based version (Bodin & Saura 2010).
refs: Bodin & Saura (2010). Ranking individual habitat patches as connectivity providers: integrating network analysis and patch removal experiments. Ecological Modelling 221: 2393-2405.

metrics.name: Betweenness contribution to IIC (varBC_IIC)
metrics.what:
The sum, over ordered pairs of other nodes, of the share of their shortest paths that pass through the node
times the IIC weight of the pair.
metrics.formula: varBC_{IIC,i} = \sum_{j\neq k;\; j,k\neq i} \frac{\sigma_{jk}(i)}{\sigma_{jk}} \cdot \frac{a_j\, a_k}{1 + nl_{jk}}

symbols.\\sigma_{jk}(i)/\\sigma_{jk}: share of shortest \( j \)-\( k \) paths through \( i \)

metrics.use: Absolute version of dBC_IIC.
refs: Bodin & Saura (2010). Ranking individual habitat patches as connectivity providers: integrating network analysis and patch removal experiments. Ecological Modelling 221: 2393-2405.

metrics.name: Betweenness importance for PC (dBC_PC)
metrics.what: The part of the PC numerator carried by most-probable paths that pass through the node, in percent.

symbols.varBC_{PC,i}: the betweenness contribution to PC of node \(i\) (the card below)

metrics.use: Probabilistic counterpart of dBC_IIC.
refs: Bodin & Saura (2010). Ranking individual habitat patches as connectivity providers: integrating network analysis and patch removal experiments. Ecological Modelling 221: 2393-2405.

metrics.name: Betweenness contribution to PC (varBC_PC)
metrics.what:
The sum of the pair weights a_j a_k p*_jk over ordered pairs whose most probable path runs through the node (the
node itself is not an endpoint).
metrics.formula: varBC_{PC,i} = \sum_{j\neq k;\; j,k\neq i,\; i\in path^{*}_{jk}} a_j\, a_k\, p^{*}_{jk}

symbols.path^{*}_{jk}: the most probable path between \( j \) and \( k \).

metrics.use: Absolute version of dBC_PC.
refs: Bodin & Saura (2010). Ranking individual habitat patches as connectivity providers: integrating network analysis and patch removal experiments. Ecological Modelling 221: 2393-2405.

metrics.name: Gain of a node to add (d...add, Conefor adding mode)
metrics.what:
With `restoration` flags and `convention="conefor"`, every index of the existing graph gets a gain column for
each candidate node (dAadd, dNCadd, dNLadd, dHadd, dCCPadd, dLCPadd, dIICadd, dFadd, dAWFadd, dPCadd).

symbols.\\mathrm{X}: the index of the existing nodes
symbols.\\mathrm{X}_{+c}: the index once candidate \( c \) is added with its links to existing nodes. dAadd is \( 100\,a_c/A \) and the flux gains use the added direct probabilities; the rest follow the pattern above.

metrics.use: Rates sites for restoration. Candidates are those with restoration flag 0; values for existing nodes are NaN.
refs: Saura & Torné (2009). Conefor Sensinode 2.2: a software package for quantifying the importance of habitat patches for landscape connectivity. Environmental Modelling & Software 24: 135-139. doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2008.05.005
metrics.python: top(tf.HabitatGraph.from_raster(land, habitat=[23, 24, 25], restoration=candidate, convention="conefor", **kw).node_importance("PC", distance=1000, probability=0.5), "dPCadd")

metrics.name: Gain of a node to add (dIICres, dPCres)
metrics.what:
Makurhini's restoration importance: for the nodes flagged 0 (possible additions), the gain of IIC or PC in
percent of the graph that includes them.

symbols.\\Delta_c: increase of the numerator of IIC or PC from adding candidate \( c \) to the existing nodes

metrics.use:
Different normalisation from Conefor's `...add` gains (share of the graph with the node, not of the existing
graph).
refs: Godínez-Gómez & Correa Ayram (2020). Makurhini: analyzing landscape connectivity. R package. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3748095

metrics.name: Link importance for IIC (dIIC_removal)
metrics.what:
The percent of IIC lost when a single link is removed. Only the links of the graph at the chosen distance are
rated.

symbols.IIC_{num}^{-ij}: numerator after removing the link between \( i \) and \( j \).

metrics.use: Finds the links worth protecting (corridors). A link inside a redundant cycle scores near 0.

metrics.name: Link importance for PC (dPC_removal)
metrics.what: The percent of PC lost when one edge (a pair above `pij_min`) is removed.

symbols.PC_{num}^{-ij}: numerator after removing the direct edge of \( i \) and \( j \) (paths may re-route through other edges).

metrics.use: Probabilistic version; pairs not above `pij_min` score 0.

metrics.name: Change of IIC or PC when a pair's value changes (dIIC_change, dPC_change)
metrics.what:
The percent change of IIC or PC when the distance of a pair is replaced by a new value, e.g. a corridor that
brings two patches closer. Positive is a loss, negative a gain.

symbols.\\mathrm{X}'': the same with the pair's new value. For IIC a pair that comes closer than the distance gains a link and any other change counts 0; for PC the new probability is not cut by `pij_min`.

metrics.use: Tests a planned corridor or a barrier before building it.
refs: Godínez-Gómez & Correa Ayram (2020). Makurhini: analyzing landscape connectivity. R package, function MK_dPCIIC_links. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3748095

metrics.name: Degree or strength
metrics.what:
The number of links of the node (binary graph) or the sum of the edge weights 1/p over its edges (weighted
graph, when a probability is given).

symbols.l_{ij}: link indicator; \( p_{ij} = P^{d_{ij}/t} \); in the weighted graph \( 1/p_{ij} \) is the length of the edge. Column `degree` (binary) or `strength`.

metrics.use: Local importance only. Note the strength sums lengths, so a larger value means weaker connections.
refs: Godínez-Gómez & Correa Ayram (2020). Makurhini: analyzing landscape connectivity. R package, function MK_RMCentrality. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3748095

metrics.name: Eigenvector centrality (eigen)
metrics.what: A node scores high when it is linked to nodes that themselves score high; scaled so the highest node is 1.

symbols.A: adjacency matrix (weights \( 1/p_{ij} \) when weighted)

metrics.use: Highlights well-connected clusters. Meaningful within one component; isolated nodes get 0.

metrics.name: Closeness centrality (close)
metrics.range: > 0, NaN for a node that reaches no other
metrics.what: The inverse of the total path length from the node to all nodes it can reach; high for nodes close to the rest.

symbols.\\ell_{ij}: shortest path length (hops, or the sum of \( 1/p \))
symbols.r_i: number of nodes reached including \( i \).

metrics.use: Only reachable nodes count, so values are not comparable between components of different size.

metrics.name: Betweenness centrality of the graph (BWC)
metrics.what:
The number of shortest paths between pairs of other nodes that pass through the node (unnormalised), as igraph
computes it; paths of equal length within 1e-10 share it.

symbols.\\sigma_{jk}: number of shortest paths between \( j \) and \( k \) (lengths 1 per link, or \( 1/p \) when weighted).

metrics.use: Unlike `BC` of the node importance table it is not normalised.

metrics.name: Component of a node (cluster)
metrics.what: The number of the connected component the node belongs to (numbered from 1). `conn.components` returns the same.

symbols.k: number of the connected component (1 to NC) of the link graph at the chosen distance

metrics.use:
To map or group patches that are connected. With python-igraph installed `centrality` also gives `memb_rw`, the
walktrap community of the node.

metrics.name: ECA of a time (ECA)
metrics.what:
The equivalent connected area of the graph of each time or scenario, EC(PC) or EC(IIC), together with its share
of the landscape (ECA_LA) and of the habitat area (ECA_area).
metrics.formula: ECA = EC(\mathrm{PC\ or\ IIC}),\quad ECA_{LA} = 100\,\frac{ECA}{LA},\quad ECA_{area} = 100\,\frac{ECA}{A}

symbols.A: habitat area of that time (the sum of the node attributes or the habitat area of raster or vector nodes)
symbols.LA: landscape area, common to all times.

metrics.use:
ECA_area near 100 means the habitat is almost fully connected; a falling value means fragmentation within the
habitat.
refs: Saura et al. (2011). Network analysis to assess landscape connectivity trends: application to European forests (1990-2000). Ecological Indicators 11: 407-416.
Godínez-Gómez & Correa Ayram (2020). Makurhini: analyzing landscape connectivity. R package, function MK_dECA. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3748095

metrics.name: Change of ECA and of habitat area (dECA, dA, rECA)
metrics.range: dECA, dA > -100 after the first time
metrics.what:
The percent change of ECA and of habitat area between consecutive times (the first time is compared with LA),
and their ratio. It separates habitat loss from connectivity loss.

symbols.LA: landscape area, used as \(ECA_{t-1}\) and \(A_{t-1}\) at the first time; `comparison` and `change` classify the pair (dECA < dA < 0: connectivity loss beyond habitat loss; dA < dECA < 0: habitat loss; equal; or a gain), as Makurhini's dECAfun

metrics.use: rECA above 1 means connectivity changes faster than the area. Needs a common landscape area.
refs: Godínez-Gómez & Correa Ayram (2020). Makurhini: analyzing landscape connectivity. R package, function MK_dECA. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3748095
metrics.value:
dA    dECA  rECA                       change
-79.372 -92.836 1.170          + Connectivity loss
  0.462   0.949 2.056 Habitat or connectivity gain

metrics.name: Composite connectivity of a focal node (IComp)
metrics.what:
For a node and the neighbourhood of nodes around it (within a search buffer), the product of the neighbourhood's
IIC (or PC) and the node's dIIC (or dPC). It is high where the surroundings are connected and the focal node
matters in them.

symbols.N(i): nodes whose polygons intersect the buffer of node \( i \); IIC and dIIC are computed on that sub-graph with the area of its bounding box as landscape (PC and dPC with `metric="PC"`). NaN with fewer than three nodes.

metrics.use: Ranks nodes locally; the neighbourhood is defined by the buffer you choose.
refs: Godínez-Gómez & Correa Ayram (2020). Makurhini: analyzing landscape connectivity. R package, function MK_Focal_nodes. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3748095

metrics.name: ProtConn ECA (ECA)
metrics.what:
The equivalent connected area of the protected areas in a region: the area of one protected patch that would
give the same PC.

symbols.a_i: area of protected node \(i\): the protected areas cut to the region, dissolved and split into separate polygons (distances between edges, or least-cost)
symbols.p^{*}_{ij}: highest product of direct probabilities along a path between \(i\) and \(j\); transboundary and region nodes take part as stepping stones, their products \(a_i a_j\) replaced by `transboundary_weight` (1 for Makurhini; 0 for Saura et al. 2017)

metrics.use: With a single protected node the result is the node's area (capped at LA).
refs: Saura et al. (2017). Protected areas in the world's ecoregions: how well connected are they? Ecological Indicators 76: 144-158.
Saura et al. (2018). Protected area connectivity: shortfalls in global targets and country-level priorities. Biological Conservation 219: 53-67.
Godínez-Gómez & Correa Ayram (2020). Makurhini: analyzing landscape connectivity. R package, function MK_ProtConn. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3748095

metrics.name: ProtConn PC (PC)
metrics.what: The probability of connectivity of the protected-area network in the region.
metrics.use: Usually read through ProtConn (its square root, in %).

metrics.name: Region area (LA)
metrics.what: The area of the region (all polygons merged) in the chosen unit.

symbols.LA: area of the region polygons, computed with GDAL areas on the projected polygons

metrics.use: The denominator of all percentages below.

metrics.name: Protected surface
metrics.what: The total area of the protected areas inside the region (non-transboundary nodes, after dissolving).

symbols.a_i: area of protected node \(i\); only nodes of type Non-Transboundary are summed

metrics.use: Overlapping protected areas are dissolved, so overlaps are not double counted.

metrics.name: Protected area (Prot)
metrics.what: The share of the region that is protected.
metrics.use: The Aichi/Kunming-Montreal style coverage indicator; says nothing about connectivity.

metrics.name: Protected connected land (ProtConn)
metrics.what:
The share of the region that is both protected and connected: the ECA of the protected-area network as a
percentage of the region.

symbols.ECA: equivalent connected area of the protected areas (above).

metrics.use:
The headline indicator; it depends on the dispersal distance and the probability assumed. Compare with Prot to
see how much of the protection is connected.
refs: Saura et al. (2017). Protected areas in the world's ecoregions: how well connected are they? Ecological Indicators 76: 144-158.
Saura et al. (2018). Protected area connectivity: shortfalls in global targets and country-level priorities. Biological Conservation 219: 53-67.

metrics.name: Protected unconnected land (ProtUnconn)
metrics.what: The part of the protected area that is not connected: Prot minus ProtConn.

symbols.Prot: share of the region that is protected
symbols.ProtConn: share of the region that is protected and connected

metrics.use: Shows how much protected land is isolated at the chosen distance.

metrics.name: Relative connectivity (RelConn)
metrics.what: The share of the protected area that is connected.

symbols.ProtConn: share of the region that is protected and connected
symbols.Prot: share of the region that is protected

metrics.use: Useful for comparing regions with different coverage.

metrics.name: Unprotected land (Unprotected)
metrics.what: The share of the region that is not protected.

symbols.Prot: share of the region that is protected

metrics.use: Complement of Prot.

metrics.name: Design of unconnected land (ProtUnconn_Design)
metrics.what:
The change in connected area when the region itself is added as a stepping-stone node. Only given when
`bound=True` and transboundary nodes exist; NaN otherwise.

symbols.ECA_{all}: ECA of the graph with the region node included.

metrics.use: A technical term of the ProtConn[Bound] decomposition.

metrics.name: ProtConn within the boundary (ProtConn_Bound)
metrics.what:
The part of the protected area that is connected through the region's boundary, as Prot minus
ProtUnconn[Design].

symbols.Prot: share of the region that is protected
symbols.ProtUnconn_{Design}: the card above; NaN unless `bound=True` with transboundary nodes

metrics.use: Technical term of the decomposition.

metrics.name: ProtConn[Prot]
metrics.what: The share of ProtConn that comes from the area of the protected nodes themselves (intra-node connectivity).

symbols.a_i: area of protected node \( i \).

metrics.use: Together with Trans and Unprot it sums to 100 (with Within and Contig, a second decomposition).

metrics.name: ProtConn[Trans]
metrics.what:
The share of ProtConn that depends on transboundary protected areas (outside the region within the transboundary
distance).

symbols.ECA_{no\\,trans}: ECA computed without transboundary nodes. 0 without transboundary nodes.

metrics.use: Needs `transboundary`. Shows how much a region relies on its neighbours.

metrics.name: ProtConn[Unprot]
metrics.what: The share of ProtConn due to dispersal between protected areas across unprotected land.

symbols.ProtConn_{Prot}: share of ProtConn from the area of the nodes

metrics.use: The part that would be lost if the matrix between reserves became impassable.

metrics.name: ProtConn[Within]
metrics.what:
The share of ProtConn that comes from within the individual protected areas before they were dissolved (so
overlapping or touching areas are treated as separate pieces).
metrics.formula: ProtConn_{Within} = \min\!\left(100\,\frac{w_1 w_2}{ProtConn},\, 100\right),\quad w_1 = 100\frac{\sqrt{\sum_k s_k^{2}}}{LA},\; w_2 = \sqrt{\frac{A_{prot}}{\sum_k s_k}}

symbols.s_k: area of piece \( k \) before dissolving (`pieces`).

metrics.use: Compare with Contig. With one dissolved node it is 100.

metrics.name: ProtConn[Contig]
metrics.what: The share of ProtConn that comes from contiguous protected areas that were merged into one node.

symbols.ProtConn_{Within}: the share of ProtConn from within the individual pieces (the card above)

metrics.use: Zero when no protected areas touch or overlap.

metrics.name: ProtConn[Within] as land
metrics.what: ProtConn[Within] expressed as percent of the region rather than of ProtConn.

symbols.ProtConn_{Within}: share of ProtConn from within the pieces
symbols.ProtConn: share of the region that is protected and connected

metrics.use: The same decomposition on the same scale as Prot.

metrics.name: ProtConn[Contig] as land
metrics.what: ProtConn[Contig] as percent of the region.

symbols.ProtConn_{Contig}: share of ProtConn from contiguous areas
symbols.ProtConn: share of the region that is protected and connected

metrics.use: As ProtConn[Within] as land.

metrics.name: ProtConn[Unprot] as land
metrics.what: ProtConn[Unprot] as percent of the region.

symbols.ProtConn_{Unprot}: share of ProtConn from dispersal across unprotected land
symbols.ProtConn: share of the region that is protected and connected

metrics.use: As ProtConn[Within] as land.

metrics.name: ProtConn[Trans] as land
metrics.what: ProtConn[Trans] as percent of the region.

symbols.ProtConn_{Trans}: share of ProtConn from transboundary areas
symbols.ProtConn: share of the region that is protected and connected

metrics.use: As ProtConn[Within] as land.

metrics.name: Importance of a protected area (dProt, dProtConn, varProtConn)
metrics.what:
With `delta=True`, each protected area (cut to the region) is rated by the share of the protected surface it
holds (dProt), by the percent of ProtConn lost when it is removed (dProtConn) and by that loss in percent of the
region (varProtConn).
metrics.formula: dProt_i = 100\frac{a_i}{\sum_k a_k},\quad dProtConn_i = 100\Bigl(1 - \sqrt{1 - dPC_i/100}\Bigr),\quad varProtConn_i = ProtConn\Bigl(1-\sqrt{1 - dPC_i/100}\Bigr)

symbols.dPC_i: node importance for PC of area \( i \) in the graph of the clipped areas (PC computed without a probability cut); \( ProtConn \) here is that graph's value.

metrics.use: Ranks protected areas for their contribution to connected protection.

families.title: Species distributions
families.source: predicts / dismo (evaluate), ecospat (Boyce), ENMeval (omission rates, p10), dismo and Liu et al. (thresholds), predicts (MESS), mop (MOP), dsmextra (ExDet)
families.intro:
Metrics that judge a species distribution model from its predictions at presences and at background points (or
absences), and measures of how far new conditions lie outside those the model was fitted to. They are the measures of the
[species distribution tutorials](../../tutorials/species-distributions/evaluation-and-thresholds/).

The cards show their values on the model of those tutorials: the Bradypus (brown-throated three-toed sloth) records and
the bioclimatic layers that ship with the library, a MaxNet model with 2000 background points and spatial folds. The
evaluation cards use the **out-of-fold predictions** of the model (`o_pres` at the presences, `o_back` at the background:
what each record gets from the model fitted without its block), the score you would report, and `ev` is their
evaluation. The threshold cards read the table of `ev` at the threshold of maximum TSS (`at`). The omission rates compare
the predictions of the model fitted on every record at the presences (`pres`, the training ones) with the out-of-fold
ones (the test ones). The extrapolation cards project the model to a scenario, `new`, with a warmest month 2 degrees
hotter and a driest quarter 20% drier than today, and compare it with the conditions of the records and background.

Conventions: the candidate thresholds of `evaluate` are the prediction values minus 0.0001, and at a threshold a
prediction at or above it counts as predicted present.
families.example:
import numpy as np
import terraflux as tf

occ = tf.load_table(tf.sdm.example_data("bradypus"))
env = tf.load_raster(tf.sdm.example_data("bioclim"))
data = tf.sdm.prepare(occ, env, thin=50_000, area=500_000, background=2000,
                      folds={"size": 500_000, "k": 5}, seed=1)
res = tf.sdm.fit(data, {"maxnet": tf.sdm.MaxNet(regmult=2, classes="lqh")})

p = res.models["maxnet"].predict_proba(data.X)[:, 1]          # the model fitted on every record, at every record
pres = p[data.y == 1]                                         # training predictions at the presences
oof = res.predictions["maxnet"].to_numpy()                    # out-of-fold: the model fitted without the record's block
ok = ~np.isnan(oof)
o_pres, o_back = oof[ok & (data.y == 1)], oof[ok & (data.y == 0)]
ev = tf.sdm.evaluate(o_pres, o_back)
at = ev.table.loc[ev.table["tss"].idxmax()]                   # the row of the confusion table at the maximum TSS

future = env.copy()                                           # a scenario: a hotter warmest month, a drier driest quarter
future.loc[{"band": "bio5"}] = env.sel(band="bio5") + 20
future.loc[{"band": "bio17"}] = env.sel(band="bio17") * 0.8
new = future.sel(band=data.predictors)

metrics.name: Area under the ROC curve (AUC)
metrics.what:
The probability that a random presence gets a higher prediction than a random background point (ties count one
half). It is independent of any threshold.

symbols.n_p, n_a: number of presences and background points
symbols.R_p: sum of the ranks of the presences in the pooled predictions (average ranks for ties). This is the Mann-Whitney statistic.

metrics.use:
With background points instead of true absences the maximum possible AUC is below 1 and depends on prevalence;
do not compare AUC across studies with different backgrounds.
refs: Hanley & McNeil (1982). The meaning and use of the area under a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Radiology 143: 29-36.
Fielding & Bell (1997). A review of methods for the assessment of prediction errors in conservation presence/absence models. Environmental Conservation 24: 38-49.

metrics.name: Point-biserial correlation (cor, pcor)
metrics.what:
The Pearson correlation between the predictions and the presence indicator (1 at presences, 0 at background),
with the two-sided p-value of a t-test.

symbols.z: 1 for presences, 0 for background; \( N = n_p + n_a \)
symbols.F_t: Student's t distribution with \( N-2 \) degrees of freedom. Returned as `cor` and `pcor`.

metrics.use:
Sensitive to the scale of the predictions. Background points are not independent absences, so read the p-value
as descriptive.
refs: dismo R package (Hijmans et al.), function evaluate.

metrics.name: Sample sizes and prevalence (np, na, prevalence)
metrics.what: The numbers of presences (np) and background points (na) used, and the share of presences in the pooled sample.

symbols.n_p, n_a: number of presences and background points after dropping missing values.

metrics.use:
With background points, the prevalence is set by the number of points you draw, not by the species; it is only
used for the equal-prevalence threshold.

metrics.name: Maximum TSS (max_tss)
metrics.what:
The highest true skill statistic over all candidate thresholds, a threshold-free summary of how well some
threshold can separate presences from background.

symbols.\\tau: candidate threshold; TPR and TNR as defined in the table of the evaluation.

metrics.use: Optimistic because the threshold is chosen on the same data. Use cross-validated predictions.
refs: Allouche et al. (2006). Assessing the accuracy of species distribution models: prevalence, kappa and the true skill statistic (TSS). Journal of Applied Ecology 43: 1223-1232. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2664.2006.01214.x

metrics.name: Confusion matrix (tp, fp, fn, tn)
metrics.what:
At each candidate threshold, the counts of presences predicted present (tp), background predicted present (fp),
presences predicted absent (fn) and background predicted absent (tn).
metrics.formula: tp_\tau = \#\{p_i \ge \tau\},\; fp_\tau = \#\{a_j \ge \tau\},\; fn_\tau = n_p - tp_\tau,\; tn_\tau = n_a - fp_\tau
metrics.use:
Basis of all the threshold-dependent measures below. With background points, fp is not a true false-positive
count.

metrics.name: Cohen's kappa
metrics.what:
The agreement between predicted and observed presence/absence beyond what chance would give from the marginal
totals.

symbols.N: number of points, \(tp+fp+fn+tn\); the column `kappa` of `ev.table`
symbols.p_o, p_e: observed agreement and the agreement expected by chance from the marginal totals

metrics.use:
Depends on prevalence, which with background points is arbitrary; many authors advise against it for
presence-background data. The `max_kappa` threshold maximises it.
refs: Cohen (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement 20: 37-46.
