Allouche et al. (2006). Assessing the accuracy of species distribution models: prevalence, kappa and the true skill statistic (TSS). Journal of Applied Ecology 43: 1223-1232. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2664.2006.01214.x

metrics.name: Correct classification rate (ccr)
metrics.what: The share of all points classified correctly (overall accuracy).
metrics.use: Misleading when presences are rare: a model predicting absence everywhere scores high.

metrics.name: Sensitivity (tpr)
metrics.what: The share of presences predicted present: how well the threshold keeps the known occurrences.

symbols.tp, fn: presences predicted present and absent (the confusion matrix); the column `tpr`

metrics.use: Reliable with presence-background data, since it only uses presences. Equals 1 minus the omission rate (fnr).

metrics.name: Specificity (tnr)
metrics.what: The share of background points (or absences) predicted absent.

symbols.tn, fp: background points predicted absent and present (the confusion matrix); the column `tnr`

metrics.use: With background points it measures how much of the area is predicted absent, not true specificity.

metrics.name: False positive rate (fpr)
metrics.what: The share of background points predicted present; the x-axis of the ROC curve.

symbols.fp, tn: background points predicted present and absent (the confusion matrix); the column `fpr`

metrics.use: With background points it is the fraction of the area predicted suitable.

metrics.name: False negative (omission) rate (fnr)
metrics.what: The share of presences predicted absent: how many known occurrences the threshold omits.

symbols.fn, tp: presences predicted absent and present (the confusion matrix); the column `fnr`

metrics.use: The omission rate at a chosen threshold; for omission on independent test data use `omission_rate`.

metrics.name: Positive predictive power (ppp)
metrics.what: The share of points predicted present that are presences.

symbols.tp, fp: presences and background points predicted present (the confusion matrix); the column `ppp`

metrics.use: Depends on prevalence, hence arbitrary with background points.

metrics.name: Negative predictive power (npp)
metrics.what: The share of points predicted absent that are really absent (background).

symbols.tn, fn: background points and presences predicted absent (the confusion matrix); the column `npp`

metrics.use: As ppp, depends on prevalence.

metrics.name: Misclassification rate (mcr)
metrics.what: The share of all points classified wrongly.

symbols.fp, fn: background points predicted present and presences predicted absent; \(N\) is their total with tp and tn; the column `mcr`

metrics.use: As ccr, misleading for rare presences.

metrics.name: Odds ratio (or)
metrics.range: or ≥ 0 (inf when fn or fp is 0)
metrics.what:
The odds of a presence being predicted present relative to the odds for a background point. Note the column name
`or` is the odds ratio, not an omission rate.

symbols.tp, tn, fn, fp: the four counts of the confusion matrix; the column `or`

metrics.use: Becomes infinite when the model has no omission or no commission at the threshold.
refs: dismo R package (Hijmans et al.), function evaluate.

metrics.name: True skill statistic (TSS)
metrics.what: Sensitivity plus specificity minus one. It is a kappa-like agreement measure that does not depend on prevalence.

symbols.TPR, TNR: sensitivity and specificity at the threshold (the two cards above); the column `tss`

metrics.use: Preferred over kappa; its maximum over thresholds defines the `max_spec_sens` threshold.
refs: Allouche et al. (2006). Assessing the accuracy of species distribution models: prevalence, kappa and the true skill statistic (TSS). Journal of Applied Ecology 43: 1223-1232. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2664.2006.01214.x

metrics.name: Continuous Boyce index
metrics.what:
Whether presences fall more often than expected in the cells the model predicts as more suitable. It uses only
presences and the distribution of predictions over the area, so it needs no absences.

symbols.w: width of the moving windows: a tenth of the range of the available predictions by default, moved in `res` = 100 steps (`nclass = k` uses k equal classes instead)
symbols.P_k, E_k: presences and background points in window \(k\); windows without background are dropped, and with `rm_duplicate` only the last of each run of equal ratios is kept
symbols.n_p, n_b: total numbers of presences and background points
symbols.\\rho_s: Spearman correlation (`method`); the result is rounded to 3 decimals

metrics.use:
Unlike ecospat, the last window ends at the maximum prediction on any scale (no "+1 trick"), so the index does
not depend on whether predictions are 0-1 or 0-1000. Needs enough presences; noisy with fewer than about 30.
refs: Boyce et al. (2002). Evaluating resource selection functions. Ecological Modelling 157: 281-300.
Hirzel et al. (2006). Evaluating the ability of habitat suitability models to predict species presences. Ecological Modelling 199: 142-152.

metrics.name: Threshold maximising kappa (max_kappa)
metrics.what: The candidate threshold with the highest kappa (first one on a tie).
metrics.use: Depends on prevalence; with background points the result varies with the number of points drawn.
refs: Liu et al. (2013). Selecting thresholds for the prediction of species occurrence with presence-only data. Journal of Biogeography 40: 778-789. doi:10.1111/jbi.12058

metrics.name: Threshold maximising sensitivity + specificity (max_spec_sens)
metrics.what: The candidate threshold where the sum of sensitivity and specificity (equivalently TSS) is highest.

symbols.TPR_\\tau, TNR_\\tau: sensitivity and specificity at threshold \(\tau\); the default method of `threshold`

metrics.use: The default recommendation for presence-background models; insensitive to prevalence.
refs: Liu et al. (2013). Selecting thresholds for the prediction of species occurrence with presence-only data. Journal of Biogeography 40: 778-789. doi:10.1111/jbi.12058

metrics.name: Threshold without omission (no_omission)
metrics.what: The highest candidate threshold that keeps every presence (no false negatives).

symbols.fn_\\tau: presences predicted absent at threshold \(\tau\); the result is NaN when no threshold has \(fn = 0\)

metrics.use: Very permissive; determined by the lowest presence prediction, so a single bad record sets it.

metrics.name: Threshold at the prevalence (equal_prevalence)
metrics.what:
The candidate threshold closest to the prevalence value itself (the share of presences in the pooled sample),
compared on the prediction scale.

symbols.\\text{prevalence}: \(n_p/(n_p+n_a)\), the share of presences in the pooled sample; this is dismo's `prevalence` method

metrics.use: Only meaningful for predictions that are probabilities; arbitrary with background points.

metrics.name: Threshold with equal sensitivity and specificity (equal_sens_spec)
metrics.what: The candidate threshold where sensitivity and specificity are closest to each other.
metrics.use: Balances errors on presences and background; the value often equals max_spec_sens.

metrics.name: Threshold for a given sensitivity (sensitivity)
metrics.what:
The highest threshold that still keeps at least the requested share of presences (default 0.9). dismo returns
the first one below it; here it is the last one at or above it.

symbols.s: the requested sensitivity (`sensitivity`, default 0.9). NaN when no threshold reaches it.

metrics.use: For conservation uses where a fixed omission is acceptable.

metrics.name: 10th percentile training presence (p10)
metrics.range: within the range of the presence predictions
metrics.what:
The prediction value that leaves 10 percent of the presences below it, so the model omits about 10 percent of
the training records by construction. It guards against a few erroneous records.
metrics.formula: \tau^{*} = p_{(k)}^{\downarrow},\quad k = \begin{cases}\lfloor 0.9\, n_p \rfloor & n_p < 10\\ \lceil 0.9\, n_p \rceil & n_p \ge 10\end{cases}

symbols.p^{\\downarrow}_{(k)}: the \( k \)-th largest presence prediction (an order statistic, as ENMeval).

metrics.use: A robust choice when records may contain errors. NaN with a single presence (\( k < 1 \)).
refs: Radosavljevic & Anderson (2014). Making better Maxent models of species distributions: complexity, overfitting and evaluation. Journal of Biogeography 41: 629-643.

metrics.name: Minimum training presence (mtp)
metrics.range: within the range of the presence predictions
metrics.what: The lowest prediction at any presence; the threshold that keeps all training presences.
metrics.use: Sensitive to a single outlying record.
refs: Pearson et al. (2007). Predicting species distributions from small numbers of occurrence records: a test case using cryptic geckos in Madagascar. Journal of Biogeography 34: 102-117.

metrics.name: Omission rate at the minimum training presence (or.mtp)
metrics.what:
The share of test presences that are predicted below the lowest training presence. It tests whether the model is
overfitted: it should be near 0.

symbols.x^{train}, x^{test}: predictions at training and test presences.

metrics.use:
Needs predictions at independent test presences (cross-validation fold). Values well above 0 indicate
overfitting.
refs: Radosavljevic & Anderson (2014). Making better Maxent models of species distributions: complexity, overfitting and evaluation. Journal of Biogeography 41: 629-643.

Kass et al. (2021). ENMeval 2.0: redesigned for customizable and reproducible modeling of species' niches and distributions. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 12: 1602-1608. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13628

metrics.name: Omission rate at the 10th percentile (or.10p)
metrics.what:
The share of test presences predicted below the 10th percentile training presence threshold. A well-fitted model
omits about 0.1.
metrics.use: Much more than 0.1 suggests overfitting; much less, an overly permissive model.
refs: Radosavljevic & Anderson (2014). Making better Maxent models of species distributions: complexity, overfitting and evaluation. Journal of Biogeography 41: 629-643.

Kass et al. (2021). ENMeval 2.0: redesigned for customizable and reproducible modeling of species' niches and distributions. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 12: 1602-1608. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13628

metrics.name: Multivariate environmental similarity surface (MESS)
metrics.range: negative = novel; up to 100 at the median
metrics.what:
For each cell, the smallest over the variables of the similarity of its value to the reference sample: 100 at
the median, falling to 0 at the reference extremes and negative outside the reference range. Negative cells are
conditions at least one variable of which the model has never seen.
metrics.formula: S_j(x) = \begin{cases}2F & F \le 50\\ 200 - 2F & 50 < F < 100\\ 100\,\dfrac{x - \min}{\max - \min} & F = 0\\ 100\,\dfrac{\max - x}{\max - \min} & F = 100\end{cases},\qquad MESS = \min_j S_j

symbols.F = 100\\,\\#\\{v \\le x\\}/n: percent of the reference values of the variable that are at or below the cell's value \( x \); min and max: extremes of the reference values. Option `full=True` also returns \( S_j \) per variable (bands `<name>_mess`).

metrics.use:
Use to mask projections into novel climates. It only looks at each variable separately; combinations of values
that never occurred together are not flagged (use ExDet or MOP for that).
refs: Elith et al. (2010). The art of modelling range-shifting species. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 1: 330-342.
metrics.value: a map: mean 1.345, from -68.22 to 90.16; 25936 cells without a value

metrics.name: Mobility-oriented parity distance (mop)
metrics.what:
For each cell, the mean distance in environmental space to its nearest reference conditions. Large values mean
the cell is unlike the conditions the model was fitted to, even inside the ranges.

symbols.d: Euclidean distance (optionally after centring and scaling both sets together) or Mahalanobis distance with the covariance of the reference conditions
symbols.n_r: number of reference points. Computed by default only in cells inside every variable's reference range (`where="in_range"`); other cells are NaN. `rescale` maps the values to 0-1.

metrics.use:
Compare with MESS (range only). The Mahalanobis form uses the reference covariance, unlike the R package, which
uses that of the tested cells.
refs: Owens et al. (2013). Constraints on interpretation of ecological niche models by limited environmental ranges on calibration areas. Ecological Modelling 263: 10-18.
metrics.value: a map: mean 64.15, from 17.44 to 734.8; 28849 cells without a value

metrics.name: MOP outside-range mask (basic, simple)
metrics.range: basic = 1 or NaN; simple ≥ 1 or NaN
metrics.what:
The band `basic` is 1 in cells where at least one variable is outside the reference range, NaN otherwise. With
`type="simple"` the band `simple` counts how many variables are outside.
metrics.formula: basic(x) = 1[\,\exists j:\; x_j < \min_j \lor x_j > \max_j\,],\qquad simple(x) = \sum_j 1[x_j < \min_j \lor x_j > \max_j]

symbols.\\min_j, \\max_j: extremes of variable \(j\) in the reference sample
symbols.x_j: value of variable \(j\) in the cell

metrics.use: A binary equivalent of MESS < 0; `simple` shows how many variables extrapolate.
metrics.value: a map: mean 1.172, from 1 to 2; 32800 cells without a value

metrics.name: MOP variables below / above range (low_combined, high_combined)
metrics.what:
With `type="detailed"`, two codes saying which variables are below and which above the reference range in each
cell: for each variable j (1-based) outside in that direction, 2^j is added.

symbols.j: position of the variable in the reference table, starting at 1. A code of 6 means variables 1 and 2 (2 + 4).

metrics.use: To map which variables drive extrapolation.
metrics.value: a map: mean 5.077, from 2 to 8; 35699 cells without a value

metrics.name: Univariate novelty (ExDet NT1)
metrics.what:
Where at least one variable is outside its reference range, the sum over the variables of how far outside it is,
in units of the reference range of that variable. It is 0 inside every range.

symbols.a_j, b_j: minimum and maximum of variable \( j \) in the reference sample. The band `exdet` holds NT1 where it is below 0.

metrics.use: Negative cells are univariate extrapolation; the more negative, the farther out.
refs: Mesgaran et al. (2014). Here be dragons: a tool for quantifying novelty due to covariate range and correlation change when projecting species distribution models. Diversity and Distributions 20: 1147-1159.
metrics.value: a map: mean -0.1908, from -0.7204 to -0.000407; 32800 cells without a value

metrics.name: Combinatorial novelty (ExDet NT2)
metrics.what:
For cells inside every variable's range, the squared Mahalanobis distance to the reference centre relative to
the largest such distance among the reference points. A value above 1 marks a combination of values (a
correlation structure) the reference sample never had.

symbols.R: reference points. The band `exdet` holds NT2 where NT1 = 0. Collinear predictors make \( \Sigma \) singular and raise an error.

metrics.use: Complements MESS and NT1: it finds novelty that no single variable shows.
refs: Mesgaran et al. (2014). Here be dragons: a tool for quantifying novelty due to covariate range and correlation change when projecting species distribution models. Diversity and Distributions 20: 1147-1159.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.1045, from 0.001738 to 0.7393; 28849 cells without a value

metrics.name: Most influential covariate (ExDet mic)
metrics.what:
The variable most responsible for the novelty of the cell (1-based position), or 0 for conditions that are
analogue.
metrics.formula: mic(x) = \begin{cases}\arg\min_j \dfrac{\min(x_j - a_j,\, b_j - x_j,\, 0)}{b_j - a_j} & NT1 < 0\\ \arg\max_k \dfrac{D^{2}(x) - D^{2}_{-k}(x)}{D^{2}_{-k}(x)} & NT2 > 1\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}

symbols.D^{2}_{-k}: squared Mahalanobis distance without variable \( k \) (reference centre and covariance recomputed). The R package dsmextra numbered the variables backwards in the combinatorial case; here it points to the right variable.

metrics.use: Use to explain why a projection extrapolates.
refs: Mesgaran et al. (2014). Here be dragons: a tool for quantifying novelty due to covariate range and correlation change when projecting species distribution models. Diversity and Distributions 20: 1147-1159.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.4939, from 0 to 3; 25937 cells without a value

families.title: Change and agreement
families.source: diffeR (Pontius & Santacruz), OpenLand (intensity analysis), lulcc (three-map comparison), MOLUSCE, r.futures.validation, Dinamica EGO (fuzzy similarity), mapaccuracy (Olofsson et al. 2014, Stehman 2014)
families.intro:
Measures that compare two maps of classes: an earlier and a later map of land use (change), a simulation and the observed
map (agreement), or a classified map and a sample of reference points (accuracy). They are the measures of the
[change detection](../../tutorials/change-detection/) and [land change](../../tutorials/land-change/) tutorials.

The cards show their values on the land use of Sibuyan Island, the Philippines, in 1997 and 2011 that ships with the
library (`lu`, two bands as the float arrays `t0` and `t1`, with 255 read as no value: 5 classes, 7 226 cells with data,
743 of them changed), and on `sim`, a simulated 2011 map made from them, since the island has no model run to judge: it
takes `t1`, undoes half of the changes (back to the 1997 class) and flips 1 percent of the cells that did not change, with
a seeded generator, so that each measure has something to say. It is not the result of any land change model. The accuracy
cards use the 2011 map, a stratified random sample of it (`pts`, 100 points at least in each class) whose reference
class is read from `sim`, standing in for the labels of an interpreter. The binary card uses forest (class 1) against
the rest, with the loss of forest as the change, and the card for the sample cross-tabulation a small toy table.

Conventions: a cross-tabulation `n` has the comparison map (or the earlier map) in the rows and the reference map (or the
later map) in the columns; cells without a value in any map are left out.
families.example:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import terraflux as tf

lu = tf.load_raster(tf.simulate.example_data("sibuyan_landuse"))      # Sibuyan Island, 1997 and 2011, 5 classes
t0 = np.asarray(lu.isel(band=0)).astype(float)
t1 = np.asarray(lu.isel(band=1)).astype(float)
t0[t0 == 255] = np.nan                                                # 255 is no value
t1[t1 == 255] = np.nan

# a simulated 2011: undo half of the changes and flip 1 percent of the cells that did not change
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
sim = t1.copy()
changed = (t0 != t1) & ~np.isnan(t0) & ~np.isnan(t1)
undo = changed & (rng.random(t0.shape) < 0.5)
sim[undo] = t0[undo]
stay = ~changed & ~np.isnan(t0)
flip = stay & (rng.random(t0.shape) < 0.01)
sim[flip] = np.where(t0[flip] == 1, 2, 1)

zones = np.where(np.arange(t1.shape[1]) < t1.shape[1] // 2, 1.0, 2.0) * np.ones(t1.shape)   # a west and an east stratum
nonforest = lambda a: np.where(np.isnan(a), np.nan, (a != 1).astype(float))                # the rest against forest (class 1)
o, r, s = nonforest(t0), nonforest(t1), nonforest(sim)

pts = tf.accuracy.sample(lu.isel(band=1), n=100, seed=1)               # a stratified sample of the 2011 map
pts["reference"] = sim[pts["row"], pts["col"]]                         # its reference labels, read from the simulation

metrics.name: Transition (cross-tabulation) matrix
metrics.what:
The number of cells of class i in the first map and class j in the second. It is the input of every disagreement
and kappa measure.
metrics.formula: n_{ij} = \#\{\text{cells with class } i \text{ in the first map and } j \text{ in the second}\}

symbols.N: total number of cells; the diagonal \(n_{ii}\) holds the persistence

metrics.use:
For change between two dates read it as from (rows) to (columns); for error as comparison (rows) and reference
(columns).

metrics.name: Gain, loss and persistence of a class (Gain, Loss, Persistence)
metrics.unit: cells (or the unit of the matrix)
metrics.what:
For each class, the cells that arrived in it (gain), left it (loss) and stayed (persistence) between two maps.
The same columns are named Omission, Commission and Agreement when the matrix compares a map with a reference.
metrics.formula: Gain_j = n_{+j} - n_{jj},\qquad Loss_i = n_{i+} - n_{ii},\qquad Persistence_i = n_{ii}

symbols.n_{ij}: rows the earlier map, columns the later map. In `analysis="error"` (rows the comparison, columns the reference) `Omission` = \( n_{+j} - n_{jj} \), `Commission` = \( n_{i+} - n_{ii} \), `Agreement` = \( n_{ii} \) (diffeR spells it "Comission").

metrics.use: Gain and loss show change by class; quantity, exchange and shift (below) split them further.
refs: Pontius & Santacruz (2014). Quantity, exchange, and shift components of difference in a square contingency table. International Journal of Remote Sensing 35: 7543-7554.

metrics.name: Quantity difference
metrics.unit: cells (or the unit of the matrix)
metrics.what:
The part of the difference between two maps that comes from a different number of cells in each class (the net
change), independent of where they are.

symbols.n_{i+}, n_{+i}: row and column totals of class \( i \). The overall row of `difference_components` halves the sum because each unit of net change counts in two classes.

metrics.use: A map with the right quantities but wrong places has Q = 0 and all its disagreement in allocation.
refs: Pontius & Millones (2011). Death to Kappa: birth of quantity disagreement and allocation disagreement for accuracy assessment. International Journal of Remote Sensing 32: 4407-4429. doi:10.1080/01431161.2011.552923

metrics.name: Exchange difference
metrics.unit: cells (or the unit of the matrix)
metrics.what:
The part of the allocation difference that is a swap: cells of class i that went to class j balanced by cells of
j that went to i.
metrics.formula: E_i = \sum_{j \neq i} 2\min(n_{ij}, n_{ji}),\qquad E = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i E_i = \sum_{i<j} 2\min(n_{ij}, n_{ji})

symbols.n_{ij}: cells of the cross-tabulation. In the overall row each swap is counted once.

metrics.use: Exchange needs two classes; a pure one-way transition has none.
refs: Pontius & Santacruz (2014). Quantity, exchange, and shift components of difference in a square contingency table. International Journal of Remote Sensing 35: 7543-7554.

metrics.name: Shift difference
metrics.unit: cells (or the unit of the matrix)
metrics.what:
The part of the allocation difference that is not an exchange: cells that move among three or more classes
without a matching reverse flow.
metrics.formula: S_i = (n_{i+} + n_{+i} - 2n_{ii}) - Q_i - E_i,\qquad S = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i S_i

symbols.Q_i, E_i: quantity and exchange of class \( i \).

metrics.use: Shift usually shrinks fastest as the resolution coarsens (see difference_resolutions).
refs: Pontius & Santacruz (2014). Quantity, exchange, and shift components of difference in a square contingency table. International Journal of Remote Sensing 35: 7543-7554.

metrics.name: Allocation and overall difference
metrics.unit: cells (or the unit of the matrix)
metrics.what:
The allocation difference is the part of the total disagreement that is not quantity (exchange plus shift); the
overall difference is everything off the diagonal.
metrics.formula: D = \sum_{i \neq j} n_{ij} = Q + A,\qquad A = E + S
metrics.use: Report quantity and allocation separately: they point to different causes (demand versus location).
refs: Pontius & Millones (2011). Death to Kappa: birth of quantity disagreement and allocation disagreement for accuracy assessment. International Journal of Remote Sensing 32: 4407-4429. doi:10.1080/01431161.2011.552923

metrics.name: Differences at coarser resolutions (Multiples, Resolution)
metrics.what:
Quantity, exchange, shift and overall difference when the maps are compared at blocks of factor^k cells. The
differences generally fall as the blocks grow, since small displacements cancel inside a block.
metrics.formula: Q^{(f)},\; E^{(f)},\; S^{(f)},\; D^{(f)} \text{ of the composite matrix of blocks of side } f

symbols.f: block side in cells (1, `factor`, `factor`², ...). At \( f = 1 \) the ordinary matrix, at coarser sizes the composite matrix (below), as a percent of the domain. Blocks cut by the edge or with a missing cell are left out, which can make the coarsest rows NaN.

metrics.use:
Shows at what spatial scale the model is right: disagreement that vanishes at 4-cell blocks was only a small
displacement.
refs: Pontius (2002). Statistical methods to partition effects of quantity and location during comparison of categorical maps at multiple resolutions. Photogrammetric Engineering and Remote Sensing 68: 1041-1049.
Pontius & Cheuk (2006). A generalized cross-tabulation matrix to compare soft-classified maps at multiple resolutions. International Journal of Geographical Information Science 20: 1-30.

metrics.name: Composite cross-tabulation (composite)
metrics.what:
A cross-tabulation at a coarser resolution in which each block of cells is a mix of classes. The agreement of a
class in a block is the smaller of its two shares; the remainder is spread over pairs of classes.
metrics.formula: n_{ii} = \frac{\sum_b w_b \min(c_{ib}, r_{ib})}{\sum_b w_b},\qquad n_{ij} = \frac{\sum_b w_b \dfrac{(c_{ib} - m_{ib})(r_{jb} - m_{jb})}{1 - \sum_k m_{kb}}}{\sum_b w_b}\; (i \neq j)

symbols.c_{ib}, r_{ib}: share of class \( i \) in block \( b \) of the comparison and the reference map; \( m_{ib} = \min(c_{ib}, r_{ib}) \)

metrics.use: The matrix whose differences `chg_resolutions` reports. Needs complete blocks.
refs: Pontius & Cheuk (2006). A generalized cross-tabulation matrix to compare soft-classified maps at multiple resolutions. International Journal of Geographical Information Science 20: 1-30.

metrics.name: Class membership of a block (memberships)
metrics.what:
The share of each class in every block of factor x factor cells; blocks with a missing cell or cut by the edge
are NaN.
metrics.use: The input of the composite method and of any fuzzy comparison at coarse resolution.
metrics.value: a map: mean 0.6314, from 0 to 1; 456 cells without a value

metrics.name: Sample cross-tabulation scaled to the population
metrics.what:
Rescales each row of a sample cross-tabulation to the known size of its class in the population, so that the
sample counts estimate map areas.

symbols.P_i: population (e.g. cells) of the row's class
symbols.n_{ij}: sample counts. Unlike diffeR the row is matched to its population by class, not by position.

metrics.use: For a stratified sample whose strata are the classes of the map.
refs: Olofsson et al. (2014). Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change. Remote Sensing of Environment 148: 42-57. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015

metrics.name: MAD quantity
metrics.what:
For two continuous maps, the part of the mean absolute deviation due to a net difference in the mean (bias) over
the strata.
metrics.use: Zero when the two maps have the same mean.
refs: Pontius et al. (2008). Components of information for multiple resolution comparison between maps that share a real variable. Environmental and Ecological Statistics 15: 111-142.

metrics.name: MAD strata
metrics.what: The part of the MAD due to deviations that cancel inside each stratum but not between strata.

symbols.h: the strata (one by default, and then this term is 0)

metrics.use:
Give a `strata` map to see whether the bias differs between regions. The term is 0 when the net deviation has
the same sign in every stratum, as here with a west and an east half.

metrics.name: MAD element
metrics.what:
The rest of the MAD: the cell-level deviations that cancel when the maps are summed over larger blocks. It falls
to zero at coarse resolutions.

symbols.MAD, MAD_{Q}, MAD_{S}: the total, quantity and strata parts of the card above and below; computed per resolution from sums of the deviations over blocks of 2, 4, 8, ... cells (`multiple=True`)

metrics.use: Shows how much of the error is a displacement at fine scale.

metrics.name: Mean absolute deviation (MAD total)
metrics.what: The mean absolute difference between two continuous maps over the cells with data.

symbols.x_c, y_c: values of cell \(c\) in the two maps
symbols.n: cells with data in both; the total of the components, `Total`

metrics.use: Unlike RMSE it is not dominated by outliers.

metrics.name: Number of changes per cell (change count)
metrics.what: For a series of maps, how many times each cell changed class, and the share of the area with each count.

symbols.x_{c,t}: class of cell \( c \) at time \( t \). Cells missing in any map get -1 and are excluded from the shares.

metrics.use: Highlights cells that flicker (map errors or shifting cultivation) versus stable change.
refs: Exavier & Zeilhofer (2020). OpenLand: software for quantitative analysis and visualization of land use and cover change. The R Journal 12(2): 359-371 (function acc_changes). doi:10.32614/RJ-2021-021

metrics.name: Interval change (PercentChange, St)
metrics.unit: % of the study area (PercentChange); % per time unit (St)
metrics.what: The share of the study area that changed in a time interval, and the same per year (annual change intensity).

symbols.C_t: area that changed in interval \( t \)
symbols.A: study area (the first period's total).

metrics.use:
The interval level of the intensity analysis; compare \( S_t \) between periods and with the uniform intensity
U.
refs: Aldwaik & Pontius (2012). Intensity analysis to unify measurements of size and stationarity of land changes by interval, category, and transition. Landscape and Urban Planning 106: 103-114.
Exavier & Zeilhofer (2020). OpenLand: software for quantitative analysis and visualization of land use and cover change. The R Journal 12(2): 359-371. doi:10.32614/RJ-2021-021

metrics.name: Uniform change intensity (U)
metrics.what:
The annual intensity that would apply if the change were spread evenly over the whole series. Intervals with St
above U are fast, below U slow.

symbols.\\Delta: the total length of the series

metrics.use: The reference line of the interval level.
refs: Aldwaik & Pontius (2012). Intensity analysis to unify measurements of size and stationarity of land changes by interval, category, and transition. Landscape and Urban Planning 106: 103-114.

metrics.name: Category gain intensity (Gtj)
metrics.what:
For each class and interval, the gross gain relative to the size of the class at the end of the interval. Gains
are active when Gtj exceeds the interval intensity St.

symbols.GG_{tj}: area gained by class \( j \) in interval \( t \) (`GG_km2`)
symbols.A_{t+1,j}: area of class \( j \) at the end of the interval.

metrics.use:
Class levels of the intensity analysis; `Test` = Y in the stationarity table says the class is active (or
dormant) in every interval.
refs: Aldwaik & Pontius (2012). Intensity analysis to unify measurements of size and stationarity of land changes by interval, category, and transition. Landscape and Urban Planning 106: 103-114.

metrics.name: Category loss intensity (Lti)
metrics.what:
For each class and interval, the gross loss relative to the size of the class at the start. Losses are active
when Lti exceeds St.

symbols.A_{t,i}: area of class \( i \) at the start.

metrics.use: As Gtj.
refs: Aldwaik & Pontius (2012). Intensity analysis to unify measurements of size and stationarity of land changes by interval, category, and transition. Landscape and Urban Planning 106: 103-114.

metrics.name: Transition intensity into a class (Rtin, Wtn)
metrics.what:
For the chosen gaining class n, how intensively it takes over each other class i (Rtin), compared with the
uniform intensity of its gains over all the classes that could be taken (Wtn). Class i is targeted by n when
Rtin > Wtn.

symbols.T_{tin}: area that changed from \( i \) to \( n \) (`T_i2n_km2`)
symbols.A_{t,i}: area of \( i \) at the start
symbols.GG_{tn}: gain of \( n \). Chosen with `gain=` of `intensity`.

metrics.use:
Tells whether a land use expands preferentially into particular classes. Targeted / avoided classes are listed
in the transition stationarity table.
refs: Aldwaik & Pontius (2012). Intensity analysis to unify measurements of size and stationarity of land changes by interval, category, and transition. Landscape and Urban Planning 106: 103-114.

metrics.name: Transition intensity out of a class (Qtmj, Vtm)
metrics.what:
For the chosen losing class m, how intensively it is lost to each other class j (Qtmj), compared with the
uniform intensity of its losses over all the classes that could take it (Vtm). Class j targets m when Qtmj >
Vtm.

symbols.T_{tmj}: area that changed from \( m \) to \( j \) (`T_m2j_km2`)
symbols.A_{t+1,j}: area of \( j \) at the end
symbols.GL_{tm}: loss of \( m \). Chosen with `loss=` of `intensity`.

metrics.use: Tells which classes replace a given land use.
refs: Aldwaik & Pontius (2012). Intensity analysis to unify measurements of size and stationarity of land changes by interval, category, and transition. Landscape and Urban Planning 106: 103-114.

metrics.name: Stationarity test (active / dormant, targeted / avoided)
metrics.what:
Counts in how many intervals each class (or transition) is above or below the uniform intensity, and says (Test
= Y) whether this holds in every interval, meaning a stable pattern.
metrics.formula: Test = \begin{cases}Y & \#\{t: G_{tj} > S_t\} = N\\ N & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}\quad\text{(likewise for } L_{ti} \text{ vs } S_t,\; R_{tin} \text{ vs } W_{tn},\; Q_{tmj} \text{ vs } V_{tm})

symbols.N: number of intervals. Labels: Active / Dormant Gain and Loss; targeted / avoided by the chosen gain and loss class.

metrics.use: Only meaningful with several intervals; with one it always says Y.
metrics.value:
To  Gain  N Stationarity Test
  2     1  1  Active Gain    Y
  3     1  1  Active Gain    Y
  4     1  1  Active Gain    Y
  5     1  1 Dormant Gain    Y

metrics.name: Cohen's kappa of two maps
metrics.what: The agreement of two maps cell by cell beyond what chance would give from the class proportions of each map.
metrics.formula: \kappa = \frac{P_o - P_e}{1 - P_e},\quad P_o = \sum_i p_{ii},\quad P_e = \sum_i p_{i+}\, p_{+i}

symbols.p_{ij} = n_{ij}/N: cross-tabulation in proportions over the classes of both maps

metrics.use:
Overall agreement can look high only because one class dominates; kappa corrects for that but conflates quantity
and location (use the next two variants or the disagreement components).
refs: Cohen (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement 20: 37-46.
MOLUSCE plugin for QGIS (validation tab).

metrics.name: Kappa for location (klocation)
metrics.what:
How well the maps agree in location given the quantities of the classes: kappa rescaled by the best agreement
possible with those quantities.

symbols.P_o, P_e: observed agreement and the agreement expected by chance (see kappa)
symbols.p_{i+}, p_{+i}: marginals of the cross-tabulation in proportions; returned as `kappa_location`

metrics.use: High when allocation is right even if the quantities are off.
refs: Pontius (2000). Quantification error versus location error in comparison of categorical maps. Photogrammetric Engineering and Remote Sensing 66: 1011-1016.
MOLUSCE plugin for QGIS (validation tab).

metrics.name: Kappa for quantity (khisto)
metrics.what:
How well the class quantities of the two maps match: the best kappa that could be reached with the quantities,
given perfect location.

symbols.P_o, P_e, P_{max}: observed agreement, expected by chance and the largest possible given the quantities (see kappa for the first two, kappa for location for the last)
symbols.\\kappa_{loc}: kappa for location; returned as `kappa_histogram`, and \(\kappa = \kappa_{loc}\,\kappa_{histo}\)

metrics.use: Low when the simulated demand differs from the observed.
refs: MOLUSCE plugin for QGIS (validation tab).

metrics.name: Correctness
metrics.what: The percent of cells with the same class in both maps.

symbols.n_{ii}: cells of class \(i\) in both maps (the diagonal of the cross-tabulation)
symbols.N: total number of cells with data

metrics.use: Inflated by persistence when most cells do not change: compare with the null model (no change).

metrics.name: Cramer's V
metrics.what:
The strength of the association between the classes of the two maps, from the chi-square of their
cross-tabulation (computed over the classes each map actually has).

symbols.r, c: number of classes of each map; V is NaN if a map has one class

metrics.use: Measures association, not agreement: a map that swaps two classes still has a high V.

metrics.name: Joint information uncertainty (JIU)
metrics.what:
The information the two maps share, relative to the information they carry in total (a normalised mutual
information).
metrics.formula: JIU = \frac{2\,\bigl(H_x + H_y - H_{xy}\bigr)}{H_x + H_y},\qquad H = -\sum p \ln p

symbols.H_x, H_y: entropies of the class distributions of the two maps

metrics.use: 1 when one map determines the other. Like V, it ignores which class is which.

metrics.name: Correlation of class values
metrics.what: The Pearson correlation between the numeric class codes of the two maps over cells with data.

symbols.x_c, y_c: class codes of cell \( c \) in the two maps.

metrics.use: Only meaningful for ordered classes; with nominal codes read it as a rough check.

metrics.name: Overall agreement and class quantity (validate.agreement)
metrics.what:
The share of cells where the simulated and the observed map are the same class, and for each class the
difference between the number of simulated and observed cells.

symbols.o_c, s_c: observed and simulated class of cell \( c \) (cells with a value in the observed, the simulated and the starting map).

metrics.use: A simple check of the demand: the quantity of each class should be close to 0.

metrics.name: Hits, misses, false alarms and wrong hits
metrics.unit: cells (agreement) or share of the cells (three-map)
metrics.what:
The four ways a simulation can treat a cell relative to the starting map. A miss is observed change simulated as
persistence; a hit is change simulated correctly; a wrong hit is change simulated as a different class; a false
alarm is persistence simulated as change.
metrics.formula:
hits = \#\{o 
eq a,\, s 
eq a,\, s = o\},\quad misses = \#\{o 
eq a,\, s = a\},\quad wrong = \#\{o 
eq a,\, s 
eq a,\, s 
eq o\},\quad false = \#\{o = a,\, s 
eq a\}

symbols.a, o, s: class of a cell in the start, observed and simulated maps. Counts in `agreement`; shares of the area in `agreement_budget` (three-map), which adds `correct_rejections` (persistence simulated as persistence).

metrics.use: Judge a simulation by these and not by overall agreement, which is dominated by persistence.
refs: Pontius et al. (2008). Comparing the input, output, and validation maps for several models of land change. Annals of Regional Science 42: 11-37.

Pontius et al. (2011). Comparison of three maps at multiple resolutions: a case study of land change simulation in Cho Don District, Vietnam. Annals of the Association of American Geographers 101: 45-62.
metrics.python: {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in tf.simulate.agreement(t1, sim, t0).items() if k != "quantity"}

metrics.name: Figure of merit
metrics.what:
The share of the area of observed or simulated change where both agree: hits divided by the sum of hits, misses,
wrong hits and false alarms. It ignores persistence, so it is not inflated by the cells that did not change.

symbols.F: false alarms. `validate.agreement` uses this form; the FUTURES binary version (below) has no wrong hits.

metrics.use:
A simulation without any change scores 0. Typical values are low (10-30 percent); compare with other models, not
with 1.
refs: Pontius et al. (2008). Comparing the input, output, and validation maps for several models of land change. Annals of Regional Science 42: 11-37.

metrics.name: Three-map agreement budget
metrics.range: 0 ≤ x ≤ 1; the five components sum to 1
metrics.what:
A comparison of the map at the start, the reference at the end and the simulated map at the end, at one or more
resolutions. It splits the area into misses, hits, wrong hits, false alarms and correct rejections, for the
whole map, for each class and for each transition.
metrics.formula:
misses = \sum_{i 
eq j} T_{iji},\quad hits = \sum_{i 
eq j} T_{ijj},\quad wrong = \sum_{i,j,k 	ext{ distinct}} T_{ijk},\quad false = \sum_{j 
eq k} T_{jjk},\quad correct\ rejections = \sum_i T_{iii}

symbols.T_{ijk}: share of the area with class \( i \) in the start map, \( j \) in the reference end map and \( k \) in the simulated end map (the three-dimensional table, `ThreeMapComparison.table()`). Per class or transition the sums are restricted to the starting class (and end class); rows with from equal to to are not meaningful.

metrics.use: At coarser resolutions (`factors`), blocks give partial credit to near misses.
refs: Pontius et al. (2011). Comparison of three maps at multiple resolutions: a case study of land change simulation in Cho Don District, Vietnam. Annals of the Association of American Geographers 101: 45-62.
Moulds et al. (2015). An open and extensible framework for spatially explicit land use change modelling: the lulcc R package. Geoscientific Model Development 8: 3215-3229 (function AgreementBudget).

level  from  to  factor  misses   hits  wrong_hits  false_alarms  correct_rejections
overall   NaN NaN       1  0.0545 0.0483      0.0000        0.0077              0.8894
overall   NaN NaN       4  0.0514 0.0476      0.0026        0.0071              0.8914

metrics.name: Three-map figure of merit (overall, class, transition)
metrics.what:
The figure of merit at the three levels of the three-map comparison: overall, for change from each class and for
each from-to transition, at each resolution.
metrics.formula: FoM = \frac{H}{1 - CR},\qquad FoM_i = \frac{H_i}{M_i + H_i + W_i + F_i},\qquad FoM_{ij} = \frac{H_{ij}}{H_{ij} + M_{ij} + F_{ij}}

symbols.H, M, W, F: hits, misses, wrong hits and false alarms for the whole map or for class \( i \); for a transition \( i \to j \) the denominator is the area of observed \( i \to j \) plus that of simulated \( i \to j \) minus the hits.

metrics.use: The overall value equals `figure_of_merit` of `validate.agreement` at factor 1.
refs: Pontius et al. (2011). Comparison of three maps at multiple resolutions: a case study of land change simulation in Cho Don District, Vietnam. Annals of the Association of American Geographers 101: 45-62 (eqs. 9-11).
Moulds et al. (2015). An open and extensible framework for spatially explicit land use change modelling: the lulcc R package. Geoscientific Model Development 8: 3215-3229 (function FigureOfMerit).

metrics.name: Error budget levels (no_no ... perfect_perfect)
metrics.what:
The agreement expected when the model has no, medium or perfect information about the quantity and location of
change: no_no, no_medium, medium_medium, medium_perfect and perfect_perfect (always 1), at the map's resolution
and at coarser ones.

symbols.r_{ck}, s_{ck}: indicator (share, after aggregation) of class \( k \) in cell or block \( c \) of the reference and the simulated map
symbols.K: number of classes. The difference between the levels shows what is gained by knowing the quantities and the locations.

metrics.use: From MOLUSCE's validation: a simulation is only worth trusting if medium_medium is well above no_medium.
refs: Pontius (2002). Statistical methods to partition effects of quantity and location during comparison of categorical maps at multiple resolutions. Photogrammetric Engineering and Remote Sensing 68: 1041-1049.
MOLUSCE plugin for QGIS (validation tab).

metrics.name: Quantity disagreement (FUTURES)
metrics.what:
The disagreement per class due to a different amount of that class in the simulated and the reference map, and
its total over the map.

symbols.n_{k+}: cells of class \( k \) in the simulation
symbols.n_{+k}: in the reference. Returned as `quantity` (per class) and `total_quantity`.

metrics.use: The same as `chg_quantity` in shares.
refs: Pontius & Millones (2011). Death to Kappa: birth of quantity disagreement and allocation disagreement for accuracy assessment. International Journal of Remote Sensing 32: 4407-4429. doi:10.1080/01431161.2011.552923
r.futures.validation, GRASS GIS addon.

metrics.name: Allocation disagreement (FUTURES)
metrics.what: The disagreement per class from cells being in the wrong place even when the amount is right, and its total.
metrics.formula: a_k = \frac{2\min\bigl(n_{k+} - n_{kk},\, n_{+k} - n_{kk}\bigr)}{N},\qquad A = \frac{1}{2}\sum_k a_k

symbols.n_{kk}: cells of class \(k\) in both maps
symbols.n_{k+}, n_{+k}: cells of class \(k\) in the simulation and in the reference; returned as `allocation` and `total_allocation`

metrics.use:
Quantity plus allocation equals 1 minus the overall agreement; it is the same split as the quantity and exchange
+ shift of diffeR.
refs: Pontius & Millones (2011). Death to Kappa: birth of quantity disagreement and allocation disagreement for accuracy assessment. International Journal of Remote Sensing 32: 4407-4429. doi:10.1080/01431161.2011.552923
r.futures.validation, GRASS GIS addon.

metrics.name: Kappa simulation
metrics.what:
A kappa whose expected agreement accounts for the change that took place: how much better the simulation agrees
with the reference than a model that knew each class's overall transition probabilities but not where. It is 0
when no better than that.
metrics.formula: \kappa_{sim} = \frac{P_o - P_e^{sim}}{1 - P_e^{sim}},\qquad P_e^{sim} = \sum_i d_i \sum_j P(s{=}j \mid o_0{=}i)\,P(r{=}j \mid o_0{=}i)

symbols.P_o: proportion of cells with the simulated class equal to the reference
symbols.d_i: share of cells of class \( i \) in the original (start) map
symbols.P(s{=}j \\mid o_0{=}i): share of start-class-\( i \) cells that are \( j \) in the simulation, and \( P(r{=}j \mid o_0{=}i) \) in the reference. Returned as `kappasimulation` when the original map is given.

metrics.use: A fairer benchmark than kappa for land change, where persistence inflates agreement.
refs: van Vliet et al. (2011). Revisiting Kappa to account for change in the accuracy assessment of land-use change models. Ecological Modelling 222: 1367-1375.

metrics.name: Binary change metrics (FUTURES)
metrics.what:
For two classes (for example undeveloped and developed) with the original map given: misses, hits, false alarms,
null successes (persistence simulated correctly) and initially developed, as shares of the cells, plus the
figure of merit, producer's and user's accuracy of the change.
metrics.formula: FoM = \frac{H}{M + H + F},\qquad producer = \frac{H}{M + H},\qquad user = \frac{H}{H + F}

symbols.H, M, F: hits, misses and false alarms of the cells that were class 0 at the start (class 1 gain is the change); `initially_developed` is the share of cells already 1. There are no wrong hits with two classes.

metrics.use: Without wrong hits, the FoM here equals the general one. Run on 0/1 maps (for example forest or not).
refs: Pontius et al. (2008). Comparing the input, output, and validation maps for several models of land change. Annals of Regional Science 42: 11-37.
r.futures.validation, GRASS GIS addon.
metrics.python: {k: round(v, 4) if isinstance(v, float) else v for k, v in tf.simulate.futures_validation(r, s, o).items() if k not in ("quantity", "allocation")}

metrics.name: Fuzzy similarity of two maps
metrics.what:
For each cell with a class, how well that class is found nearby in the other map: 1 if present in the cell,
2^(-d/2) for the nearest cell of the class at d cells inside a square window, 0 if none. The map mean is the
similarity.

symbols.d_c: distance in cells from \( c \) to the nearest cell of the same class in the other map inside the \( w \times w \) window around \( c \) (\( m_c = 0 \) if there is none)
symbols.m^{rev}_c: the reverse membership, taken where the other map has a class too (`decay="constant"` gives 1 everywhere in the window). The two means are `first_mean`, `second_mean`; the smaller is `minimum` (Dinamica's two-way similarity).

metrics.use: Tolerates small displacements, unlike cell-by-cell agreement. The result depends on the window size and decay.
refs: Hagen (2003). Fuzzy set approach to assessing similarity of categorical maps. International Journal of Geographical Information Science 17: 235-249.
Dinamica EGO software (CSR, UFMG).

metrics.name: Similarity of the changes (per window)
metrics.what:
The fuzzy similarity of the observed change and the simulated change: only cells that changed since the start
are compared, each in its new class, in windows of growing size. The result per window is the smaller of the two
means.

symbols.\\bar{s}^{sim}_w: mean similarity over the simulated changes
symbols.\\bar{s}^{obs}_w: over the observed changes, both in a window of side \( w \). Columns `simulated`, `observed`, `minimum` and the number of cells of each.

metrics.use:
Dinamica EGO's validation: a simulation is acceptable when the minimum similarity reaches about 0.5 at the
window of the spatial tolerance you accept. Windows are odd (1 = exact).
refs: Hagen (2003). Fuzzy set approach to assessing similarity of categorical maps. International Journal of Geographical Information Science 17: 235-249.
Dinamica EGO software (CSR, UFMG).

metrics.name: Overall accuracy (with standard error)
metrics.what:
The proportion of the map's area that is correctly classified, estimated from a stratified random sample of
reference points; given with its standard error and confidence interval.
metrics.formula: OA = \sum_j \hat{p}_{jj},\quad \hat{p}_{ij} = W_i\,\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{i+}},\quad SE(OA) = \sqrt{\sum_i W_i^{2}\,\frac{U_i(1 - U_i)}{n_{i+} - 1}},\quad CI = z\,SE

symbols.W_i = A_i/A: mapped area share of stratum (map class) \( i \)
symbols.n_{ij}: sample points of map class \( i \) with reference class \( j \)
symbols.z: normal quantile of `confidence` (0.95). With `strata` of their own (`estimator="stehman"`) the estimator of Stehman (2014) with finite population correction is used.

metrics.use:
Not the share of sample points that agree, unless the sample is proportional. Needs a design-based sample
(`accuracy.sample`).
refs: Olofsson et al. (2014). Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change. Remote Sensing of Environment 148: 42-57. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015
Stehman (2014). Estimating area and map accuracy for stratified random sampling when the strata are different from the map classes. International Journal of Remote Sensing 35: 4923-4939.
metrics.value:
overall_accuracy  overall_se  overall_ci  samples  cells  confidence
           0.9408        0.01      0.0196    500.0 7226.0        0.95

metrics.name: User's accuracy (with standard error)
metrics.what:
For each map class, the probability that a cell mapped as that class really is that class: 1 minus the
commission error.

symbols.\\hat{p}_{jj}, \\hat{p}_{j+}: estimated area share of the cells mapped as class \(j\) that are \(j\), and of all cells mapped as \(j\)
symbols.n_{jj}, n_{j+}: sample points mapped and referenced as \(j\), and mapped as \(j\); columns `user_accuracy`, `user_se`, `user_ci`

metrics.use: Tells the map user how far to trust a class.
refs: Olofsson et al. (2014). Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change. Remote Sensing of Environment 148: 42-57. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015

metrics.name: Producer's accuracy (with standard error)
metrics.what:
For each reference class, the probability that a cell that really is that class was mapped as such: 1 minus the
omission error, weighted by the mapped areas.

symbols.\\hat{p}_{jj}: estimated area share of the cells that are class \(j\) in both the map and the reference
symbols.\\hat{p}_{+j}: estimated area share of reference class \(j\); the standard error follows Olofsson et al. (2014), eq. 6; columns `producer_accuracy`, `producer_se`, `producer_ci`

metrics.use: Differs from the share of the class's points correctly mapped because the strata have different sizes.
refs: Olofsson et al. (2014). Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change. Remote Sensing of Environment 148: 42-57. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015

metrics.name: Estimated class area (with confidence interval)
metrics.what:
The area of each class estimated from the sample (error-adjusted), instead of counted on the map, with its
standard error and confidence interval. It corrects for the classification errors.

symbols.A: total number of cells
symbols.\\hat{p}_{+j}: estimated area share of class \( j \). Columns `area_share`, `area_cells`, `area_ha` and their `se` / `ci`; hectares use `cell_area` (m2).

metrics.use:
Report these areas with their intervals, particularly for rare classes and change, where the map count is
biased.
refs: Olofsson et al. (2013). Making better use of accuracy data in land change studies: estimating accuracy and area and quantifying uncertainty using stratified estimation. Remote Sensing of Environment 129: 122-131.
Olofsson et al. (2014). Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change. Remote Sensing of Environment 148: 42-57. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015

metrics.name: Estimated error matrix (area proportions)
metrics.what:
The confusion matrix with each cell given as an estimated proportion of the map area, so that it accounts for
the unequal sampling of the strata. The matrix of sample counts is also returned.

symbols.\\hat{p}_{ij}: estimated share of the area mapped as class \(i\) whose reference class is \(j\) (rows the map, columns the reference; cells without sample points are NaN)
symbols.n_{ij}, n_{i+}: sample points of map class \(i\) with reference class \(j\), and all those of class \(i\)

metrics.use:
The base from which user's, producer's and overall accuracy and the areas are derived; report it with the sample
size.
refs: Olofsson et al. (2014). Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change. Remote Sensing of Environment 148: 42-57. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015

families.title: Fragmentation
families.source: GuidosToolbox (FAD, FOS, contagion, clustering, entropy, landscape mosaic) and GraySpatCon / Riitters et al.
families.intro:
Moving-window measures of how much habitat surrounds each habitat cell and how it is arranged: the foreground area
density (FAD) and its six fragmentation classes, the fixed observation scale (FOS) with its three methods, Riitters'
contagion and clustering, the spatial entropy, GraySpatCon's statistics of a percentage map, and the landscape mosaic
of agriculture, natural and developed land. They are the measures of the
[fragmentation tutorials](../../tutorials/fragmentation/fragmentation-and-habitat-loss/), and of GuidosToolbox.

The cards use the three maps of those tutorials: `forest`, the forest map of GuidosToolbox's sample (1000 x 1000 cells
of 25 m, coded 0 missing, 1 background, 2 forest); `cover`, GraySpatCon's sample of the percentage of tree cover of the
conterminous United States (1289 x 1990 cells of 2.43 km, 0 to 100, 255 missing); and `three`, the CORINE land cover
around Hannover in the mosaic's three groups (1 agriculture, 2 natural, 3 developed, 0 missing: the water is in none).

A window is a square of an odd number of cells around each cell. The maps of percentages are bytes, as in
GuidosToolbox: 0 to 100 on the habitat, 101 on the background and 102 on missing cells, so their values are whole
percent; the cards keep the habitat cells (`.where(forest == 2)`), so that the mean of a map is the mean over the
habitat.
families.example:
import terraflux as tf

# forest of GuidosToolbox's sample (1000 x 1000 cells of 25 m): 0 missing, 1 background, 2 forest
forest = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("input"))
# % tree cover of the conterminous United States (GraySpatCon's sample): 0-100, 255 missing
cover = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("gscinput"))
# CORINE around Hannover in the landscape mosaic's three groups: 1 agriculture, 2 natural, 3 developed, 0 missing
three = tf.reclassify(tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("clc")), [(1, 12, 3), (12, 23, 1), (23, 40, 2)], others=0)

metrics.name: Foreground area density (FAD)
metrics.what:
The share of habitat (foreground) among the cells of a window centred on each habitat cell: how much of the
neighbourhood is habitat. It is the basis of the six fragmentation classes, from rare to intact.

symbols.n_f: the habitat cells (code 2) in the window
symbols.n_v: the valid cells of the window, all but the missing (0) and the non-fragmenting special background (4); at the border of the map the window is clipped, not padded

metrics.use:
Use it for the local amount of habitat at one scale of observation, the window; quote the window in metres with the
result. It says how much habitat there is around a cell, not how it is arranged: contagion and clustering add that.
The value is quantised as in GuidosToolbox: the proportion is cut to steps of 1/254, rounded to a whole percent and
held at 99 unless the window has no background at all, so 100 means an all-habitat window.
refs: Riitters, K. H., Wickham, J. D., O'Neill, R. V., Jones, K. B., Smith, E. R., Coulston, J. W., et al. (2002). Fragmentation of continental United States forests. *Ecosystems*, 5(8), 815-822. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10021-002-0209-2

metrics.name: Multiscale FAD
metrics.what:
The mean of the FAD maps of several windows (by default 7, 13, 27, 81 and 243 cells), which blends the near and the
broad neighbourhood in one map. It is classified into the same six classes as FAD.

symbols.FAD^{(k)}_i: the FAD of cell \(i\) in window \(k\), in whole percent; the cells that are not habitat keep their codes of background and missing

metrics.use:
Use it to rank habitat cells by the habitat around them across scales, when no single scale is the right one for
the question. Quote the list of windows with the result.

metrics.name: FOS by foreground area density
metrics.what:
The fixed observation scale (FOS) map with the FAD method: the share of habitat in the window, taken as the
connectivity of each habitat cell, with GuidosToolbox's reports (class shares, ECA, coherence). On a map of
percent cover the habitat is the cover at or above a threshold, and the value is the mean cover in the window.

symbols.n_f: the habitat cells of the window; on a percent map, the cells with a cover of at least `gray_threshold` (30 by default), and the value is the window's mean cover
symbols.n_v: the valid cells of the window (the special background 4 counted as missing)

metrics.use:
The same reading as FAD. Fragmentation in GuidosToolbox's sense is the complement, 100 % less this connectivity.
[`tf.fos`][terraflux.fos.fos] reads a map of 0 to 100 as percent cover by its values (`grayscale=True` forces it).

metrics.name: FOS by foreground edge density
metrics.what:
The connectivity of each habitat cell from the pairs of neighbouring cells in its window: a pair of two habitat
cells counts fully, a habitat-background pair half, a background pair nothing. It mixes the amount of habitat with
how much edge cuts it.

symbols.E_{ff}: the pairs (a cell and its right or lower neighbour, both inside the window) with both cells habitat
symbols.E_{fb}: the pairs with one habitat and one background cell
symbols.E_{v}: the pairs without a missing cell; the cells outside the map count as missing, so the window is padded, not clipped. On a map of 100 for habitat and 0 for background, this is GraySpatCon's clustering, the mean of \((i + j)/2\) over the pairs

metrics.use:
Lower than FAD where the habitat is cut by many edges, so the difference between the two maps points to edge. On a
percent map it is the same mean of the pairs' values.

metrics.name: FOS by foreground area clustering
metrics.what:
The connectivity of each habitat cell as the share of habitat-habitat pairs among all the valid pairs of
neighbouring cells in the window. Binary maps only.

symbols.E_{ff}: the horizontal and vertical pairs of neighbours, both inside the window, with both cells habitat
symbols.E_{v}: the pairs without a missing cell (missing and non-fragmenting special background left out)

metrics.use:
Choose it to measure how clustered the habitat is rather than how much there is; it is the FOS form of the
moving-window clustering (FAC) card.
refs: Vogt, P., & Riitters, K. (2017). GuidosToolbox: universal digital image object analysis. *European Journal of Remote Sensing*, 50(1), 352-361. https://doi.org/10.1080/22797254.2017.1330650

metrics.name: Contagion (Pff)
metrics.what:
The chance that a neighbour of a habitat cell is habitat too, counted over the pairs of neighbouring cells of a
window. High values mean that the habitat is aggregated; the value is mapped on the habitat cells only.

symbols.E_{ff}: the horizontal and vertical pairs of neighbours with both cells habitat (code 2)
symbols.E_{fb}: the pairs with one habitat and one background (code 1) cell; the pairs with a missing cell are left out, and the cells outside the map count as missing

metrics.use:
Pff looks only at the pairs that involve habitat, so a window of solid habitat gives 1 and one with a single habitat
cell gives 0, whatever the amount around. Read it with FAD (Pf): Riitters' fragmentation categories (interior,
perforated, edge, transitional, patch) are a rule on the two. `as_byte=False` gives a proportion with no value off
the habitat; the default byte map follows GuidosToolbox (steps of 1/254, whole percent, 99 unless exactly 1, 101
background, 102 missing).
refs: Riitters, K., Wickham, J., O'Neill, R., Jones, B., & Smith, E. (2000). Global-scale patterns of forest fragmentation. *Conservation Ecology*, 4(2), 3. https://doi.org/10.5751/ES-00209-040203
Vogt, P., & Riitters, K. (2017). GuidosToolbox: universal digital image object analysis. *European Journal of Remote Sensing*, 50(1), 352-361. https://doi.org/10.1080/22797254.2017.1330650
aliases: conditional probability of habitat next to habitat

metrics.name: Foreground area clustering (FAC)
metrics.what:
The share of all the valid pairs of neighbouring cells in the window that are habitat-habitat. Unlike Pff it keeps
every pair of the window in the denominator, so it grows both with clustering and with the amount of habitat.

symbols.E_{ff}: the pairs of neighbours (a cell and its right or lower one) with both cells habitat
symbols.E_{v}: all the pairs of neighbours without a missing cell

metrics.use:
Prefer it to Pff when the measure should also reflect how much of the window is habitat. The byte coding is that
of Pff.

metrics.name: Rare (FAD below 10 %)
metrics.what:
The share of the habitat cells whose window is almost all background (FAD under 10 %): habitat scarcely surrounded
by more habitat.

symbols.FAD_i: the FAD of cell \(i\), in whole percent

metrics.use:
Read the six class shares together: they add up to 100 % of the habitat, and each depends on the window, so compare
them only at one window size.

metrics.name: Patchy (FAD 10 to 40 %)
metrics.what: The share of the habitat cells with a FAD of 10 % up to 40 %: habitat in small amounts among mostly other cover.

symbols.FAD_i: the FAD of cell \(i\), in whole percent

metrics.use: With rare, the habitat that lives in a matrix of something else.
refs: Riitters, K. H., Wickham, J. D., O'Neill, R. V., Jones, K. B., Smith, E. R., Coulston, J. W., et al. (2002). Fragmentation of continental United States forests. *Ecosystems*, 5(8), 815-822. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10021-002-0209-2

metrics.name: Transitional (FAD 40 to 60 %)
metrics.what: The share of the habitat cells with a FAD of 40 % up to 60 %: about as much habitat as background around the cell.

symbols.FAD_i: the FAD of cell \(i\), in whole percent

metrics.use:
These cells sit where a matrix of habitat turns into a matrix of non-habitat, the zone where a little more loss
changes which cover dominates.
refs: Riitters, K. H., Wickham, J. D., O'Neill, R. V., Jones, K. B., Smith, E. R., Coulston, J. W., et al. (2002). Fragmentation of continental United States forests. *Ecosystems*, 5(8), 815-822. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10021-002-0209-2

metrics.name: Dominant (FAD 60 to 90 %)
metrics.what:
The share of the habitat cells with a FAD of 60 % up to 90 %: the habitat is the matrix, with a clear share of other
cover.

symbols.FAD_i: the FAD of cell \(i\), in whole percent

metrics.use: With interior and intact, the habitat that sits within mostly habitat.
refs: Riitters, K. H., Wickham, J. D., O'Neill, R. V., Jones, K. B., Smith, E. R., Coulston, J. W., et al. (2002). Fragmentation of continental United States forests. *Ecosystems*, 5(8), 815-822. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10021-002-0209-2

metrics.name: Interior (FAD 90 % to under 100 %)
metrics.what:
The share of the habitat cells with a FAD of at least 90 % but not a full 100 %: almost entirely surrounded by
habitat. In FOS with five classes, this class holds the intact cells too.

symbols.FAD_i: the FAD of cell \(i\), in whole percent; it is 100 only for a window with no background cell

metrics.use: Habitat deep inside large areas of it; intact is the strictest class.
refs: Riitters, K. H., Wickham, J. D., O'Neill, R. V., Jones, K. B., Smith, E. R., Coulston, J. W., et al. (2002). Fragmentation of continental United States forests. *Ecosystems*, 5(8), 815-822. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10021-002-0209-2

metrics.name: Intact (FAD 100 %)
metrics.what: The share of the habitat cells whose whole window is habitat, with no background cell in it.

symbols.FAD_i: the FAD of cell \(i\); 100 only when every valid cell of the window is habitat

metrics.use:
A strict measure that shrinks fast as the window grows: on the example it is 52 % of the forest in windows of 7
cells, 7 % in windows of 27 and 0 in windows of 81 and 243, as for almost any real landscape.
refs: Riitters, K. H., Wickham, J. D., O'Neill, R. V., Jones, K. B., Smith, E. R., Coulston, J. W., et al. (2002). Fragmentation of continental United States forests. *Ecosystems*, 5(8), 815-822. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10021-002-0209-2

metrics.name: FOS class shares (5 or 6 classes)
metrics.what:
The share of the habitat cells in each fragmentation class of a FOS map: rare (below 10), patchy (10 to 40),
transitional (40 to 60), dominant (60 to 90), interior (90 to 100) and, with six classes, intact (exactly 100).
With five classes, interior covers 90 to 100.

symbols.v_i: the FOS value of habitat cell \(i\), in whole percent
symbols.lo_c, hi_c: the edges of class \(c\) above; the last class takes \(v_i \le 100\) (five classes) or \(v_i = 100\) (intact)

metrics.use:
The `stats` of the result has a row per class, and the shares add up to 100. The classes have the same names for
the three methods but not the same meaning: say which method and window they come from.
refs: Riitters, K. H., Wickham, J. D., O'Neill, R. V., Jones, K. B., Smith, E. R., Coulston, J. W., et al. (2002). Fragmentation of continental United States forests. *Ecosystems*, 5(8), 815-822. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10021-002-0209-2

The mean FAD over all the habitat cells of the map, at one window: how much habitat an average habitat cell has

metrics.name: Average FOS value
metrics.what:
The mean of the FOS map over the habitat cells, which GuidosToolbox reports as "Average FAD (or FED, FAC) at
WS" and the window.

symbols.FOS_i: the FOS value of cell \(i\) with the chosen method

metrics.use: The headline number of a FOS run; quote the method and the window with it.
refs: Vogt, P., & Riitters, K. (2017). GuidosToolbox: universal digital image object analysis. *European Journal of Remote Sensing*, 50(1), 352-361. https://doi.org/10.1080/22797254.2017.1330650

metrics.name: Average connectivity (AVCON) of FOS
metrics.what:
The average FOS value scaled by the habitat's share of the reporting unit, so that a map with little habitat scores
low however dense that habitat is.

symbols.\\overline{FOS}: the average FOS value of the habitat cells
symbols.N_r: the cells of the reporting unit, all those that are not missing

metrics.use: Good for comparing units with unequal amounts of habitat, but it mixes amount and arrangement in one number.
refs: Vogt, P., & Riitters, K. (2017). GuidosToolbox: universal digital image object analysis. *European Journal of Remote Sensing*, 50(1), 352-361. https://doi.org/10.1080/22797254.2017.1330650

metrics.name: Equivalent connected area (ECA) of FOS
metrics.what:
The area of a single patch that would be as connected as the habitat of the map: the patches add up as the square
root of the sum of their squared areas, so one large patch counts more than many small ones of the same total.

symbols.a_p: the area, in cells, of habitat patch \(p\) (8-connected by default, 4 with `connectivity=4`)

metrics.use:
Follow the habitat's connectivity through time with it, beside the habitat area. It is in cells here, and it takes
the patches as connected components with no dispersal distance: the [connectivity](../connectivity/) cards give the
ECA of a habitat graph with one.
refs: Saura, S., Estreguil, C., Mouton, C., & Rodríguez-Freire, M. (2011). Network analysis to assess landscape connectivity trends: application to European forests (1990-2000). *Ecological Indicators*, 11, 407-416.

metrics.name: Coherence (COH)
metrics.what:
ECA as a percentage of the largest it could be, with all the habitat in one patch: 100 % when the habitat is one
patch, less as it splits.
metrics.use: It does not depend on the size of the reporting unit, unlike the coherence over the reporting unit.
refs: Saura, S., Estreguil, C., Mouton, C., & Rodríguez-Freire, M. (2011). Network analysis to assess landscape connectivity trends: application to European forests (1990-2000). *Ecological Indicators*, 11, 407-416.

metrics.name: Coherence over the reporting unit (COH_ru)
metrics.what:
ECA divided by the area of the whole reporting unit rather than by the habitat's: low both when the habitat is
scarce and when it is split.

symbols.ECA: the equivalent connected area, in cells
symbols.N_r: the cells of the reporting unit, all those that are not missing

metrics.use: Use it to compare units of the same size, or when the whole unit is what the question is about.
refs: Saura, S., Estreguil, C., Mouton, C., & Rodríguez-Freire, M. (2011). Network analysis to assess landscape connectivity trends: application to European forests (1990-2000). *Ecological Indicators*, 11, 407-416.

symbols.n: the number of habitat patches (8-connected by default)
symbols.N_r: the cells of the reporting unit

metrics.name: Spatial entropy
metrics.what:
The Shannon entropy of the differences between every cell and its eight neighbours, among habitat, background and
missing, scaled to 0-100: 0 for a uniform map, rising as the pattern gets more mixed.

symbols.d: the coded difference between a cell and one of its 8 neighbours (habitat 7, background 3, missing 0; the border of the map is replicated)
symbols.p_d: the share of the \(8N\) pairs of a cell and a neighbour with difference \(d\), \(N\) the cells of the map
symbols.1.5 \\ln 2: the normalising maximum (1.5 bits); the result is clipped to 0-100

metrics.use:
One number for the heterogeneity of a map. It is not the Shannon diversity of the classes: it counts transitions
between neighbours, not class areas. It is highest near 50 % habitat, so compare it between maps with similar
amounts of habitat, or read it with FAD.
refs: Vogt, P., & Riitters, K. (2017). GuidosToolbox: universal digital image object analysis. *European Journal of Remote Sensing*, 50(1), 352-361. https://doi.org/10.1080/22797254.2017.1330650

metrics.name: Spatial entropy in a window
metrics.what:
The same normalised entropy within a square window around each cell, which maps where the pattern is mixed. The
window spans `2 * (window_size // 2) + 1` cells, so an even size gives the next odd one; the default is 50.

symbols.p_d: within the window around cell \(x\), the share of the pairs of a cell and a neighbour (8 directions) with difference \(d\); the window is clipped at the border of the map

metrics.use:
Use it to find the zones of transition of a pattern: dark where the window is all habitat or all background,
bright where they are most intermingled. A window needs many cells for a stable count of the differences.
refs: Vogt, P., & Riitters, K. (2017). GuidosToolbox: universal digital image object analysis. *European Journal of Remote Sensing*, 50(1), 352-361. https://doi.org/10.1080/22797254.2017.1330650

metrics.name: Landscape mosaic (19 classes)
metrics.what:
The mix of agriculture, natural (*forest* in the library's names) and developed land in a window around each cell,
as one of 19 classes of the triangle of compositions: the three corners of a pure cover, three classes where one
cover dominates alone, six where one dominates with a second, three where one dominates with both others, and four
mosaics where none reaches 60 %. A name lists the covers from the most abundant.
metrics.formula: (p_a, p_f, p_d) \mapsto c \in \{1, \dots, 19\}, \qquad p_a + p_f + p_d = 1

symbols.p_a, p_f, p_d: the shares of agriculture (input 1), natural (2) and developed (3) among the classified cells of the window; input 0 is missing and left out, and the window is padded with missing cells at the border of the map
symbols.c: the class of the cell, from the table; a pure class needs a share of 1 (to single-precision rounding)

metrics.use:
The classes, with \(p_a\), \(p_f\) and \(p_d\) the shares of agriculture, natural and developed in the window
(class edges at multiples of 10 %; the side an edge falls on follows the comparisons of the code):

| Code | Class | Shares in the window |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Agriculture (>60%) | \(p_a \ge 0.8\), \(p_f < 0.1\), \(p_d < 0.1\), not pure |
| 2 | Developed (>60%) | \(p_d \ge 0.8\), \(p_a < 0.1\), \(p_f < 0.1\), not pure |
| 3 | Forest (>60%) | \(p_f \ge 0.8\), \(p_a < 0.1\), \(p_d < 0.1\), not pure |
| 4 | Agriculture-Developed | \(0.6 \le p_a < 0.9\), \(0.1 \le p_d \le 0.4\), \(p_f < 0.1\) |
| 5 | Agriculture-Forest | \(0.6 \le p_a < 0.9\), \(0.1 \le p_f \le 0.4\), \(p_d < 0.1\) |
| 6 | Developed-Forest | \(0.6 \le p_d < 0.9\), \(0.1 \le p_f \le 0.4\), \(p_a < 0.1\) |
| 7 | Developed-Agriculture | \(0.6 \le p_d < 0.9\), \(0.1 \le p_a \le 0.4\), \(p_f < 0.1\) |
| 8 | Forest-Agriculture | \(0.6 \le p_f < 0.9\), \(0.1 \le p_a \le 0.4\), \(p_d < 0.1\) |
| 9 | Forest-Developed | \(0.6 \le p_f < 0.9\), \(0.1 \le p_d \le 0.4\), \(p_a < 0.1\) |
| 10 | Agriculture-Forest-Developed | \(0.6 \le p_a < 0.8\), \(0.1 \le p_f < 0.3\), \(0.1 \le p_d < 0.3\) |
| 11 | Developed-Agriculture-Forest | \(0.6 \le p_d < 0.8\), \(0.1 \le p_a < 0.3\), \(0.1 \le p_f < 0.3\) |
| 12 | Forest-Agriculture-Developed | \(0.6 \le p_f < 0.8\), \(0.1 \le p_a < 0.3\), \(0.1 \le p_d < 0.3\) |
| 13 | Mosaic Agriculture-Developed | \(0.3 \le p_a < 0.6\), \(0.3 \le p_d < 0.6\), \(p_f < 0.1\) |
| 14 | Mosaic Agriculture-Forest | \(0.3 \le p_a < 0.6\), \(0.3 \le p_f < 0.6\), \(p_d < 0.1\) |
| 15 | Mosaic Developed-Forest | \(0.3 \le p_d < 0.6\), \(0.3 \le p_f < 0.6\), \(p_a < 0.1\) |
| 16 | Mosaic Agriculture-Developed-Forest | all three from about 0.1 to under 0.6: the centre of the triangle, what no other class takes |
| 17 | Pure Forest (100%) | \(p_f = 1\) |
| 18 | Pure Agriculture (100%) | \(p_a = 1\) |
| 19 | Pure Developed (100%) | \(p_d = 1\) |

A pure class and the dominant class of the same cover (17 and 3, 18 and 1, 19 and 2) make together the area that
cover dominates. What counts as natural or as agriculture (pastures?) changes every class: say how the land cover
was grouped. The library names the classes in `tf.LM19_CLASSES`; the card's value is the share of the cells with
data in each class, from [`tf.landscape_mosaic_stats`][terraflux.mosaic.landscape_mosaic_stats].
refs: Riitters, K., Wickham, J., O'Neill, R., Jones, B., & Smith, E. (2000). Global-scale patterns of forest fragmentation. *Conservation Ecology*, 4(2), 3. https://doi.org/10.5751/ES-00209-040203

Riitters, K. H., Wickham, J. D., & Wade, T. G. (2009). An indicator of forest dynamics using a shifting landscape mosaic. *Ecological Indicators*, 9(1), 107-117. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolind.2008.02.003
Vogt, P., & Riitters, K. (2017). GuidosToolbox: universal digital image object analysis. *European Journal of Remote Sensing*, 50(1), 352-361. https://doi.org/10.1080/22797254.2017.1330650

tf.landscape_mosaic_stats(three, window_size=27).groupby("recode_name_19")["percentage"].sum()
