families.title: Habitat patterns
families.source: GuidosToolbox (MSPA, SPA, parcellation, contortion) / Soille & Vogt 2009
families.intro:
The pattern classes of a binary habitat map, and a few indices of how the map is divided into parcels and how
contorted its objects are, as GuidosToolbox computes them. **MSPA** (morphological spatial pattern analysis) sorts every
habitat cell into one of seven classes by its place in the pattern (core, islet, perforation, edge, loop, bridge,
branch) and the background into openings and the rest; **SPA** is its simplified form, with a fixed edge of one cell
and two to six classes. They are the measures of the [habitat patterns tutorials](../../tutorials/habitat-patterns/mspa/).

The cards show their values on the forest map of GuidosToolbox's sample, the one those tutorials use
(`tf.example_data("input")`: 1000 x 1000 cells of 25 m, coded 0 missing, 1 background, 2 forest). A class card gives
the class's share of the mapped (non-missing) area and of the habitat, as
[`tf.mspa_stats`][terraflux.mspa.mspa_stats] (`pct_data`, `pct_foreground`) and the `stats` of
[`tf.spa`][terraflux.spa.spa] (`pct_data`, `pct_fg`) report them; the same tables have the cells of each class. MSPA is
run with an edge width of 2 cells (50 m) and 8-connectivity of the habitat; the class codes of the map are core 17,
islet 9, perforation 5, edge 3, loop 65, bridge 33, branch 1, background 0, core-opening 100, border-opening 220 and
missing 129, and with `internal=True` (the default) the habitat cells of internal features carry their code plus 100.
The parcellation tables have a row per class of the map: 1 the background, 2 the forest.
families.example:
import terraflux as tf

# forest of GuidosToolbox's sample (1000 x 1000 cells of 25 m): 0 missing, 1 background, 2 forest
forest = tf.load_raster(tf.example_data("input"))

metrics.name: MSPA core
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what:
The habitat cells that lie farther than the edge width from any non-habitat cell: the interior of the patches. Every
other class of the habitat is defined by how its cells relate to the core.

symbols.N_{core}: the cells of class core (codes 17 and, for internal features, 117), farther than `edge_width` cells from the nearest non-habitat cell
symbols.N_{fg}: the habitat cells, the sum of the seven habitat classes (core, islet, perforation, edge, loop, bridge, branch)
symbols.N_{data}: the cells that are not missing (habitat, background and openings)

metrics.use:
The edge width is the one setting that decides the result, and it should match the distance over which the
species feels the edge: on the example, the core is 75 % of the habitat with an edge of 1 cell and 62 % with an
edge of 2. Report the edge width (in metres) with the share.
refs: Soille, P., & Vogt, P. (2009). Morphological segmentation of binary patterns. *Pattern Recognition Letters*, 30(4), 456-459. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2008.10.015

Vogt, P., Riitters, K. H., Estreguil, C., Kozak, J., Wade, T. G., & Wickham, J. D. (2007). Mapping spatial patterns with morphological image processing. *Landscape Ecology*, 22(2), 171-177. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-006-9013-2

metrics.name: MSPA islet
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what:
The habitat objects too small to hold any core: whole patches, separate from the rest of the habitat, that no bridge
or loop reaches.

symbols.N_{islet}: the cells of class islet (codes 9 and 109)
symbols.N_{fg}: the habitat cells; the share of the mapped area divides by \(N_{data}\), the cells that are not missing, instead

metrics.use:
Islets are the small patches of the map, possible stepping stones. Their share grows with the edge width, because
ever larger objects fall below the size that holds a core (3.3 % of the habitat with an edge of 1 cell on the
example, 6.1 % with 2).
refs: Soille, P., & Vogt, P. (2009). Morphological segmentation of binary patterns. *Pattern Recognition Letters*, 30(4), 456-459. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2008.10.015

metrics.name: MSPA perforation
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what:
The band of habitat, as wide as the edge width, around the holes inside a core: the inner boundary of the patches,
where the edge is the outer one.

symbols.N_{perf}: the cells of class perforation (codes 5 and 105)

metrics.use:
Perforation points to gaps inside the habitat (clearings, ponds, small settlements); edge points to the rim of the
patches. Read the two together to tell a forest cut from inside from one eaten from its border.
refs: Soille, P., & Vogt, P. (2009). Morphological segmentation of binary patterns. *Pattern Recognition Letters*, 30(4), 456-459. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2008.10.015

metrics.name: MSPA edge
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what:
The band of habitat, as wide as the edge width, along the outer boundary of a core: the rim of the patch where it
meets the non-habitat around it.

symbols.N_{edge}: the cells of class edge (codes 3 and 103)

metrics.use:
The share of edge measures how exposed the habitat is to its surroundings (light, wind, predators, people). It
depends on the edge width, so compare it only between maps run with the same width and cell size.
refs: Soille, P., & Vogt, P. (2009). Morphological segmentation of binary patterns. *Pattern Recognition Letters*, 30(4), 456-459. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2008.10.015

metrics.name: MSPA loop
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what: Narrow strips of habitat that leave a core and come back to the same core: corridors that join a core to itself.

symbols.N_{loop}: the cells of class loop, those in an edge or a perforation included (codes 65, 67, 69 and their internal codes 165, 167, 169)

metrics.use:
Loops give alternative routes within one core area, not between areas, so they add redundancy rather than
connectivity. The share counts the loops that run through an edge or a perforation too (see the transition classes).
refs: Soille, P., & Vogt, P. (2009). Morphological segmentation of binary patterns. *Pattern Recognition Letters*, 30(4), 456-459. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2008.10.015

metrics.name: MSPA bridge
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what: Narrow strips of habitat that join two different cores: the structural corridors of the pattern.

symbols.N_{bridge}: the cells of class bridge, those in an edge or a perforation included (codes 33, 35, 37 and their internal codes 133, 135, 137)

metrics.use:
Bridges are the links when the cores are taken as the nodes of a habitat network (the
[MSPA network tutorial](../../tutorials/habitat-networks/mspa-network/)). They are structural: whether a species
uses them depends on its behaviour, not on the map. The share counts the bridges through an edge or a perforation too.
refs: Soille, P., & Vogt, P. (2009). Morphological segmentation of binary patterns. *Pattern Recognition Letters*, 30(4), 456-459. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2008.10.015

metrics.name: MSPA branch
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what:
Narrow strips of habitat attached to the rest of the pattern at one end only: dead-end spurs from a core, an edge, a
bridge or a loop.

symbols.N_{branch}: the cells of class branch (codes 1 and 101)

metrics.use:
Branches add habitat that connects nothing; for dispersal they lead nowhere, though they may still be habitat for
species of the edge.
refs: Soille, P., & Vogt, P. (2009). Morphological segmentation of binary patterns. *Pattern Recognition Letters*, 30(4), 456-459. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2008.10.015

metrics.name: MSPA core-opening
metrics.what:
The background cells of the holes enclosed by core (only with `internal=True`): openings inside the core area, told
apart from the openings that lie between the rims of patches.

symbols.N_{data}: the cells that are not missing

metrics.use:
With the border-openings it separates the background that lies inside the habitat from the background outside it.
It is background, so it has no share of the habitat.
refs: Soille, P., & Vogt, P. (2009). Morphological segmentation of binary patterns. *Pattern Recognition Letters*, 30(4), 456-459. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2008.10.015

metrics.name: MSPA border-opening
metrics.what:
The background cells of the holes in the habitat that are not core-openings (only with `internal=True`): background
enclosed by habitat whose boundary does not touch a core.

symbols.N_{data}: the cells that are not missing

metrics.use: Read it with the core-opening; the rest of the background is class 0.
refs: Soille, P., & Vogt, P. (2009). Morphological segmentation of binary patterns. *Pattern Recognition Letters*, 30(4), 456-459. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2008.10.015

metrics.name: MSPA background
metrics.what: The non-habitat cells that are in no opening: the part of the mapped area that is neither habitat nor enclosed by it.

symbols.N_{data}: the cells that are not missing

metrics.use:
Background, the openings and the seven habitat classes add up to the mapped area. Missing cells (code 129) are in no
share.

metrics.name: MSPA internal features (+100)
metrics.unit: class code; the card's value is a count of cells
metrics.what:
With `internal=True` (the default) the habitat cells that lie inside a core-opening get the code of their class plus
100, so that features inside the habitat can be told from those outside: a branch inside a clearing is 101, outside
it 1. [`tf.mspa_stats`][terraflux.mspa.mspa_stats] counts them with their class.

symbols.c: the MSPA code of the cell's class; core-opening (100) and border-opening (220) are codes of their own

metrics.use: Set `internal=False` for the plain classes. The card counts the cells of internal features on the example.
metrics.python:
m = tf.mspa(forest, edge_width=2, internal=True)
int(m.isin([c + 100 for c in (1, 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, 35, 37, 65, 67, 69)]).sum())   # cells of internal features

metrics.name: MSPA transition classes
metrics.unit: class code; the card's value is a count of cells
metrics.what:
The bridges and loops that run through an edge or a perforation have codes of their own: 35 bridge in edge, 37
bridge in perforation, 67 loop in edge, 69 loop in perforation. [`tf.mspa_stats`][terraflux.mspa.mspa_stats] adds
them to bridge and loop.

symbols.c: the MSPA code of the cell; plus 100 for internal features

metrics.use:
The `transition` option changes only the colour table of a written map (shown as bridge or loop when on, as edge or
perforation when off), never the codes or the shares.
metrics.python:
m = tf.mspa(forest, edge_width=2)
{tf.MSPA_CLASSES[c]: int(m.isin([c, c + 100]).sum()) for c in (35, 37, 67, 69)}
metrics.value: {'Bridge in Edge': 12178, 'Bridge in Perforation': 195, 'Loop in Edge': 8585, 'Loop in Perforation': 2813}

metrics.name: SPA core (contiguous in SPA2)
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what:
The interior habitat cells of the simplified pattern analysis, with the edge width fixed at one cell and
8-connectivity. In SPA2 the class is called *contiguous* and also holds what the other variants call edge and
perforation.

symbols.N_{core}: the cells coded 17; in SPA2 the contiguous cells (core, edge and perforation)
symbols.N_{fg}: the habitat cells, the mapped cells less the background (class 0 and the core-openings)

metrics.use:
Use SPA for a quick, coarse classification: the variant (2, 3, 5 or 6) is the number of habitat and opening classes
it reports. At an edge of one cell the core of SPA equals the core of MSPA.
refs: Vogt, P., & Riitters, K. (2017). GuidosToolbox: universal digital image object analysis. *European Journal of Remote Sensing*, 50(1), 352-361. https://doi.org/10.1080/22797254.2017.1330650

metrics.name: SPA edge
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what: The one-cell rim along the outer boundary of the core (variants 5 and 6).
metrics.use: The same idea as MSPA's edge, with the width fixed at one cell.

metrics.name: SPA perforation
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what: The one-cell rim around the holes inside the core (variants 5 and 6).
metrics.use: In variant 3 these cells are part of the margin.

metrics.name: SPA islet
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what:
The habitat objects without core (variant 6 only): too small to hold a cell whose whole 3 x 3 neighbourhood is
habitat.
metrics.use: Variant 5 puts these cells in the margin.

metrics.name: SPA margin (small linear features in SPA2)
metrics.unit: % of the mapped area, % of the habitat
metrics.what:
The habitat left once the other classes are taken out: the thin or small features that an opening of 3 x 3 cells
removes. In SPA3 it is all the habitat that is not core, in SPA5 what is not core, edge or perforation, in SPA6 also
not islet; SPA2 calls it small linear features (SLF).

symbols.N_{fg}: the habitat cells; the classes of one variant add up to it

metrics.use:
Its meaning changes with the variant (on the example, 24.9 % of the habitat in SPA3, 9.2 % in SPA5, 6.0 % in SPA6),
so compare margins only within one variant.

metrics.name: SPA core-opening
metrics.what:
The background cells in the holes of the core (variants 3, 5 and 6); the rest of the background is *other
background*. They enter the porosity.

symbols.N_{co}: the cells coded 100, reported as Core-Opening

metrics.use: The area of the holes inside the habitat, in cells: multiply by the cell's area for hectares.

metrics.name: SPA porosity
metrics.what: The share of the contiguous habitat and its inner openings that is opening: how perforated the habitat is.

symbols.C: the contiguous habitat cells (core, edge and perforation; in SPA3, which has no edge class, the core only)

metrics.use:
Compare porosity only between maps run with the same SPA variant (on the example, 1.42 % in SPA5 and SPA6, 1.71 % in
SPA3). SPA2 does not report it.
refs: Vogt, P., & Riitters, K. (2017). GuidosToolbox: universal digital image object analysis. *European Journal of Remote Sensing*, 50(1), 352-361. https://doi.org/10.1080/22797254.2017.1330650

metrics.name: Number of parcels
metrics.what:
The number of parcels of each class: the connected regions of touching cells of the same class (8-connectivity by
default). Every class of the map counts, the background too; the `global_stats` of the result have the total of the
whole map.

symbols.n_c: the number of parcels of class \(c\), a parcel being a largest set of cells of \(c\) that touch by a side (`connectivity=4`) or by a side or a corner (8); class 0 (missing) is left out

metrics.use:
The count depends on the connectivity rule and on the resolution: 4-connectivity splits parcels that touch only at a
corner, and a finer map sees more small ones.

metrics.name: Average parcel size (APS)
metrics.what: The mean area of the parcels of a class, or of all the parcels of the map.

symbols.A_c: the area of class \(c\), in cells
symbols.n_c: the number of parcels of class \(c\)
symbols.A: the data area, the cells that are not missing
symbols.n: the number of parcels of all classes

metrics.use:
An arithmetic mean: a few very large parcels among many small ones give a middle value that describes neither.
The area-weighted size (AWAPS) is closer to what a cell of the class lies in.

metrics.name: Area-weighted average parcel size (AWAPS)
metrics.what:
The size of the parcel that a cell of the class, picked at random, belongs to: the mean parcel size when each
parcel counts in proportion to its area.

symbols.a_i: the area of parcel \(i\) of class \(c\), in cells

metrics.use:
Closer than APS to what an organism living in the class meets. For the whole map the divisor is the data area and
the sum runs over all the parcels.

metrics.name: Effective mesh size of a class (AWAPS over the data area)
metrics.range: more than 0, at most the data area
metrics.what:
The sum of the squared areas of a class's parcels divided by the area of the whole map: Jaeger's effective mesh size
of the class, in cells (the `AWAPS/data` column).

symbols.a_i: the area of parcel \(i\) of class \(c\), in cells
symbols.A: the data area, the cells of the map that are not missing

metrics.use: The values of the classes add up to the AWAPS of the whole map. Multiply by the cell's area for hectares.
refs: Jaeger, J. A. G. (2000). Landscape division, splitting index, and effective mesh size: new measures of landscape fragmentation. *Landscape Ecology*, 15(2), 115-130. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1008129329289

metrics.name: Division index
metrics.what:
The chance that two cells of a class, picked at random, fall in different parcels. In the class table it is computed
within the class (the divisor is the class's area); the whole map's value uses the data area.

symbols.a_i: the area of parcel \(i\) of class \(c\)
symbols.A_c: the area of class \(c\); for the whole map, the data area \(A\)

metrics.use:
0 for a single parcel, close to 1 for many small ones. Jaeger's division of a class divides by the whole landscape
instead, so the two differ for any class that does not cover the map.
refs: Jaeger, J. A. G. (2000). Landscape division, splitting index, and effective mesh size: new measures of landscape fragmentation. *Landscape Ecology*, 15(2), 115-130. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1008129329289

metrics.name: Degree of parcellation (PARC)
metrics.what:
The logarithm of the inverse of the sum of the squared shares of the parcels, scaled to 0-100, with 100 reached when
that sum falls to one in a million. It spreads out the low end of the division index, and so tells apart landscapes
that are almost undivided.

symbols.a_i: the area of parcel \(i\) of class \(c\)
symbols.A_c: the area of class \(c\); for the whole map, the data area
symbols.-\\ln 10^{-6}: about 13.82, the value of \(-\ln S\) that gives 100 %

metrics.use:
The `PARC[%]` column. Use it to compare the division of maps of different sizes or resolutions, where the division
index crowds near 0 or 1.
refs: Jaeger, J. A. G. (2000). Landscape division, splitting index, and effective mesh size: new measures of landscape fragmentation. *Landscape Ecology*, 15(2), 115-130. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1008129329289

metrics.name: Contortion of habitat objects
metrics.what:
How contorted the outline of each habitat object is: the number of straight runs of its boundary in x and in y, less
a fixed offset. Compact objects score low, elongated or branching ones high.

symbols.r_x, r_y: the number of runs of equal non-zero steps in x and in y along the traced boundary of the 8-connected object
symbols.7: the offset of the start and end markers (5 and 6) of the tracing

metrics.use:
The value depends on the grid and the resolution, so compare objects of the same map. The output map holds
\(K + 1\) on each object (0 missing, 1 background, 2 the objects left out: smaller than `min_area` or without a
3 x 3 core); the card subtracts the 1. `return_display=True` rescales the values to 3-255 for display.
metrics.python:
k = tf.contortion(forest, min_area=100)   # K + 1 on every object of 100 cells or more
k.where(k > 2) - 1
metrics.value: a map: mean 9.32, from 2 to 41; 596828 cells without a value
